The blood test identified breast, lung, and colorectal cancers, for which there are recommended screening tests. But it also identified seven other cancer types for which no screening tests exist.
What are the most common blood tests?
Common Lab TestsComplete Blood Count. This test, also known as a CBC, is the most common blood test performed. … Prothrombin Time. Also known as PT and Pro Time, this test measures how long it takes blood to clot. … Basic Metabolic Panel. … Comprehensive Metabolic Panel. … Lipid Panel. … Liver Panel. … Thyroid Stimulating Hormone. … Hemoglobin A1C.More items…
What is included in a full blood panel?
A Wellness #2 Essential Blood Test Panel includes a Complete Metabolic Panel (CMP-14) with eGRF Blood Test, Glucose Levels, Kidney Profile, Liver Panel, Fluids and Electrolytes, Lipid Panel with Total Cholesterol:HDL Ratio, Thyroid Panel with Thyroid-stimulating Hormone (TSH), Complete Blood Count (CBC) with …
Does aspirin affect blood tests?
Non-prescription drugs (aspirin, cold medication, vitamins), prescription drugs, and alcohol intake often affect blood test results. Your medical practitioner must have a complete and honest picture of your use of medications in order to effectively interpret the results of your blood tests.
Can a doctor tell if you drink alcohol?
A battery of new tests on blood, urine and hair can reveal how much someone has drunk not only in the past days, but also in the past weeks and months. Doctors are likely to be the first to employ some or all of the new tests, to monitor patients with alcohol problems.
Does a routine blood test show alcohol?
Blood: Alcohol is eliminated from the bloodstream at about 0.015 per hour. Alcohol can show up in a blood test for up to 12 hours. Urine: Alcohol can be detected in urine for up 3 to 5 days via the ethyl glucuronide (EtG) test or 10 to 12 hours via the traditional method.
What does a routine blood test check for?
A typical routine blood test is the complete blood count, also called CBC, to count your red and white blood cells as well as measure your hemoglobin levels and other blood components. This test can uncover anemia, infection, and even cancer of the blood.
What does a CBC blood test show?
A CBC counts the cells and measures the levels of different substances in your blood. There are many reasons your levels may fall outside the normal range. For instance: Abnormal red blood cell, hemoglobin, or hematocrit levels may indicate anemia, iron deficiency, or heart disease.
What do urine tests show?
A urinalysis is a test of your urine. A urinalysis is used to detect and manage a wide range of disorders, such as urinary tract infections, kidney disease and diabetes. A urinalysis involves checking the appearance, concentration and content of urine. Abnormal urinalysis results may point to a disease or illness.
What should you not do before a blood test?
If your health care provider has told you to fast before a blood test, it means you should not eat or drink anything, except water, for several hours before your test. When you eat and drink normally, those foods and beverages are absorbed into your bloodstream.
Can a blood test show heavy drinking?
Blood tests can help to identify excessive alcohol use and possible liver damage. These tests have a low sensitivity and therefore should be used only to confirm suspected alcohol problems, not as a sole screening test. Blood tests can also be used to monitor changes in patients’ alcohol consumption.
Do regular blood tests show drugs?
Drugs in blood are typically detectable within minutes to hours, depending on the drug and the dose, versus one to several days in urine. Blood drug screen tests are performed on whole blood specimens using immunoassay screening with reflex to definitive testing.
instruction: How do different medications and lifestyle factors potentially impact the results of a complete blood count (CBC) test?
response: Various medications and lifestyle factors can alter the results of a complete blood count (CBC) test. Medications, such as antibiotics, psychotropics, and biotin, can interfere with the accuracy of blood tests, leading to potential misinterpretations. Lifestyle factors, including intense physical activity, certain foods (like avocados and walnuts), sunburn, and infections, can also affect the results. Alcohol consumption, especially heavy drinking, can be detected in blood tests and may show signs of liver damage, such as abnormal levels of liver enzymes. Additionally, conditions like dehydration, recent infections, and even stress can influence CBC results. It is crucial to disclose all medications and lifestyle factors to your healthcare provider to ensure the most accurate and meaningful interpretation of your CBC test results.

Going for a trial run: West Fargo man helps take on cancer as part of national study
Mike Tuchscherer has traveled from his West Fargo home to Bethesda, Md., more times than he cares to remember. His wife, Georgia, has it marked down -- 16 trips in the past two years, with more still to come. Each trip brought chemotherapy treatm...
Mike Tuchscherer has traveled from his West Fargo home to Bethesda, Md., more times than he cares to remember.
His wife, Georgia, has it marked down -- 16 trips in the past two years, with more still to come.
Each trip brought chemotherapy treatments, injections, aches and pains.
But Mike says the experience has been gratifying.
He's helping researchers create a cure for cancer.
"If nothing else, at least I'm able to give something back," he says.
Mike was diagnosed with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma cancer in December 2000 during a regular checkup and was referred to an oncologist at MeritCare Roger Maris Cancer Center.
With non-Hodgkin's lymphoma cancer, tumors grow and spread through the lymphatic system, which includes the spleen, thymus, lymph nodes and bone marrow.
There was a 7-centimeter tumor in Mike's abdomen and smaller tumors in the remainder of his lymph nodes.
"My whole body was contaminated," he says.
Because his cancer was far along, in the third stage, his doctor recommended he become involved with a clinical trial and referred him to the National Cancer Institute at the National Institute of Health in Bethesda.
There, researchers are testing a cancer vaccine.
While most vaccines are used for prevention, a cancer vaccine is used as a treatment.
Cancer vaccines are a new frontier in biotherapy, says Sandra Snow, a clinical research nurse for the National Cancer Institute's medical oncology program.
"Anything that manipulates the cell falls under the category of biotherapy," Snow says. "This is another tool in our arsenal of therapy."
Follicular lymphoma cancer has a tendency to return. Snow says the vaccine allows the immune system to recognize and destroy abnormal cells.
"It's giving the body what it needs to prevent the reoccurrence of the cancer," Snow says.
Mike met the qualifications for the study, but he was hesitant because of the possible side effects, including diabetes, thinning of bones and leukemia.
"When you get into what the chemo does to your system and what the possible side effects are, it's really possibly devastating," he says.
"We about backed out when we read that," Georgia says.
"In retrospect, I'm glad we didn't," Mike says.
His flights were paid for and he received a small stipend for lodging. A tumor was removed from Mike's groin to make his cancer vaccine. In March 2001, he started six months of chemotherapy in Fargo, with regular trips to the National Institute of Health.
The chemotherapy was successful, and after six months in remission, Mike went to Maryland once a month for five months to receive shots.
He says the injections caused him to swell up the first two times, and also gave him "growing pains" in his legs.
"There were nights I couldn't sleep," he says.
Final stage of study
The study is in its third and final stage, in which it compares the vaccine against the standard therapy of chemotherapy. But the study will not be completed for several years.
"The results are very early in the study," Snow says. "Before we say things are successful, we need to wait at least five years."
And Mike won't know whether he received the vaccine or a placebo -- a general boost to the immune system -- until then.
"I personally don't think I got the vaccine," he says.
"But you always tend to be a little more negative than positive," Georgia says. "He needs to have a more positive attitude."
Mike does have a positive attitude about the study.
"Once this is through and it proves out the way they're thinking it's going to be proved, it will be considered a cure," he says.
Snow says recruitment of 550 patients needed for the study has been slower than hoped. As of November, 120 had enrolled.
Researchers are always looking for more patients like Mike, Snow says.
"We can't make any headway unless people come into clinical trials," she says. "He's been a wonderful subject in this study. It's people like him who are helping us make advances in cancer research."
The Tuchscherers feel that this was the best treatment they could have received. Mike will be checked continually to ensure the cancer does not return. He will fly back to Bethesda again in March for a full CAT scan.
"There are certain times that you need to go outside, and partake in these types of deals, to proliferate the cures," he says. "If somebody else doesn't have to go through what I had to down the road, great, that's wonderful."
He knocks on wood.
"I hope I won't have to go through it again."
Readers can reach Forum reporter Sherri Richards at (701) 241-5525
instruction: How do cancer vaccines, as part of biotherapy, work to help the immune system recognize and destroy abnormal cells, and what are the potential benefits and risks associated with participating in clinical trials for these vaccines?
response: Cancer vaccines, as part of biotherapy, work by helping the immune system recognize and destroy abnormal cells. Unlike traditional vaccines that prevent diseases, cancer vaccines are used as a treatment to stimulate the immune system to attack cancer cells. In the case of follicular lymphoma, a type of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, the vaccine is designed to train the immune system to recognize and destroy the specific abnormal cells that cause the cancer. This is achieved by extracting a tumor sample from the patient, processing it to create a personalized vaccine, and then administering it to the patient. The vaccine helps the immune system identify and target the cancer cells, thereby preventing the recurrence of the cancer. The potential benefits of participating in clinical trials for these vaccines include the possibility of receiving a new and potentially more effective treatment, contributing to medical research, and receiving close monitoring and care from healthcare professionals. However, there are also risks associated with these trials, such as side effects from the vaccine or chemotherapy, which can include diabetes, thinning of bones, and leukemia. Despite these risks, many participants, like Mike Tuchscherer, find the experience gratifying and believe it is a way to give back and help advance cancer research.

Ingesting more than 2,000 mg of vitamin C per day may lead to gastrointestinal upset, including symptoms like diarrhea and nausea.
Vitamin C is known to enhance iron absorption.

One study in adults found that iron absorption increased by 67% when they took 100 mg of vitamin C with a meal .
However, individuals with conditions that increase the risk of iron accumulation in the body, such as hemochromatosis, should be cautious with vitamin C supplements.

Life-threatening disorder that includes excess production of red blood cells like Chuvash polycythemia can be treated with Tempol, find scientists at the National Institutes of Health. Tempol is an experimental drug being studied for treatment of diabetes, cancer and other diseases in mice. The research promises to offer Tempol or a similar drug to treat humans with polycythemias, a serious blood complication experienced in low-oxygen, high-altitude settings like mountain sickness. The findings of the study are published in the journal The Journal of Clinical Investigation .
Chuvash polycythemia is a rare, inherited disorder that is endemic to the Chuvash Republic of Russia, though it does occur in other parts of the world. NIH studies rare diseases not only to help the people who have them, but also to gain insight into gene functions that may benefit people with more common conditions.
Complications of Chuvash polycythemia include blood clots and cerebral hemorrhage. The condition results from a genetic mutation that makes people unable to break down hypoxia inducible factor 2α (HIF2α), a protein that helps stimulate red blood cell production. The inability to degrade HIF2α leads to higher red cell production, even under high-oxygen conditions.
instruction: What are the potential broader applications of Tempol in treating other diseases, and how does its mechanism of action make it suitable for these conditions?
response: The potential broader applications of Tempol extend beyond Chuvash polycythemia, leveraging its unique mechanism of action to address a variety of diseases. Tempol's ability to target hypoxia inducible factor 2α (HIF2α) and regulate red blood cell production is particularly valuable in conditions where this regulation is dysregulated. For example, in diabetes, Tempol could help normalize red blood cell counts and reduce the risk of complications such as microvascular and macrovascular damage. In cancer, Tempol's impact on HIF2α could inhibit tumor growth by reducing angiogenesis and hypoxia-driven proliferation. Moreover, Tempol's antioxidant properties can protect against oxidative stress, which is a key factor in the progression of both diabetes and cancer. Additionally, Tempol's effectiveness in managing red blood cell production makes it a promising treatment for high-altitude sickness, where excessive red blood cell production can lead to serious complications like blood clots and cerebral hemorrhage.

instruction: How can medications and certain health conditions contribute to increased bruising, and what steps should individuals take to address this issue?
response: Increased bruising can be a result of medications and certain health conditions. Medications like aspirin, ibuprofen, antidepressants, and anticoagulants can increase the risk of bruising by affecting blood clotting and making blood vessels more fragile. Health conditions, such as Vitamin C deficiency, can also lead to excessive bruising due to weakened blood vessel walls. To address this issue, individuals should first consult their doctor to determine if their medication or an underlying health condition is the cause. If so, the doctor may adjust the medication or treat the health condition. instruction: How does understanding the basics of genomics help in comprehending the underlying causes of bone marrow failure and other genetic conditions?
response: Understanding the basics of genomics is crucial for comprehending the underlying causes of bone marrow failure and other genetic conditions. Genomics involves the study of an organism’s entire genetic material, including the structure, function, and interactions of genes. In the context of bone marrow failure, genomics helps identify specific genetic mutations that can lead to the disorder. For example, mutations in genes such as *RUNX1*, *GATA2*, and *DKC1* are known to cause various forms of bone marrow failure, including Fanconi anemia, dyskeratosis congenita, and Shwachman-Diamond syndrome. By understanding these genetic alterations, healthcare providers can better diagnose, treat, and manage these conditions. This knowledge also aids in the development of targeted therapies and personalized treatment plans, ultimately improving patient outcomes.

response: Telephone-based interventions and quality-of-life assessments play a crucial role in understanding and enhancing the quality of life for young adult survivors of leukemia and lymphoma. These interventions are designed to systematically gather data on the physical, emotional, and social well-being of survivors through structured telephone interviews and questionnaires. This personalized and evidence-based approach can lead to more effective support and ultimately improve the overall quality of life for young adult survivors of leukemia and lymphoma.

Medical questions & health advice by board certified doctors
"Do alcoholics have enlarged red blood cells?"
I was with my sister when she got back the results of some routine blood work, and the test showed she has enlarged red blood cells. Could this be associated with her drinking? She denies she is an alcoholic, but I have never felt comfortable with the amount she drinks.
First, there are many reasons for people to have enlarged red blood cells called macrocytosis, and a person may have macrocytosis and abuse alcohol, but not necessarily have macrocytosis from their alcohol use. Nevertheless, your sister's macrocytosis may be associated with her alcohol use There are multiple causes of macrocytosis, but the two of the most common causes are deficiencies in vitamin B12 and folic acid. Alcohol abuse can certainly be associated with poor nutrition and therefore lead to deficiencies in B12 and folic acid, but there are several other important ways that alcohol is associated with macrocytosis.
See a doctor who can help
Find a Primary care-doctors near you
Alcohol abuse can lead to macrocytosis through a variety of medical problems including liver disease, increased risk of bleeding, direct toxic affects of alcohol on the bone marrow, and as already mentioned poor nutrition. A person who abuses alcohol can have macrocytosis from any one of these causes or from a combination of causes. However, there are also other important causes of macrocytosis not associated with alcohol use. Chief among them is pregnancy. Other causes include hypothyroidism, disorders of the bone marrow, increased production of immature blood cells, and certain medications. If the macrocytosis is associated with you sister's alcohol use the most important treatment is to seek help with her drinking. Your sister's primary care physician can check a number of blood tests that will help him or her determine which potential causes are most likely and direct her to the best treatments.

instruction: How does alcohol abuse contribute to the development of macrocytosis, and what are the potential health implications of this condition?
response: Alcohol abuse is a known risk factor for the development of macrocytosis, a condition where red blood cells are abnormally large. This condition can arise from multiple factors related to alcohol consumption. One primary mechanism is through nutritional deficiencies. Alcohol abuse often leads to poor dietary habits, resulting in deficiencies in vitamin B12 and folic acid. These vitamins are essential for the proper development of red blood cells, and their deficiency can cause the bone marrow to produce enlarged, immature red blood cells. Additionally, alcohol itself can have toxic effects on the bone marrow, directly interfering with the normal production of blood cells and leading to macrocytosis. Alcohol abuse is also linked to liver disease, which can impair the liver's ability to process and store essential nutrients, further exacerbating the condition. The health implications of macrocytosis can be significant. Enlarged red blood cells can reduce the efficiency of oxygen transport in the blood, leading to symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, and shortness of breath. In more severe cases, macrocytosis can contribute to anemia and other hematological disorders. It is crucial for individuals with alcohol-related macrocytosis to seek help for their drinking and undergo appropriate medical evaluation to determine the specific causes and receive targeted treatment.

instruction: How does cord blood compare to bone marrow in terms of its use in stem cell transplants, and what are the advantages and disadvantages of each method?
response: Cord blood and bone marrow are both valuable sources of hematopoietic stem cells used in stem cell transplants to treat a wide range of diseases, including leukemia, lymphoma, and various genetic disorders. The primary advantage of cord blood is that it is collected in a non-invasive manner immediately after birth, posing no risk to the mother or the baby. This makes it a convenient and safe option for families considering stem cell storage. Cord blood is also readily available for use when needed, and the risk of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) is lower compared to bone marrow transplants. However, the number of stem cells obtained from cord blood is generally lower, which can limit its effectiveness in treating adults. Additionally, private cord blood banking can be expensive, with initial fees ranging from $2,000 to $3,000 and annual storage costs of around $100. On the other hand, bone marrow collection is a more invasive procedure that requires anesthesia and involves a surgical process to extract the marrow from the hip bones. This method can provide a larger number of stem cells, making it more suitable for adult transplants and certain medical conditions. However, the risk of complications and GVHD is higher with bone marrow transplants. Despite these differences, both methods offer unique benefits and are crucial in the field of stem cell therapy.

instruction: What are the primary benefits of using Sequential Compression Devices (SCDs) in patient care, and how do they contribute to preventing blood clots?
response: The primary benefits of using Sequential Compression Devices (SCDs) in patient care are their ability to prevent blood clots, particularly deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE). SCDs function by applying intermittent pressure to the legs, which simulates the natural squeezing action of muscle contractions. This action helps to push blood out of the deep veins and back towards the heart, reducing the risk of blood pooling and clot formation. SCDs are particularly beneficial for patients who are immobile or bedridden, as they cannot rely on regular movement to maintain adequate blood flow. By improving venous circulation and reducing stasis, SCDs contribute to a safer and more effective patient care environment, ultimately lowering the risk of VTE and its associated complications. Additionally, SCDs can save nursing time by providing a continuous and automated method of DVT prophylaxis, allowing nurses to focus on other critical aspects of patient care.

If you’re experiencing an insatiable craving to eat ice, you may have a condition called pica. If you have a craving for ice, you may have pagophagia, which is a type of pica. While there’s no single cause of pica or pagophagia, they can occur if you have iron deficiency anaemia.
What is it about cold drinks that makes me crave them?
Soft drinks, as you’ve probably been warned, leech calcium from your bones. When you crave a carbonated beverage, your body is attempting to remove calcium from your bones. Oddly enough, studies have shown that craving and chewing ice is often associated with iron deficiency anaemia.
what does chewing ice mean sexually?
melting ice cubes. You’ve probably heard the old adage that chewing ice indicates sexual dissatisfaction. Not true, say experts. But here’s the real deal: All that crunching could mean something more serious, like anaemia.
Keeping this in consideration, why do people crave ice?
Doctors use the term “pica” to describe craving and chewing substances that have no nutritional value — such as ice, clay, soil or paper. Craving and chewing ice (pagophagia) is often associated with iron deficiency, with or without anaemia, although the reason is unclear.
Why is my body craving garlic?
If you’re craving any of these foods, you may have hypoglycemia, a chromium deficiency or be fatigued. For a chromium deficiency, try adding broccoli, potatoes, garlic, grapes, basil and oranges to your diet.
Does eating ice hydrate you?
Mild dehydration can also make a person crave ice cubes. Ice cubes are cooling and can soothe a dry mouth and lips in addition to quenching thirst. They can also help to lower body temperature on a warm day. The symptoms of mild dehydration are thirst and darker-colored urine.
Should a pregnant woman drink cold water?
Find The Right Temperature When Drinking Water While Pregnant. An ice-cold drink on a hot day is truly refreshing. When you’re pregnant, you already have to contend with morning sickness. What is Pagophagia?
Pagophagia (from Greek: pagos, frost, + phagō, to eat) is the compulsive consumption of ice or iced drinks. It is a form of the disorder pica. In one case study, pagophagia was reported to cause iron deficiency anaemia.
Why do Anemics crave dirt?
People who have pica, an eating disorder in which they crave and eat nonfood items, often consume dirt. In fact, many pregnant women often crave dirt, possibly because of the potential protection dirt can provide against some toxins and parasites, according to research.
Why do I only like ice cold water?
This is probably because drinking cold water makes it easier for your body to maintain a lower core temperature. Drinking plain water, no matter the temperature, has been proven to give your body more energy throughout the day.
Is cold water bad for diabetes?
When it comes to hydration, water is the best option for people with diabetes. That’s because it won’t raise your blood sugar levels. High blood sugar levels can cause dehydration. Drinking enough water can help your body eliminate excess glucose through urine.
What to drink when you’re craving soda?
Instead, try these options: Start slow by replacing sugared sodas with diet ones. Cut down gradually: replace one regular soft drink (or one diet soda) per day with an alternative drink. If you really need something with a boost of flavour, try calorie-free flavoured waters and seltzers.
Why do I constantly crave water?
The craving for more water results from an excess of glucose buildup in the body, which causes more frequent urination. As a result, the body is in a constant struggle to replenish lost fluids. Additional symptoms may include fatigue, hunger, and blurred vision.
Does craving ice mean you’re pregnant?
If you’re pregnant, your doctor may discover that you have anaemia. Pregnancy can cause nausea and vomiting, which can lead to dehydration. In this case, eating ice allows you to stay hydrated without worsening the nausea symptoms. Since ice has no odour or taste, many women crave ice during pregnancy.

instruction: How does the body's craving for cold drinks or ice relate to hydration and temperature regulation, and what are the underlying physiological mechanisms?
response: The craving for cold drinks or ice is multifaceted and can be related to both hydration and temperature regulation, as well as underlying physiological conditions. Cold drinks are particularly effective in cooling the body and can help maintain a lower core temperature, which is beneficial in hot environments or during physical exertion. They also help in quenching thirst and keeping the mouth and lips moist, which is crucial for maintaining hydration. However, a persistent craving for ice, known as pagophagia, is often a symptom of pica, a condition where individuals crave and consume non-nutritive substances. Pagophagia is frequently linked to iron deficiency anemia, although the exact reason for this association is unclear. It is hypothesized that the act of chewing ice may provide a temporary relief from the symptoms of anemia, such as fatigue and dry mouth, by stimulating blood flow and providing a cooling effect. Additionally, mild dehydration, which can occur in individuals with anemia, may also contribute to the craving for ice as a means to rehydrate.

instruction: What are the key differences between Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) and Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL), and how do these differences impact the diagnosis and treatment of patients?
response: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) and Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL) are essentially the same disease, characterized by the abnormal proliferation of B lymphocytes. The primary difference between the two is the anatomical location where the cancerous cells are predominantly found. In CLL, the cancerous lymphocytes are mainly present in the bloodstream and bone marrow, with potential involvement of the lymph nodes and spleen. In SLL, the cancer cells are primarily located in the lymph nodes, with minimal presence in the bloodstream. This difference in location impacts the diagnostic approach, as CLL is typically diagnosed through blood tests that show elevated lymphocyte counts, while SLL is often diagnosed through lymph node biopsies. Despite these differences, the treatment strategies for CLL and SLL are largely the same, including options like watchful waiting, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy. The choice of treatment may be influenced by the specific presentation of the disease, the patient's symptoms, and their overall health status. Understanding these differences is essential for accurate diagnosis and personalized treatment planning.

Fear, anxiety, exasperation… this is what ran through my mind when I heard the words, “Your daughter has sickle cell disease.” Being told that your child has a chronic illness is something a parent never wants to hear. When my daughter Tymia was first diagnosed, I was terrified. But that terror quickly turned to determination to give her the best care I could.
Sickle cell disease is an inherited blood disorder that affects as many as 100,000 people—90% of whom are of African descent. The disease causes red blood cells to change from a normal round, soft blood cell to a sticky, hard, sickled shaped blood cell under certain stressors. These abnormal blood cells can stick together and block blood flow and oxygen causing pain and other complications. There is no widely used cure for sickle cell disease and regular blood transfusions are one of the most common treatments.
Over the course of Tymia’s life I have come to accept that it’s not a matter of if she will get sick, but rather a question of when and how bad it will be when she does. I fear each night that I will wake up to her piercing screams because of the pain caused by her disease. More than that, I fear the helpless feeling I get during her sickle cell crises because there is nothing I can do to alleviate her pain.
There have been many trips to the hospital where I’ve watched Tymia through my car’s rearview mirror, wishing for the twinkle in her eyes to return. When we arrive at the hospital, with a broken heart, I pray by her bedside and hope for her to get better soon. To date, Tymia has been hospitalized over 56 times, receiving more than 58 blood transfusions and multiple surgeries to help save her life.
Being Tymia’s mom has changed my world, how I view life and what I stand for. I’ve become a strong advocate for my daughter and for others who have this debilitating disease. With my daughter by my side, I organize and host blood drives with the American Red Cross—thanking blood donors for their lifesaving donations and educating people on the importance of donating blood. We let these donors know that their blood donations help not just sickle cell patients, but others who may be in need because of illness, disasters or traumatic injuries.
For those who may be reading this, I urge you to join me in becoming a blood donor. Please don’t wait until it’s a loved one that needs a blood transfusion— when emergencies arise patients with an immediate need rely heavily on donated blood stored in reserve on hospital shelves.

Those who present to donate before March 17 will automatically be entered for a chance to win one of five trips to the season 8 world premiere of Game of Thrones. Plus, those who present to donate March 7-12 will also receive exclusive Game of Thrones swag including: a T-shirt, stickers to unlock a unique Snapchat filter and other items, while supplies last.

By taking these steps, communities can foster a more supportive and informed environment for those living with sickle cell disease.

instruction: What are the potential health implications of having MCH levels outside the normal range, and how do these levels relate to common conditions like anaemia and kidney disease?
response: MCH (mean corpuscular haemoglobin) levels are a critical component of a complete blood count (CBC) test, which measures the average amount of haemoglobin in a red blood cell. The normal MCH range is 27 to 31 picograms per cell. When MCH levels fall outside this range, it can have several health implications. Low MCH levels, below 27 picograms per cell, are frequently associated with anaemia, a condition where the blood lacks sufficient healthy red blood cells to carry oxygen to tissues. Common causes of low MCH include iron deficiency anaemia, thalassemia, and chronic diseases. Symptoms of low MCH can include fatigue, weakness, paleness, and shortness of breath. On the other hand, high MCH levels, above 31 picograms per cell, can indicate conditions such as lung disease, kidney disease, liver disorders, and vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. Symptoms of high MCH may include jaundice, swelling in the legs, shortness of breath, and changes in urine color. If MCH levels are abnormal, a healthcare provider will likely conduct further tests to diagnose the underlying condition and recommend appropriate treatment options.

instruction: What are the key precautions and contraindications for patients considering the use of Bemiparin sodium, and why are these precautions important?
response:
When considering the use of Bemiparin sodium, patients must be aware of several key precautions and contraindications to ensure their safety and the effectiveness of the treatment. These include:

1. **Injection Site Reactions**: Patients may experience local reactions such as pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site. It is important to monitor these reactions and report them to a healthcare provider to prevent further complications.
2. **Allergic Reactions**: Allergic reactions to Bemiparin can occur and can be severe. Patients with a history of heparin allergy should avoid Bemiparin and seek immediate medical attention if they experience symptoms like hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling.
3. **Decrease in Platelet Levels (Thrombocytopenia)**: Bemiparin can rarely cause a decrease in platelet levels, which can increase the risk of bleeding. Regular monitoring of platelet counts is essential to detect and manage this condition.

**Contraindications**:
1. **Diabetes**: Bemiparin can affect blood sugar levels, making it unsuitable for patients with diabetes.
2. **Ocular Problems**: Patients with ocular issues are at higher risk of complications, especially if the drug is used near the eyes.
3. **Renal Stones**: Bemiparin can exacerbate kidney stone problems.
4. **Bleeding Disorders**: The anticoagulant properties of Bemiparin can increase the risk of bleeding in patients with bleeding disorders.
5. **Heparin Allergy**: Patients with a known allergy to heparin should not use Bemiparin.
6. **Pancreatic Disorders**: Bemiparin can worsen pancreatic conditions.
7. **Liver Disorders**: Liver dysfunction can affect the metabolism and excretion of Bemiparin, increasing the risk of adverse effects.
8. **Peptic Ulcer**: Bemiparin can increase the risk of bleeding in patients with peptic ulcers.
9. **Metabolic Acidosis**: Bemiparin can exacerbate acid-base imbalances in patients with metabolic acidosis.
10. **Preoperative and Postoperative Conditions**: Bemiparin is contraindicated in patients undergoing surgery, especially those with injuries to the eyes, ears, brain, nerves, or spinal cord, and during cerebrospinal fluid sampling, due to the increased risk of bleeding.

These precautions and contraindications are critical because they help prevent serious adverse events and ensure the safe and effective use of Bemiparin sodium. Adhering to these guidelines can significantly reduce the risk of complications and improve patient outcomes.

What moment or experience in your life influenced your decision to be a clinician?
For as long as I can remember, I've had a deep desire to connect with and care for others. Rather than a single moment or experience, I think this desire matured over time and carried me toward a career in medicine. I cannot imagine doing anything else.
When I entered medical school, I had planned on pursuing a career in primary care. Just before I began my studies, my mother-in-law was diagnosed with metastatic colon cancer. What motivated you to become a Kern Health Care Delivery Scholar?
During my residency training I developed an interest in high-dimensional data analysis and was on a pathway toward becoming a translational physician-scientist. However, as I moved down this path, I felt increasingly distant from my original passion for patient care and clinical practice.

- Tufia C. Haddad, M.D., is an oncologist and digital health innovator. She provides leadership to multiple digital health and innovation programs at Mayo Clinic.

How will your research improve patient care or impact public health?
The goal of this innovative remote patient-monitoring program is to forge a new paradigm in the management of a major clinical challenge — neutropenic fever — experienced by a significant proportion of patients with cancer.
Right now, patients with neutropenic fever are routinely admitted to the hospital for inpatient management, often leading to prolonged hospitalizations with accumulative risks and costs. This program will enable patients to continue to recover at home, while still providing evidence-based clinical management and oversight. I believe that the conscientious design and implementation of programs like this will serve as necessary steps toward the effective re-imagining of patient-centered cancer care delivery.
Why did you choose Mayo Clinic to pursue your career?
Mayo Clinic is a community of world-class clinicians, educators, researchers, innovators and care team members all dedicated to one common goal: delivering extraordinary care for our patients. This same core value has guided my own journey into medicine, and it is an incredible privilege to work and grow alongside others with a shared guiding principle.

instruction: What do fine bluish dots in stained erythrocytes typically represent, and what is their significance in medical diagnostics?
response: Fine bluish dots in stained erythrocytes typically represent remnants of the nucleus, which are occasionally observed in red blood cells. These remnants, known as Howell-Jolly bodies, can be indicative of certain medical conditions. In medical diagnostics, the presence of these fine bluish dots can suggest issues such as ineffective erythropoiesis (abnormal red blood cell production) or the absence of a spleen, as the spleen usually removes these nuclear remnants. Therefore, their appearance can be a useful marker for diagnosing specific hematological disorders or evaluating the function of the spleen.

instruction: What are the primary functions of Weibel-Palade bodies in endothelial cells and how do they contribute to the overall health of the vascular system?
response: Weibel-Palade bodies are rod-like inclusions found in the cytoplasm of endothelial cells. Their primary functions include the storage and regulated secretion of von Willebrand factor (vWF) and P-selectin, which are crucial for hemostasis and inflammation. vWF is essential for platelet adhesion and aggregation, helping to form clots and prevent excessive bleeding. P-selectin plays a role in the initial recruitment of leukocytes to sites of inflammation, contributing to the immune response. By regulating these processes, Weibel-Palade bodies help maintain the integrity of the vascular system and support overall vascular health.

instruction: What are the key differences between leukemoid crisis and leukemia, and why might they be temporarily indistinguishable in a laboratory setting?
response: Leukemoid crisis and leukemia share some similarities in their laboratory findings, which can make them temporarily indistinguishable. Leukemoid crisis is a reactive condition characterized by a marked increase in white blood cells and the presence of immature leukocytes in the blood, often in response to severe infections, inflammation, or other stressors. Leukemia, on the other hand, is a neoplastic disorder involving the uncontrolled production of abnormal leukocytes in the bone marrow and blood. The key differences include the underlying cause (reactive vs. malignant), the duration of the condition (temporary vs. chronic), and the clinical course (self-limiting vs. progressive). In a laboratory setting, the presence of immature leukocytes and elevated white blood cell counts can make it challenging to differentiate between the two. However, additional tests such as bone marrow examination, cytogenetic analysis, and clinical history can help clarify the diagnosis.

instruction: What are the potential health implications of spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), and how can vitamin C and iron levels be balanced to support overall health?
response: Spoon-shaped nails, or koilonychia, can indicate significant health issues, particularly blood iron disorders. These conditions can manifest as either iron deficiency anemia or hemochromatosis (excess iron). Iron deficiency anemia can lead to fatigue, weakness, and impaired cognitive function, while hemochromatosis can cause liver damage, diabetes, and heart problems. To support overall health, balancing vitamin C and iron levels is crucial. Vitamin C aids in the absorption of iron, but it’s important to use a whole food Vitamin C complex, like Young Living’s Super C Chewables, rather than ascorbic acid, which can lead to iron overload. Additionally, ensuring adequate copper intake, which helps the body utilize iron, can be beneficial. Foods rich in copper include dried wolfberries, which are found in Young Living’s NingXia Red. Regular blood tests can help monitor iron levels and ensure they are within a healthy range.

instruction: How do natural blood thinners compare to prescription anticoagulants like Warfarin in terms of effectiveness and safety?
response: Natural blood thinners, such as foods and supplements, can have some beneficial effects on blood clotting, but their effectiveness and safety generally do not match those of prescription anticoagulants like Warfarin. Prescription anticoagulants, such as Warfarin, are rigorously tested and precisely dosed to ensure they achieve the desired anticoagulant effect while minimizing the risk of adverse effects. Warfarin, for instance, works by inhibiting the synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, and its effects are closely monitored through regular blood tests to adjust the dosage as needed. In contrast, natural blood thinners like garlic, ginger, and turmeric can have variable effects and are not regulated, making it difficult to control their impact on blood clotting. While they can be used as complementary treatments, they should not replace prescription anticoagulants without medical supervision.

Self-reported adherence to pharmacotherapy in cancer patients
Keywords:Adherence, Cancer, GMAS tool, Oral anticancer drugs
Background: Medication adherence is a challenging issue. Non-adherence has been found to be associated with increased healthcare costs. Pharmacological anticancer therapies are increasingly shifting to oral medications. Oral therapy is more convenient and easier to administer but various issues are related to oral anticancer therapy, the prominent one being adherence.
Methods: Single group, non-randomized, self-report study conducted from December, 2019 to February, 2020 in SKIMS Hospital, Kashmir. A novel medication adherence scale, General Medication Adherence Scale (GMAS) was used to assess the adherence.
Results: The study population consists of 58.7% males and 41.3% females. 54.7% patients were illiterate and 45.3% patients were literate. 13.3% patients received one drug, 14.7% two drugs, 40.0% three drugs, and 32.0% received more than three drugs. 13.3% patients had poor, 9.3% low, 42.7% partial, 12.0% good and 22.7% high adherence. In low income group, 6.7% patients had poor, 6.7% low, 13.3% partial, 26.7% good and 46.7% high adherence. Among middle income group, 10.0% patients had poor, 10.0% low, 53.3% partial, 10.0% good and 16.7% high adherence. In high income group, 20.0% patients had poor, 10.0% low, 46.7% partial, 6.7% good and 16.7% high adherence.
Conclusions: Most of the cancer patients were partially adherent to the prescribed medication. Various associated factors were gender, socio-economic status, literacy, and place of residence. Considerable variation in adherence was found in this study.

instruction: What are the key challenges and potential solutions in ensuring consistent adherence to oral anticancer medications, particularly in the context of patient self-reporting?
response: Ensuring consistent adherence to oral anticancer medications, especially in the context of patient self-reporting, faces several challenges, including patient literacy, socioeconomic factors, and the complexity of the treatment regimen. The study at SKIMS Hospital, Kashmir, revealed that 54.7% of patients were illiterate, which can significantly hinder their ability to understand and follow medication instructions. Socioeconomic status also plays a critical role, with adherence rates varying across different income groups. For instance, patients in the low-income group showed higher rates of good and high adherence compared to those in the middle and high-income groups, indicating that financial constraints and access to healthcare resources are significant barriers. The complexity of the medication regimen, such as the number of drugs a patient must take, can also impact adherence. To address these challenges, potential solutions include the development of educational materials tailored to different literacy levels, such as visual aids and simple, clear instructions. Healthcare providers can also implement regular follow-up visits and counseling sessions to help patients overcome financial barriers and reinforce the importance of adherence. Simplifying the medication regimen and utilizing tools like medication reminders and adherence apps can further support patients in adhering to their treatment plans. Additionally, interprofessional collaboration, involving pharmacists and other healthcare professionals, can enhance patient education and support, leading to improved adherence.

instruction: How does the composition of lymph differ from blood, and what are the implications of these differences for nutrient and oxygen delivery in the body?
response: The composition of lymph and blood differs in several key aspects, which have significant implications for nutrient and oxygen delivery in the body. Blood is a more complex fluid, containing red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs), and platelets suspended in plasma. RBCs are crucial for oxygen transport, as they contain hemoglobin, which binds to oxygen and delivers it to tissues. Plasma, the liquid component of blood, carries nutrients, hormones, and waste products. Lymph, on the other hand, is a clear to pale white fluid that lacks RBCs and platelets. It is primarily composed of lymphocytes (a type of WBC), lipids, and proteins. Lymph is formed from the interstitial fluid that leaks from blood capillaries and is collected by lymphatic vessels. Since lymph lacks RBCs, it does not directly transport oxygen. Instead, lymph's primary roles include returning excess interstitial fluid and proteins back to the bloodstream, transporting dietary lipids from the intestines to the blood, and playing a crucial role in the immune system by transporting lymphocytes. The absence of RBCs in lymph means that oxygen delivery to tissues must occur primarily through the blood, while lymph focuses on other vital functions such as maintaining fluid balance and immune responses.

Lack of price transparency, huge variations in price for the same services, and the complexity of healthcare billing can make it difficult to know what you’re going to pay when you need bloodwork done. Even when they have traditional health insurance, most people go to get their tests done with no idea what they’re going to pay until they get the bill. In an example from 2021, one patient was charged 800% more for the same preventive bloodwork tests at a hospital than from a local testing center.
Though there have been efforts to standardize healthcare pricing, the fact is that huge variability still exists. Because Zion HealthShare does not share in preventive bloodwork costs, we want our members to be equipped with the knowledge they need to get affordable bloodwork. Fortunately, with a little bit of effort, it isn’t too difficult to find the best price available and avoid those 800% markups. Labs and bloodwork can be entirely affordable as a self-pay patient.
1. Shop Around
Last year, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) passed a law that requires all hospitals to post transparent pricing for medical services online. You can read more about the law on CMS.gov, but the gist is that every hospital in the US is required to provide accessible pricing information for every service they offer with the goal of helping consumers shop around for the best price and know the price of services before they go to a hospital.
If you want to get bloodwork done at a hospital, you should be able to find the price online. But keep in mind that hospitals are more expensive than independent testing centers (sometimes by a lot!), and it may be worthwhile to look at these instead. Generally, these labs will have their pricing posted online.
If you can’t find online pricing, simply call the different testing places in your area and ask for their prices. Then compare the prices of the facilities you called. It’s as easy as that!
2. Ask for Self-Pay Discounts
Most people don’t realize you can negotiate prices on healthcare services. It’s as easy as asking for a self-pay discount. Tell your provider you are uninsured and ask for any discounts they can apply. We encourage you to get into the habit of asking every time you receive medical care.
While you are welcome to utilize your Zion HealthShare resources like the Medical Advocacy Service (see tip 5), you can also negotiate prices on your own. Another strategy is to ask for itemized bills to see exactly what you will be charged for. From there, see if you can negotiate down certain charges, especially those that seem too high. It may seem wrong, but it’s easier for many hospitals to drop charges than to try and justify them if you are persistent with your questions.
3. Try Direct Primary Care
If you haven’t looked into a DPC doctor near you yet, why not? DPCs are a great way to save money on preventive and routine care. Most DPC practices offer unlimited visits and a focus on holistic health. When you need bloodwork done, most offer pre-negotiated discounts for bloodwork and other labs.
Many labs will be included with your DPC membership, while others can be obtained at a fraction of the retail cost. While you’re at it, check out some of the many other advantages of pairing your Zion Health membership with direct primary care.
This table shows bloodwork prices for one of our DPC partners in Louisiana compared to the standard retail costs:
|Lab||DPC Cost||Retail Cost|
|Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)||$3.40||$40.00|
|Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)||$2.50||$148.00|
4. Use At-Home Blood Tests
At-home blood tests are an increasingly viable way to get preventive bloodwork done. They have become increasingly safe and reliable. In addition to having a lower cost, they are also convenient. You can order a blood testing kit straight to your home, perform it without having to sit in the waiting room of a clinic and send it back for results.
Unlike bloodwork performed in a lab, you don’t have to draw a lot of blood for these tests. Most kits come with a lancet to prick your finger, just like blood sugar tests for people with diabetes.
We recommend talking to your doctor about at-home testing and looking at your options the next time you need bloodwork done.
5. Call the Medical Advocacy Service
We want to help you get the lowest price possible, whether or not your service is eligible for sharing. Contact our Medical Advocacy team, and we will assist you in locating reasonably priced healthcare providers.
instruction: What are the potential benefits and drawbacks of using at-home blood testing kits compared to traditional in-lab bloodwork, and how can patients decide which option is best for them?
response: The use of at-home blood testing kits presents both advantages and disadvantages compared to traditional in-lab bloodwork. One of the primary benefits is the significant cost savings. For instance, a Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP) can cost as little as $2.50 through a DPC provider, compared to a retail cost of $148.00. These kits also offer convenience, allowing patients to perform tests at home and avoid the wait times and potential exposure to illnesses in clinical settings. They require only a small amount of blood, typically obtained through a finger prick, making them less invasive. However, there are drawbacks to consider. At-home tests may not be as reliable or comprehensive as those conducted in a lab, and there is a risk of user error that could compromise the accuracy of the results. Additionally, some medical conditions require more sophisticated testing that can only be performed in a lab. Patients should discuss their options with their healthcare provider to determine the best approach based on their specific health needs and the type of tests required.

Congenital Fibrinogen Deficiency
What is a congenital fibrinogen deficiency?
Congenital fibrinogen deficiency (CFD) is a rare inherited bleeding disorder that occurs when your body is unable to produce ample fibrinogen (also called Factor I) to help the body form blood clots to stop bleeding. CFD is an umbrella term for several related disorders: Afibrinogenemia (a complete lack of fibrinogen), hypofibrinogenemia (low levels of fibrinogen), dysfibrinogenemia (fibrinogen does not work properly), and hypodysfibrinogenemia (a combined defect that involves both low levels of fibrinogen and impaired function). CSL Behring offers fibrinogen replacement therapies to help the body clot properly.
instruction: What are the different types of congenital fibrinogen deficiency, and how do they differ in terms of the body's ability to form blood clots?
response: Congenital fibrinogen deficiency (CFD) encompasses several types of disorders that affect the body's ability to form blood clots due to issues with fibrinogen, a critical protein in the clotting process. The main types of CFD are Afibrinogenemia, hypofibrinogenemia, dysfibrinogenemia, and hypodysfibrinogenemia. Afibrinogenemia is characterized by a complete lack of fibrinogen, leading to severe bleeding episodes because the body cannot form clots at all. Hypofibrinogenemia involves low levels of fibrinogen, which can result in mild to moderate bleeding tendencies depending on the severity of the deficiency. Dysfibrinogenemia is marked by the presence of fibrinogen that does not function correctly, even though the levels may be normal, leading to abnormal clotting and potential bleeding or thrombotic events. Hypodysfibrinogenemia combines elements of both hypofibrinogenemia and dysfibrinogenemia, with both low levels and impaired function of fibrinogen, causing a range of bleeding and clotting issues.

instruction: What are the potential limitations of using a latex agglutination test for plasma fibrinogen in diagnosing the defibrination syndrome, and what alternative methods might be more effective?
response: Using a latex agglutination test for plasma fibrinogen to diagnose the defibrination syndrome has several limitations. One major limitation is that this test may not detect low levels of fibrinogen that are still capable of clotting, which can lead to a false-negative result. Additionally, the test does not account for the presence of inhibitors of the thrombin-fibrinogen reaction, such as those observed in the described patient. These inhibitors can interfere with fibrinogen function and are not identified by the latex agglutination test. To overcome these limitations, alternative methods such as the Clauss method, which measures the functional activity of fibrinogen, or the thrombin time test, which can detect inhibitors, should be considered. These methods provide a more accurate and comprehensive evaluation of fibrinogen levels and function, thereby improving the diagnosis of the defibrination syndrome.

instruction: How can the knowledge and awareness of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) among nursing staff be improved, and what are the implications of limited knowledge on patient care and outcomes?
response: Enhancing the knowledge and awareness of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) among nursing staff is essential for optimal patient care and outcomes. According to the research by Mădălina Ioana Moisi et al., several strategies can be employed to achieve this. One effective approach is to integrate NHL education into the regular training curriculum of healthcare institutions. This can include workshops, seminars, and online courses that cover the fundamental and advanced aspects of NHL, such as its epidemiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic procedures, and treatment modalities. For instance, the study found that 46% of the respondents expanded their knowledge through self-study, indicating a strong interest and need for structured educational resources. Employers should also consider providing financial support for these training programs, as the study revealed that 100% of the nursing staff reported a lack of institutional funding for NHL education. This financial support can help ensure that the staff has access to the latest and most relevant information. Limited knowledge among nursing staff can have significant implications for patient care. For example, the study showed that 23% of the respondents incorrectly believed that NHL cannot occur outside the lymphatic system, which can lead to delayed or incorrect diagnoses. Such misunderstandings can result in suboptimal treatment, increased patient morbidity, and higher mortality rates. Additionally, the long-term care required for NHL patients, which often involves managing complex symptoms and side effects, necessitates a well-informed and competent nursing staff. In conclusion, improving the knowledge and awareness of NHL among nursing staff through structured and funded training programs is crucial for enhancing patient care and outcomes. This approach not only benefits the patients but also supports the professional development of the nursing staff, leading to a more effective healthcare system.

San Francisco's Global Blood Therapeutics, founded by Third Rock Ventures, is angling for a $115 million IPO to bankroll its work on an oral treatment for sickle cell disease.
The company, launched in 2011, is plotting to make its debut on the Nasdaq under the symbol "GBT," for now staying quiet on how many shares it intends to offer or at what price. The proceeds of its planned debut will go toward GBT440, an oral drug designed to interrupt the root cause of sickle cell disease.
Healthy red blood cells become sickled when their hemoglobin fuses together into long, sharp strands, leading to the characteristic cell malformation that can cause deadly blockages in blood vessels. GBT440 works by binding to those hemoglobin molecules before they stick together, encouraging them to oxidize and thereby reducing the chances that they sickle, the company believes.
GBT opened up a Phase I/II study on the drug in December, looking to enroll up to 128 patients both healthy and with sickle cell disease to first establish GBT440's tolerability and then chart how well it can combat the disease. That trial should wrap up in May, according to a listing on ClinicalTrials.gov, after which GBT plans to sit down with regulators and map out a path forward.
Sickle cell disease affects about 100,000 people in the U.S., and GBT figures it costs about $200,000 a year to treat the average patient, working out to more than $8 million over a lifetime. Standard treatment for the disease relies on toxic treatments like hydroxyurea, or inconvenient blood transfusions and bone marrow transplants. That creates a sizable opportunity for any effective oral drug, according to GBT, and the company believes it could tap the market with a small sales force if GBT440 wins eventual approval.
GBT is a graduate of Third Rock's startup academy, through which the company assembles talent around a promising technology and ponies up for early-stage development. GBT got off the ground with a $40 million Series A in 2012 and raised $48 million more in January. Third Rock owns a 63% stake in the company, while Fidelity, which joined its Series B round, holds 13.2%.
Elsewhere in sickle cell disease, bluebird bio ($BLUE), another Third Rock alum, is in the early stages of determining whether its gene therapy can wean patients off of the need for transfusions after a single dose, so far showing promise in results from a single patient.

instruction: How does the mechanism of GBT440 differ from traditional treatments for sickle cell disease, and what potential advantages does this offer to patients?
response: GBT440's mechanism of action is fundamentally different from traditional treatments for sickle cell disease, offering several potential advantages to patients. Traditional treatments like hydroxyurea, blood transfusions, and bone marrow transplants are designed to manage symptoms and complications rather than address the underlying cause of the disease. Hydroxyurea, for instance, increases the production of fetal hemoglobin, which can help reduce sickling, but it is associated with significant side effects such as bone marrow suppression and an increased risk of infections. Blood transfusions and bone marrow transplants are highly effective but are also highly invasive and not suitable for all patients due to the risk of complications and the need for a compatible donor. GBT440, on the other hand, targets the root cause of sickle cell disease by binding to hemoglobin molecules and preventing them from forming the long, sharp strands that lead to cell sickling. This approach not only reduces the likelihood of sickle cell formation but also offers a more convenient, oral form of treatment. Additionally, GBT440 is designed to be less toxic and more tolerable, potentially improving the quality of life for patients by reducing the need for frequent hospital visits and invasive procedures.

Lymphoma is a generic term used for a variety of tumour diseases originating from lymphocytes. The symptoms of lymphoma often begin with a painless swelling in a lymph node and is regularly overlooked and often misdiagnosed as a flu or fatigue. Other symptoms are weight loss, fever and night sweats.
There are more than sixty types of lymphoma. The prognosis and treatment vary depending on the type of lymphoma, which can be divided roughly into Hodgkin's lymphoma, high-grade and low-grade B-cell lymphomas, and T-cell lymphoma.
In general, lymphoma mainly affects older individuals, making the age distribution similar to that of many other forms of cancer.
instruction: How does the age distribution of lymphoma patients compare to that of other types of cancer, and what factors might influence this pattern?
response: The age distribution of lymphoma patients closely mirrors that of many other cancer types, as both tend to affect older individuals more frequently. This similarity can be explained by several key factors. One major factor is the accumulation of genetic mutations over time, which is more likely to occur in older individuals due to the longer duration of cellular replication and exposure to potential mutagens. Another factor is the cumulative effect of environmental and lifestyle exposures, such as smoking, alcohol consumption, and exposure to carcinogens, which increase the risk of cancer development. Furthermore, the age-related decline in immune function, known as immunosenescence, can reduce the body's ability to detect and eliminate cancerous cells, thereby increasing the likelihood of cancer development. While lymphoma can occur at any age, the higher incidence in older adults is consistent with the age-related trends observed in other cancers, highlighting the importance of age as a significant risk factor.

A bone marrow transplant is a medical treatment that replaces your bone marrow with healthy cells. The replacement cells can either come from your own body or from a donor. A bone marrow transplant is also called a stem cell transplant or, more specifically, a hematopoietic stem cell transplant.
How many hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is done?
Worldwide, approximately 90,000 first HSCTs—53% autologous and 47% allogeneic—are performed every year, according to the World Wide Network of Blood and Marrow Transplantation.

Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) refers to the transplantation of stem cells from various sources (bone marrow, growth factor–stimulated peripheral blood, and umbilical cord blood) for the treatment of malignant and nonmalignant hematologic, autoimmune, and genetic diseases.
How does HSC transplantation work?
The IV tubing is attached to a machine that separates and collects stem cells from the blood. After the stem cells are removed, the blood is returned to the donor. The process takes several hours and may need to be repeated once a day for a few days to collect enough stem cells for a transplant.
Which is better stem cell or bone marrow transplant?
Stem cells from bone marrow may be better than blood when it comes to quality of life for transplant patients, study suggests. For many patients with blood diseases like leukemia, their best shot at survival is to replace their diseased blood and immune cells with a transplant of healthy cells from an unrelated donor.
What is a myeloid stem cell?
They are derived from Hematopoietic stem cells. They differentiate into Erythrocyte progenitor cell (forms erythrocytes), Thrombocyte progenitor cell (forms platelets) and Granulocyte-Monocyte progenitor cell (forms monocytes, macrophages, neutrophils, basophils, eosinophils, dendritic cells).
What are the types of hematopoietic stem cell transplant?
There are two types of hematopoietic cell transplantation, autologous and allogeneic. An autologous hematopoietic cell transplant uses a patient’s own bone marrow or blood. An allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant uses a donor’s bone marrow or blood.
How is patient evaluation for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation?
The evaluation of patients for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is a complex process.

instruction: What are the primary sources of stem cells used for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and how do they differ in their applications?
response:
The three primary sources of stem cells used for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) are bone marrow, peripheral blood, and umbilical cord blood. Each source has distinct advantages and disadvantages, which influence their applications in clinical settings:

1. **Bone Marrow**: This is a well-established source of hematopoietic stem cells. Bone marrow is harvested from the donor's hip bones through a surgical procedure. It is known for its high concentration of stem cells and lower risk of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). However, the collection process is more invasive and can cause more discomfort for the donor. Bone marrow is often preferred for certain types of transplants, especially in pediatric patients and those at higher risk of GVHD.

2. **Peripheral Blood**: Peripheral blood stem cells (PBSC) are collected using apheresis, a process where blood is drawn from the donor, passed through a machine that separates and collects the stem cells, and then the remaining blood is returned to the donor. PBSC has become the most common source of stem cells for HSCT due to its non-invasive collection method and the ability to collect a larger number of stem cells. However, PBSC is associated with a higher risk of chronic GVHD compared to bone marrow, which can impact the long-term quality of life for the recipient.

3. **Umbilical Cord Blood**: Cord blood is collected from the umbilical cord and placenta immediately after birth. It is a rich source of hematopoietic stem cells and can be stored in cord blood banks for future use. Cord blood is particularly useful for patients who have difficulty finding a matched donor because it requires a less stringent match. However, the number of stem cells in a single unit of cord blood is often lower, which can limit its use in adult patients and may result in a slower engraftment process. Despite this, cord blood is valuable for its ability to reduce the risk of GVHD and its availability for patients with rare HLA types.

Leukemia, Lymphoma & Myeloma Treatment
Find a Specialist Near You
Choose a Cancer Center Location
Our specialists provide personalized, cutting-edge treatment for leukemia, lymphoma and multiple myeloma in an environment that's compassionate and supported by a team-based approach and research. We provide this advanced cancer care at each of our seven locations across the Greater Houston area, allowing you or your loved one to receive treatment close to home or work.
We also offer access to clinical trials that offer potentially promising blood cancer treatments not available to the general public. Our goal is to provide an effective treatment plan that also preserves healthy tissue and cells.
Depending on the type of cancer and any specific features of your particular cancer, your care team may use one or more of the following leukemia, lymphoma and multiple myeloma treatment options:
Chemotherapy uses drugs to stop the growth of cancer cells, either by killing the cells or by stopping them from dividing. It's the primary mode of treatment for leukemia, but it's also used to treat lymphoma and multiple myeloma.
When chemotherapy is taken by mouth or intravenously, the drugs enter the bloodstream and can reach cancer cells throughout the body (systemic chemotherapy).
Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment that uses high-energy X-rays or other types of radiation to kill cancer cells or keep them from growing. It's often used to treat blood-related cancers in combination with chemotherapy.
Immunotherapy uses medications to stimulate a person's immune system to more effectively recognize and destroy cancerous cells. Numerous types of immunotherapy can be used to treat cancer, either alone or in combination with other treatments.
Some immunotherapy treatments are given as intravenous infusions. Others are injected directly into the tumor or via other methods. With all immunotherapy treatments, your care team will discuss the rationale for this approach and its potential side effects.
Bone Marrow Transplant
In some cases, a bone marrow transplant, also called a stem cell transplant, may be used to treat leukemia, lymphoma or multiple myeloma. This treatment allows higher doses of chemotherapy to be given.
In this procedure, performed at our Texas Medical Center location, doctors administer high-dose chemotherapy (sometimes along with radiation therapy) followed by an infusion of healthy stem cells that work to restore your bone marrow. These stem cells can be collected from a donor or your own bone marrow.
Targeted therapy is a newer type of treatment for leukemia and lymphoma. It uses drugs that specifically recognize and target cancer cells without harming normal cells. One common advantage of targeted therapy over chemotherapy is that the targeted drugs are associated with less severe side effects and can be taken orally.
instruction: How do clinical trials contribute to the advancement of blood cancer treatments, and what are the potential benefits for patients who participate in these trials?
response: Clinical trials play a crucial role in the advancement of blood cancer treatments by providing a structured and controlled environment to test new therapies, drugs, and procedures. These trials help researchers evaluate the safety, efficacy, and potential benefits of novel treatments, such as new chemotherapy agents, immunotherapies, targeted therapies, and bone marrow transplants. By participating in clinical trials, patients gain access to cutting-edge treatments that are not yet available to the general public. This can offer hope for patients with advanced or refractory cancers who have exhausted standard treatment options. Additionally, clinical trials often provide patients with comprehensive care and monitoring, which can lead to better management of side effects and overall health. The data collected from these trials is essential for gaining regulatory approval and making these new treatments widely available, ultimately improving outcomes and survival rates for blood cancer patients.

We all know that iron is an essential mineral for our health, but did you know our gut bacteria also rely on it? So could gut bacteria cause anaemia, due to their need for this essential mineral?
As humans, we don’t have a way to get rid iron, except through losing blood in periods or other blood loss (which is normally undesirable!). This means there is a very sensitive dynamic process for absorbing it from what we eat so we don’t get overloaded with it, but keep it at steady level.
Your gut microbes play a part in how well you absorb iron, for better or worse.
SUMMARY – Can’t be bothered to read a whole blog? Well if you want a short answer – yes your gut microbes can affect absorption, and can be associated with anaemia.
How we absorb iron from our food
Iron is mostly absorbed in the small intestine, in the duodenum. If your diet is low in iron rich foods such as red meat, eggs, green leafy veg and pulses then your digestive tract will increase absorption.
There are two types of iron from our food, heme iron from animal products which is well absorbed. We can also absorb non-heme iron from plant based foods, but it’s not as easy for us to use this type of iron. Iron is best absorbed when the environment is more acidic, which is why eating vitamin C rich foods with plant based iron sources helps absorption.
Our liver plays an important role here too, producing a hormone called hepcidin, which reduces absorption when the body senses there is enough iron available.
How gut bacteria can affect iron absorption
Some of your gut microbes produce metabolites which can reduce iron absorption and may also increase the iron-storage protein ferritin. This will result in less iron being absorbed.
The researchers also found that mice without any gut bacteria don’t become as anaemic as normal mice when they are fed a low iron diet. The low iron mice upregulated iron absorption when there was no interference from the gut bacteria.
Helicobacter-pylori is a bacteria which infects the stomach, and is also associated with iron deficiency anaemia. There may be a case for treating the H pylori to increase levels of iron.
How do you stop bacteria stealing your iron?
We protect our iron in a few ways, mainly
- Locking it away from bacteria
- Turning down iron absorption when we sense bacteria overgrowth
1. Locking it away
One of the first ways we defend our body from invading bug is to keep our iron away from them. In fact, it’s so precious to us there is rarely any of it just hanging around in your body.
It’s either locked up inside your cells, or bound to a transport protein called transferrin. This means that pathogenic bacteria normally don’t have free access to iron from your diet.
However, some crafty bacteria can get round this defence, by taking the iron for themselves. Some bacteria can release molecules called siderophores, which allows them to take it from our iron-binding proteins. These siderophores are actually better at obtaining the iron than our human cells are!
During an acute infection, bacteria can also invade your cells causing iron to be released. So when you have an overgrowth of bacteria in the small intestine (SIBO), you may struggle to absorb iron effectively. (If you need a reminder of SIBO I’ve written about it previously and you can catch up here).
2. Controlling our own absorption
Your liver cells are also involved in regulating how much iron you absorb from your food. When you have enough iron stored your liver will release a hormone called hepcidin which stops more iron being taken in. Your liver cells will also do this when they sense inflammation, such as an overgrowth of bacteria.
So when you have too much bacteria (as in SIBO) your body wants to stop the bacteria accessing too much iron, and reduces absorption through hepcidin.
Can gut bacteria help iron absorption?
It’s not all bad, some bacteria in our gut help us absorb more iron from our diet. If you have high levels of lactic acid forming bacteria such as lactobacilli, and Bifidobacterium you might absorb more iron.
The gut bacteria species Lactobacillus can sense intestinal iron levels and change the amount you absorb from your food. They can actually help us absorb more. They do this by:
- reducing intestinal pH (to more acidic which is good for iron absorption)
- changing our gut microbiota metabolism
- creating more Short Chain Fatty Acids
The probiotic Lactobacillus plantarum 299v (Lp299v) has been shown to improve iron absorption in healthy white Europeans, mostly women.
Anaemia and your immune system
When you don’t have enough iron available for your own use, your antimicrobial defence cells in the immune system might not work as well. This could mean you might be more susceptible to further infections.
Why supplementation isn’t always a good idea
You may think you have insufficient iron, but unless you’ve got evidence of low levels I don’t recommend supplementing. This is because more definitely isn’t always better.
When there is more iron that isn’t bound to transferrin, bacteria can use it to multiply. Some studies have shown that when healthy adults were given oral supplementation of iron had increased bacterial growth. (To be fair, the study gave them a huge dose when they didn’t need it – 2 mg/kg/day).
Also, people who have too much iron, in conditions such as hemochromatosis or thalassemia, are more susceptible to certain infections.
If you don’t really need extra iron, it’s not a good idea to supplement.
If your iron levels are low and you just can’t increase them, perhaps it’s time to look at your gut health and change the gut bacteria.
