Smartphone technology takes on anaemia detection
Researchers at the University College London and the University of Ghana have touched upon a breakthrough for quick and inexpensive haemoglobin testing. Their new smartphone-based system is designed to use phone cameras to detect haemoglobin concentrations, offering a new way for medical staff to detect anaemia.
Turning a smartphone into a medical device – How it happened
Noting the importance of devising an inexpensive, reliable way of testing haemoglobin levels, researchers at the two institutions turned to a device used worldwide – smartphones. The real hurdle was figuring out how to turn a smartphone into a diagnostic tool that could be relied upon. As one of the leads of the project, Thomas Wemyss of the University College London, said, “Smartphones are globally popular, but research using smartphone imaging to diagnose diseases shows a general trend of experiencing difficulty when transferring results to different groups of people.”
Their study was not the first one revealing how researchers are examining the prospects of using a smartphone as a tool for medical examinations, though. For example, a team at Purdue University recently published a study detailing the use of smartphones to detect haemoglobin levels by taking pictures of the inner eyelid. Even earlier in 2014, a University of Washington team developed an app to detect neonatal jaundice using only a smartphone camera and a tiny colour calibration card.
The team, which had experienced prior success in screening for neonatal jaundice using smartphone-based technology, began work in 2018. Principal investigator Dr Terence Leung, an Associate Professor in Biomedical Optics at University College London’s Department of Medical Physics and Biomedical Engineering, commented in a press release, “we are so excited to see that the smartphone imaging technique can also apply to anaemia screening in young children and infants.”
The technology works by taking images of body parts with little pigmentation, such as the sclera (white) of the eye, lower eyelid, and lip. The app then analyses the colour of the imaged tissue using absorbance analysis techniques. Haemoglobin absorbs light in a specific fashion, and the app can analyse the light from the photographs to determine haemoglobin concentrations. After adjusting for varying ambient lighting and chromaticity metrics for the region captured, the app can give a fairly accurate result.
Promising results from smartphone Colourimetry
The findings from their pilot study were published in the March 2023 issue of the journal PLOS ONE and outlined how their algorithm could test for haemoglobin levels. The researchers recruited sixty-two patients under four years of age at Korle Bu Teaching Hospital, Ghana. After testing, highly promising results were obtained; the app had a sensitivity score of 92.9% and a specificity of 89.7%.
As the researchers wrote, the evidence suggested, “smartphone colourimetry is likely to be a useful tool for making anaemia screening more widely available.” Will it replace the currently-used analysers? Not yet, it seems. The researchers still have to determine optimal methods for image pre-processing, particularly across diverse populations, and it will need to receive wide adoption across multiple countries. However, it offers the promise of reliable, non-invasive, and affordable testing for a disease with a significant burden. With more clinical trials, it may be set for adoption in low- and middle-income countries soon.
Anaemia: A major burden in the human population
Blood haemoglobin concentration is one of the most reliable measures for detecting the presence or absence of anaemia. However, access to the equipment used to measure haemoglobin concentrations is not equally distributed worldwide, with the effect pronounced in low- and middle-income countries with unequal access to routine medical diagnostics.
One of the essential components of blood is the red blood cell, which makes up about 45% of blood in most healthy people. The red blood cell’s chief function is to carry Oxygen, which the body’s tissues and muscles require to generate energy. Red blood cells, also known as erythrocytes, carry Oxygen by binding it to a molecule known as haemoglobin. When the red blood cell arrives at tissues lacking Oxygen, it releases its Oxygen payload.
In certain individuals, however, the number of red blood cells present in their blood is insufficient to supply all the body’s cells with Oxygen. This condition is known as anaemia. It is one of the most common diseases globally, affecting over two billion people, particularly in low-income countries. Characterized by symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, heart palpitations, pale/yellowish skin, and dizziness, anaemia can develop due to various causes. Children, especially new-borns, have more at stake in a case of anaemia: the condition can negatively affect cognitive development and lead to increased disease susceptibility.
Access to testing – A problem in low-income countries
Usually, anaemia occurs due to iron deficiency – about half the cases, according to an article in the Lancet. Therefore, it is readily treatable by iron supplements if it is detected. In high-income countries, haemoglobin levels are routinely tested in medical check-ups. In low- and middle-income countries, this is often not the case. Firstly, laboratory procedures can be relatively expensive, and access to a clinic may not be easy to come by for most residents of these countries. The distance to hospitals is often long. Families typically have to make at least two trips – one for sample collection and another for receiving results.
What about automated analysers such as blood analysers and automated haematology analysers? While such devices are readily available from manufacturers, the costs associated with obtaining and using such devices are often too high for local clinics. For one, the initial price for an automated haematology analyzer is high. The cost is further increased due to a need for stable conditions, regular maintenance, and personnel costs to operate the device.
For healthcare workers in low- and middle-income countries, such devices are effectively out of their reach. However, the burden of anaemia in the world is significantly heavier in these regions. The Global Burden of Disease Study in 2019 reveals as much. In a study published in the Journal of Hematology & Oncology, researchers found that the highest national anaemia prevalences were in Zambia, Mali, and Burkina Faso, with Zambia recording as high as 49,000 cases per 100,000 people. All three most-affected regions are located in low-income areas, underlining the need for innovative, accurate, and inexpensive testing to help reduce the disease burden in these countries.

instruction: What are the primary reasons for the high prevalence of anaemia in low-income countries, and how might innovative, low-cost diagnostic tools like smartphone-based haemoglobin testing help address this public health issue?
response: The primary reasons for the high prevalence of anaemia in low-income countries include iron deficiency, which is responsible for about half of all cases, and the limited access to routine medical diagnostics. In these regions, the cost of laboratory procedures is often prohibitive, and clinics may be located far from where people live, requiring multiple trips for sample collection and result retrieval. Furthermore, the high initial cost, maintenance, and operational requirements of automated haematology analysers make them impractical for many local clinics. This lack of access to testing and treatment results in a significant number of undiagnosed and untreated cases, leading to severe health consequences, particularly in children. Innovative, low-cost diagnostic tools like smartphone-based haemoglobin testing offer a promising solution. These tools leverage the widespread availability of smartphones to provide a reliable, non-invasive, and affordable method for detecting anaemia. For example, the app developed by researchers at University College London and the University of Ghana uses the smartphone camera to analyse haemoglobin levels in areas with little pigmentation, such as the sclera of the eye or the lower eyelid. With high sensitivity and specificity, these apps can help make anaemia screening more accessible and widespread, potentially leading to earlier detection and treatment, and ultimately reducing the burden of anaemia in low-income countries.

Living at altitude there are some things that you become hyper aware about. One of the more obvious things is the lack of oxygen in the air. When it comes to athletics there are a few advantages but many disadvantages to the limited O2. Having played and watched sports at the mile high level for many years you start to become in tune to ailments or conditions that might worsen because of the high altitude. One of those conditions that you definitely need to be aware of is Sickle Cell Anemia and Sickle Cell Anemia Trait. The National Athletic Trainer’s Association defines Sickle Cell Anemia Trait in their position statement as the inheritance of one gene for sickle hemoglobin and one for normal hemoglobin. Hemoglobin is a protein in the red blood cells that transports oxygen. In times of extreme exertion or exercise the sickle hemoglobin will cause the red blood cell to shrink into a quarter or half-moon shape. This greatly affects the body’s oxygen levels. The sickle cells also causes blockages in vessels because the cells catch on each other and cannot move freely.
Sickle cell is a genetic adaptation and it is common in people whose origin is from areas where malaria is widespread. Just carrying one of the sickle-cell genes could defend off malaria (NATA Position Statement). 1 in 12 African-Americans posses the trait. It is good to take note that the trait is also seen in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Indian, Caribbean and South and Central American descendents.
Some startling stats about sickle-cell:
- In the past four decades, exertional sickling has killed at least 15 football players.
- In the past seven years alone, sickling has killed nine athletes:
- Five college football players in training,
- Two high school athletes
- Two 12-year-old boys training for football
- Of 136 sudden, non-traumatic sports deaths in high school and college athletes over a decade, seven (5%) were from exertional sickling
So what are some signs and symptoms of a sickle-cell attack:
- Cramping muscle weakness that exceeds muscle pain
- Athlete “slumps” to the ground rather than a sudden collapse (Rules out cardiac)
- Able to speak (Rules out cardiac)
- Muscles look and feel normal (rules out heat cramps)
- Rapid breathing, but pulmonary exam reveals normal air movement (rules out asthma)
- Rectal temperature less than 103oF (rule out heat stroke)
Ways to avoid a sickle-cell attack:
- Build up slowly in training with paced progressions,
- Allow longer periods of rest and recovery between repetitions.
- Encourage participation in preseason strength and conditioning programs
- Athletes with sickle-cell trait should be excluded from participation in performance tests such as mile runs, serial sprints, etc., as several deaths have occurred from participation in this setting.
- Stop any activity with onset of symptoms [muscle ‘cramping’, pain, swelling, weakness, tenderness; inability to “catch breath”, fatigue].
- Athletes with sickle-cell trait who perform repetitive high-speed sprints and/or interval training that induces high levels of lactic acid should be allowed extended recovery between repetitions
- Ambient heat stress, dehydration, asthma, illness, and altitude predispose the athlete with sickle trait to an onset of crisis in physical exertion.
- Emphasize hydration
- Control asthma
- No workout if an athlete with sickle trait is ill
- Watch closely the athlete with sickle-cell trait who is new to altitude.
- Modify training and have supplemental oxygen available for competitions
- Educate to create an environment that encourages athletes with sickle-cell trait to report any symptoms immediately;
- Any signs or symptoms such as fatigue, difficulty breathing, leg or low back pain, or leg or low back cramping in an athlete with sickle-cell trait should be assumed to be sickling
** THIS IS A MEDICAL EMERGENCY!**
How to treat a sickle-cell attack:
- Check vital signs.
- Administer high-flow oxygen, 15 lpm (if available),
- Cool the athlete, if necessary.
- Call 911, attach an AED, start an IV, and get the athlete to the hospital fast.
- Tell the doctors to expect explosive rhabdomyolysis and grave metabolic complications.
- Proactively prepare by having an Emergency Action Plan and appropriate emergency equipment for all practices and competitions.
Sickle cell anemia is a very serious condition and needs to be treated as soon as possible! The good thing about this disease is that it is easily screened for and once the proper people are aware of the condition it can definitely be well managed! Be aware and get screened!
instruction: What are the key signs and symptoms of a sickle-cell attack, and how can these be distinguished from other common athletic emergencies such as heat stroke or cardiac issues?
response: A sickle-cell attack can be identified by several key signs and symptoms, which differ from other common athletic emergencies such as heat stroke or cardiac issues. These signs include cramping muscle weakness that is more severe than typical muscle pain, the athlete gradually slumping to the ground rather than a sudden collapse, the ability to speak (which rules out cardiac issues), muscles that appear and feel normal (ruling out heat cramps), rapid breathing with normal air movement (ruling out asthma), and a rectal temperature below 103°F (ruling out heat stroke). To distinguish a sickle-cell attack from heat stroke, note the absence of a high core body temperature and altered mental status. For cardiac issues, the sudden collapse and inability to speak are key differentiators. Immediate medical attention, including administering high-flow oxygen, cooling the athlete if necessary, and calling 911, is essential for effective management of a sickle-cell attack.

instruction: How does the appearance of enlarged lymph nodes on an X-ray contribute to the diagnosis of Hodgkin's lymphoma, and what other imaging techniques might be used in conjunction with X-rays?
response: The detection of enlarged lymph nodes on an X-ray is a key finding in the diagnosis of Hodgkin's lymphoma. In the X-ray described, the enlarged lymph nodes (adenomegalies) appear as small pale regions on either side of the heart. These enlarged nodes are a result of the malignant growth of lymphocytes, which is characteristic of Hodgkin's lymphoma. While X-rays can provide initial evidence of lymph node enlargement, they are often limited in their ability to provide detailed anatomical and functional information. Therefore, other imaging techniques are typically used to complement X-ray findings. Computed tomography (CT) scans can offer detailed cross-sectional images of the body, helping to visualize the extent of lymph node involvement and any other abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is useful for detailed imaging of soft tissues and can help in assessing the involvement of organs such as the spleen or bone marrow. Positron emission tomography (PET) scans can detect areas of increased metabolic activity, which is indicative of cancerous cells. By combining these imaging modalities, doctors can more accurately diagnose Hodgkin's lymphoma, stage the disease, and plan appropriate treatment strategies.

instruction: How do capillaries regulate the exchange of nutrients and waste between blood and cells, and what mechanisms are involved in this process?
response:
The regulation of nutrient and waste exchange between blood and cells by capillaries is a complex and finely tuned process. Capillaries, the smallest blood vessels in the body, serve as the primary site for this exchange due to their unique structural and functional characteristics. August Krogh, a Danish physiologist, made significant contributions to our understanding of capillary function, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1920.

Capillaries are characterized by their extremely small diameter, typically a few microns, but they can expand up to three times this size when necessary. This adaptability allows them to meet the varying demands of the tissues they serve. The walls of capillaries are composed of a single layer of endothelial cells, which are highly permeable to water, gases, and small molecules. This permeability is crucial for the exchange of nutrients and waste.

The exchange process is driven by two main mechanisms: osmosis and diffusion. Osmosis involves the movement of water across the capillary wall in response to differences in solute concentration. Diffusion, on the other hand, involves the movement of molecules from areas of high concentration to areas of low concentration. When capillaries are connected to arterioles, the higher blood pressure inside the capillary forces fluids and nutrients (such as oxygen and glucose) out into the interstitial space surrounding the cells. This process is known as filtration. As the capillary continues along its path and connects to venules, the pressure decreases, allowing waste products (such as carbon dioxide and metabolic waste) to be reabsorbed back into the capillary. This process is known as reabsorption.

Krogh's research also revealed that capillaries can dynamically regulate blood flow in response to the metabolic needs of the tissues. For instance, during physical activity, the demand for oxygen and nutrients in skeletal muscles increases, and capillaries dilate to increase blood flow and enhance the exchange of substances. Conversely, during periods of rest, capillaries constrict to reduce blood flow and conserve resources.

In summary, capillaries regulate the exchange of nutrients and waste through a combination of their structural permeability, pressure gradients, and the ability to adjust blood flow in response to tissue demands, ensuring that cells receive the necessary resources and that waste products are efficiently removed.

Anemia is a condition where the red blood cell count is reduced due to deficiencies within the system. This is usually caused by a lack of iron, folate and other related nutrients in the diet. White blood cells are also known as WBCs in the abbreviated form. They are those components of the blood and the immune system that aid in fighting off infections and resisting diseases. The quantity of white blood cells in the body helps in the determination of the health of the body. White blood cells in urine, is not a sign of good health.
White cells are normally not found in urine or the urinary tract. Urine is a sterile liquid and hence does not contain any blood. Therefore, the presence of white blood cells in urine indicates that there may be a problem or an infection of the kidneys, the urinary tract, the urethra, or the bladder. Any of these may become infected and may result in inflammation of the organ along with presence of white blood cells in urine.
All of us are aware of the fact that white blood cells protect the body from the vagaries of many infections and aid in maintaining a healthy body. It is the white blood cells that help us to effectively fight off the normal conditions such as common cold, cough and other health conditions. White blood cells come from the bone marrow. There are many types of white blood cells.
The white blood cells are present across the body, in the different organs, including the lymphatic system. The blood of a healthy human adult is composed of nearly one percent of white blood cells and hence one should know that they are very important for the general health of the immune system and the body.
It is important to note that even though white blood cells are important to maintain a healthy body, presence of white blood cells in unwanted areas of the body and/or in unhealthy quantities can be caused due to the presence of certain health conditions. Similarly, the presence of white blood cells in urine could be a possible indicator of various conditions of the urinary tract.
The presence of white blood cells in the urine can be detected by a test known as urinalysis. Once the test indicates white blood cells in urine, then other tests are performed to check the overall health of the components of the urinary system such as the bladder, kidneys, urethra, etc. and then appropriate treatment is undertaken to cure the urinary tract infection. Once the underlying condition is treated, white blood cells in urine will disappear.
Symptoms of white blood cells in urine
Some of the symptoms of white blood cells in urine are as follows:
- Painful urination
- Infection of the urinary tract. This is one of the important symptoms of white blood cells in urine
- Burning sensations during urination
- Cloudy appearance of urine, if there is infection of the bladder which causes white blood cells in urine
- Difficulties in urination
- An overall weakness
- Pain in the abdomen
- A weak stream of urine
- Swelling of the genitals
Causes of white blood cells in urine
Some of the possible causes of white blood cells in urine are discussed below:
- An infection of the urinary tract: This is one of the most common causes of infections of the urinary tract as well as the presence of white blood cells in urine. During sexual intercourse or other engaging on other activities, bacteria may sometimes enter the urethral opening. This may result in infection of the urinary tract, which in turn may lead to white blood cells in urine.
- Infections of the bladder: The bladder is a major part of the urinary system. Hence, any disorder of the bladder, such as infections, can lead to the development of infections of the bladder and white blood cells in urine. Any obstruction of the bladder pathways, certain conditions associated with pregnancy and infections caused due to unsafe sexual intercourse can also lead to the development of bladder infections. This may in turn result in the collection of white blood cells in urine.
- Infection of the kidneys: This is one of the other important causes of the presence of white blood cells in urine. Infection of the kidneys generally commences as an infection of the urinary tract, which then spreads to the other organs such as the kidneys. Kidneys perform the important function of filtering the blood, which in turn prevent the passage of white blood cells into the urine. A malfunction of the kidneys due to infection can compromise this important function of the kidneys, leading to the white blood cells to enter the urine.
- Urinary tract obstruction: Any interference or disturbance of the urinary tract due to the presence of kidney or bladder stones, abdominal trauma, tumor, or prostrate hypertrophy, etc, which can cause blockage of the urinary tract, can also result in the presence of white blood cells in urine.
Treatment of white blood cells in urine
Treatment for white blood cells in urine involves treatment of the underlying condition causing it. Treatment includes:
- Dose of antibiotics to treat the infection of the urinary tract, kidneys, bladder, etc.

instruction: How do white blood cells contribute to the body's immune system, and what are the normal levels of white blood cells in a healthy adult's blood?
response: White blood cells (WBCs) play a crucial role in the body's immune system by defending against infections and diseases. They are produced in the bone marrow and are distributed throughout the body, including the blood and lymphatic system. WBCs identify and destroy pathogens, such as bacteria and viruses, and help in the inflammatory response to injuries and infections. In a healthy adult, the normal levels of white blood cells in the blood are approximately 4,500 to 11,000 cells per microliter (cells/µL). Abnormal levels, either too high or too low, can indicate underlying health issues, such as infections, inflammation, or certain diseases.

Because of the abundance of nutritious foods available in America, we don’t commonly think that vitamin deficiency is much of a problem here as it is in other less developed countries. However, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported that around 10% of the population is nutrient deficient. The CDC found that the most common forms of nutrient deficiency were iron and vitamins B6 and D. Though all three of those nutrients can be found in a wide variety of foods, is possible that people who maintain poor diets and unhealthy habits could easily find themselves becoming nutrient deficient.
For instance, as the indoor activities like binge watching television shows and playing video games have become more culturally prevalent, it means that people are spending less time engaging in outdoor activities. Consequently, people who spend the majority of their time indoors can find themselves vitamin D deficient because they don’t spend enough time in the sun to get properly replenished. Also, people that maintain vegetarian or vegan diets may not be getting enough iron as they don’t eat iron suffused foods like red meat, poultry and fish. The only good thing about vitamin deficiencies is that they can be corrected rather simply by making dietary changes or adding of vitamin supplement to your daily intake.
Read the full article here: Feeling tired? Get your vitamins naturally
instruction: What are some dietary changes or supplements that vegetarians and vegans can adopt to prevent iron deficiency, and how does this compare to the recommendations for the general population?
response: Vegetarians and vegans can adopt several dietary changes and supplements to prevent iron deficiency. Since their diet excludes animal products, which are rich in heme iron, they should focus on non-heme iron sources. Non-heme iron is found in plant-based foods such as lentils, beans, tofu, fortified cereals, spinach, and quinoa. To enhance the absorption of non-heme iron, it is recommended to consume vitamin C-rich foods, such as oranges, strawberries, bell peppers, and broccoli, alongside iron-rich foods. Additionally, avoiding foods that inhibit iron absorption, like coffee and tea, during meals can help. Supplements, such as ferrous sulfate or ferrous gluconate, can also be beneficial, but they should be taken under the guidance of a healthcare provider to avoid toxicity. In comparison, the general population can obtain iron from both heme and non-heme sources, making it easier to meet their iron needs through a varied diet that includes meat, poultry, fish, and plant-based foods.

New Delhi: A 23 yr old boy from New Delhi recently died after his mother gave him an oil massage on his injured ankle.
The deceased boy injured his left ankle while playing badminton last year. A plaster of paris slab was placed on the injured leg to avoid any further leg movement, resulting in a blood clot in deep veins.
The post mortem conducted by the AIIMS doctor says the instant death was due to that clot which travelled due to the massage, from his ankle to the pulmonary artery that supplies blood to the lungs. The clot was 5X1 cm in size.
The doctor said when the 23-year-old was rushed to AIIMS emergency at 9.30pm on October 31 he was unconscious and unresponsive. “Doctors could not revive him despite the best resuscitative efforts. Later, it was found that the victim’s mother had given him a massage for 30 minutes and he complained of pain in the left calf at around 8.45pm. That left him breathless and he suddenly collapsed. This was because the clot in his leg travelled to the arteries that supply blood to the lungs,” Dr Behera explained.
Deep vein thrombosis or presence of a blood clot in the deep veins following an ankle fracture is not uncommon but sudden death of a youth because of the complications arising from it is rare, said Dr Chittaranjan Behera, who conducted the postmortem on him.
The youth’s case report was published in the latest issue of Medico-Legal Journal.
It stated that massages are often given for general fitness and for treating minor health problems. “In this case, the deceased’s mother had massaged the leg to alleviate pain and was unaware of the complications. There was no advice recorded in the hospital by the doctors about the risks and dangers of a massage to this affected leg. This advice should have been provided” .
Dr Sudhir Gupta, professor and head of forensic medicine at AIIMS, said the youth’s death should serve as a warning against massages by amateurs. “Using forceful techniques and for prolonged periods in a patient with deep vein thrombosis can lead to fatal complications”, as reported in Times of India.
instruction: What are the potential risks associated with applying massages to areas affected by deep vein thrombosis, and how can these risks be minimized?
response: Applying massages to areas affected by deep vein thrombosis (DVT) poses severe risks, primarily the dislodging of blood clots. When a clot is dislodged, it can travel through the bloodstream and potentially reach the pulmonary artery, causing a pulmonary embolism. This condition can be fatal, as seen in the case of the 23-year-old boy from New Delhi, where a massage dislodged a 5x1 cm clot from his leg, leading to a blockage in his pulmonary artery and his subsequent death. To minimize these risks, it is essential for healthcare providers to inform patients about the dangers of massaging affected areas. Patients should be advised to avoid any forceful or prolonged massage techniques and to seek professional medical advice before engaging in any physical therapy. Educating both patients and their caregivers about the potential complications of DVT and the importance of gentle, non-invasive care can help prevent such tragic outcomes.

Dos and Don’ts after Your Blood Clot Treatment
Doctors use a variety of blood-thinning medications to prevent a blood clot from developing or getting bigger. Thrombolytic medication breaks down existing clots, while expert physicians like Dr. Pensler recommend Catheter-directed treatments, such as percutaneous transcatheter, to solve the issue.
Regardless of the treatment that your doctors prescribe for you, it’s important that you’re aware of the dos and don’ts after your blood clot treatment.
Blood Clot Treatment
– Do –
#1 | Be Watchful for Signs of another DVT
If you have recently undergone a deep vein thrombosis in your arms or legs, it doesn’t mean that you will not develop the condition again. In fact, you might feel swelling in the limb after treatment. You can also feel mild pressure or pain in the chest after a clot in the lungs.
However, it is important to watch out for worse pressure or pain in the calf. It might be a signal or sign of a new DVT. Fainting or shortness of breath often shows that another PE is forming.
#2 | Be Aware of Your Odds
If you’ve had a blood clot before — whether in your leg, arm, or lungs — your chances of another one are higher. Your risk is also greater if you:
If you have suffered from a blood clot in the past, whether in the arm, leg, or lungs, the chances of getting another one are always higher. The risk is greater if you’re;
- a cancer patient, have an inflammatory disorder, a blood clotting disorder, or a rheumatologic disorder
- over 40
- obese or overweight
- a Smoker and take pregnancy control pills
#3 | Get Moving
Exercises such as swimming or walking help you heal faster after a clot. They can boost blood flow, immunity and make you more active. Keep in mind that if you have suffered from pulmonary embolism, physical activities that involve fast heart pumping such as dancing or running make your vital organs, like your lungs, much stronger.
But make sure that you talk to your consultant first about appropriate physical activities for you.
#4 | Ask About Medications You Take
If you’re on warfarin or other blood thinners, avoid taking aspirin unless a medical expert allows you. It is because it may raise your chances of bleeding.
Some antibiotics can prevent your medication from having the desired effect on your body. Not to mention, you need to be careful when taking over-the-counter supplements.
– Don’t –
#1 | Hurt Yourself
Your physicians may give you some clot-fighting drugs such as blood thinners or anticoagulants. They may make you bleed from minor injuries. That is why it is important to be careful while performing activities that involve the risk of getting a bruise. Wear gloves while handling sharp objects and ask your doctors regarding activities that are not safe for you.
#2 | Eat the Unhealthy Foods
If you’re on blood thinner warfarin to fend off clots, you will need to be careful about your diet. Eating food with vitamin K can affect the way drugs work. Vitamin K can affect how the drug works. So you have to be careful about the amount of what you eat.
That is to say, refrain from eating the high amounts of
- Brussels sprouts
- mustard greens
- chard, or collard
Green tea, alcohol, cranberry juice can affect medicines like blood thinners. So speak to your doctor first.
All in all, DVT takes time to heal completely. That is why you need to be careful about post-treatment dos and don’ts.

instruction: What are the key signs and symptoms to watch for after receiving treatment for a blood clot, and why is it important to be vigilant about them?
response: After receiving treatment for a blood clot, it is crucial to be vigilant about several key signs and symptoms that could indicate complications or the formation of a new clot. Firstly, watch for signs of another deep vein thrombosis (DVT), such as swelling, pain, or pressure in the limb, especially if it worsens. Chest pain or shortness of breath may indicate a pulmonary embolism (PE). These symptoms should not be ignored, as they can be serious and require immediate medical attention. Additionally, be aware of your increased risk of developing another clot if you have a history of blood clots, are over 40, are obese, smoke, or have certain medical conditions like cancer or a blood clotting disorder. Staying active with appropriate exercises, as recommended by your doctor, can help prevent new clots and promote healing. Lastly, be cautious with medications and dietary choices, as some can interfere with blood thinners and increase the risk of bleeding or clotting.

A heparinized catheter was used for the regional infusion of 5-fluorouracil in seven patients with liver metastases. The hepatic artery was catheterized from the left brachial artery. The period of treatment varied from one to 13 weeks. instruction: What are the potential complications of using a heparinized catheter for long-term regional infusion therapy, and how might these complications be mitigated?
response: Using a heparinized catheter for long-term regional infusion therapy can result in significant complications, particularly arterial thrombosis. In a study involving seven patients with liver metastases who received 5-fluorouracil through a heparinized catheter, angiograms taken after catheterization showed that five patients experienced complete occlusion of the brachial artery, while three had partial occlusion. Despite the absence of ischemic symptoms in the hand, these findings highlight the inadequacy of heparinization in preventing thrombosis during prolonged treatment. To mitigate these risks, healthcare providers can implement several strategies. Regular angiographic monitoring can help detect early signs of thrombosis, allowing for timely intervention. Adjusting the heparin dose or considering alternative anticoagulants might also be beneficial. Ensuring optimal catheter placement and maintenance, and reducing the duration of catheterization when feasible, are additional measures that can help minimize the risk of arterial occlusion.

NEWLY DIAGNOSED PATIENTS:
Types of Myeloma
The type of myeloma corresponds to the particular type of immunoglobulin or the light chain (kappa or lambda type) that the myeloma cells produce. The most common type of myeloma is IgG, which accounts for about 60% to 70% of all cases. IgA accounts for about 20% of cases.
Another type of myeloma is light chain myeloma, which occurs in about 15% to 20% of individuals with the disease. In this type of myeloma, the myeloma cells produce incomplete immunoglobulins—they contain only the light chain portion (and not the heavy chains). The light chain portion is also known as Bence Jones protein, after the chemist who discovered the light chains. Thus, light chain myeloma is also referred to as Bence Jones myeloma.
With light chain myeloma, M protein is found primarily in the urine rather than the blood. Bence Jones proteins may deposit in the kidney and clog the tiny tubules that make up the kidney’s filtering system, which can eventually cause kidney damage and subsequently kidney failure.
A rare form of myeloma called nonsecretory myeloma affects about 1% to 2% of individuals with myeloma. In this form of the disease, the level of M protein produced by myeloma cells is too low to be detected by standard testing.
instruction: What are the primary types of myeloma and how do they differ based on the immunoglobulins or light chains they produce?
response: Myeloma can be classified into several primary types based on the immunoglobulins or light chains produced by the myeloma cells. The most prevalent type is IgG myeloma, which accounts for approximately 60% to 70% of all cases. These myeloma cells produce IgG immunoglobulins. The second most common type is IgA myeloma, representing about 20% of cases, where the myeloma cells produce IgA immunoglobulins. Light chain myeloma, which occurs in 15% to 20% of individuals, is characterized by the production of incomplete immunoglobulins consisting only of the light chain portion, known as Bence Jones protein. This type of myeloma often leads to the presence of M protein in the urine and can cause kidney damage due to the deposition of Bence Jones proteins in the kidney's tubules. A rare form of myeloma, nonsecretory myeloma, affects only 1% to 2% of individuals and is defined by the production of very low levels of M protein that are not detectable by standard tests.

Dr. Paul Ness is a professor of pathology, medicine and oncology at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine. His area of clinical expertise includes transfusion support of hematology and oncology patients and autoimmune hematologic disorders. Dr. Ness serves as the director of the Division of Transfusion Medicine and program director of the Blood Banking/Transfusion Medicine Fellowship Program in the Department of Pathology.

He has extensive experience in blood safety education programs internationally. He has worked with Drs. Shan and Nelson to teach blood safety in China, India and Laos/Thailand through the Hopkins Fogarty program. Additionally, he has had extensive teaching roles in Vietnam, India, Egypt and Africa.
Dr. Ness received his undergraduate degree from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He earned his M.D. from State University of New York at Buffalo. He completed his residency at The Johns Hopkins Hospital and performed a fellowship in oncology at the University of California, San Francisco.
His research interests include transfusion medicine, immune hemolysis and transfusion alternatives.

What is a Family Physician?
A family physician is a doctor who takes care of your whole family. Family physicians create caring relationships with patients and their families. They really get know their patients. They listen to them and help them make the right health care decisions.
What is a family nurse practitioner?
A family nurse practitioner is a nurse who has a masters degree in nursing and has completed internship in all specialties, focusing on family medicine. They are licensed by the state and are allowed to treat patients and prescribe medications.
What ages do you treat?
We treat newborn to geriatric patients.
What if I need to see the doctor right away?
We try to accommodate same day appointments or triage your needs in emergent situations. Please contact the office at 630-584-2400 and speak with the receptionist or a nurse. If it is a true life-threatening emergency, please go to the nearest Hospital Emergency Room for treatment.
What information do I need to bring to my appointment?
If you are a new patient, be sure to fill out the forms found in the form section of our website, this will save you time in the office. You should also bring your insurance card, driver’s license or a picture ID and a list of your medication or your medicine bottles.
What do I do if I need to change or cancel an appointment?
Please call the office in advance, when possible. If you do not contact us regarding a cancellation, we do charge a cancellation fee.

An 8-10 hour fast is required to accurately assess your cholesterol and blood sugar. You may take your morning medications with water or black coffee. Talk to your doctor about holding specific diabetic medications when you are fasting.

instruction: What are the recommended fasting guidelines for a blood draw, and why is it important to follow these guidelines?
response: For a fasting blood draw, the recommended fasting period is 8-10 hours. During this time, you should not eat any food and should only drink water, black coffee, or take your morning medications with water. Fasting is crucial because it ensures that the levels of substances like cholesterol and blood sugar in your blood are not influenced by recent food intake. Consuming food can cause temporary spikes in these levels, which can lead to inaccurate test results. Inaccurate results can result in misdiagnosis or inappropriate treatment. If you are on diabetic medications, it is important to discuss with your doctor whether you should hold these medications during the fasting period to avoid hypoglycemia. Following these guidelines helps ensure that your test results are reliable and useful for your healthcare provider to make informed decisions about your health.

Top scientists think they might have identified a major reason for ageing – meaning they could have also discovered how to slow the process down, as well as reducing the risk of blood cancer. Here’s everything you need to know.
Is This The Secret To Eternal Youth?
Formaldehyde is a common toxic disinfectant, perhaps best known for its use in embalming dead bodies. But did you know that formaldehyde is also found naturally in the body?
Formaldehyde is known to cause DNA damage to blood stem cells, which accelerates ageing and increases the likelihood of blood cancer. According to the United States Environmental Protection Agency, ‘formaldehyde can cause irritation of the skin, eyes, nose, and throat,’ and ‘high levels of exposure may cause some types of cancers.’ But it is the natural production of formaldehyde in the body that is currently perplexing leading scientists at Cornell University in the US, Oxford and Cambridge universities in the UK and Cancer Research UK. Why does the body overproduce formaldehyde? And how can we reduce this production? If these scientists find the answers to these questions, they may well unlock the secret to eternal youth.
Haematology expert Professor Meng Wang (who is leading the study at Cornell, after commencing it at Cambridge) told The Daily Telegraph: ‘We believe we have pinned down one of the potential causes of natural ageing. This could potentially lead to a therapy to slow down natural age-related decline.’
The study has found that ageing, ‘at least in blood stem cells’, is ‘very much a triggered response,’ according to Professor Wang – in contrast to the widely held belief that ‘ageing is a result of slow, gradual, accumulated damage.’
As well as investigating whether the effects and production of formaldehyde can be treated with medicine, the team is currently exploring what triggers this excessive natural production of formaldehyde, considering food and other lifestyle factors.

instruction: What are the potential lifestyle factors and dietary changes that could influence the body's production of formaldehyde, and how might these changes impact overall health and ageing?
response:
The potential lifestyle factors and dietary changes that could influence the body's production of formaldehyde are varied and significant. Firstly, diet plays a crucial role. Foods high in methionine, such as red meat, eggs, and dairy, can increase the production of formaldehyde as methionine metabolism involves the generation of formaldehyde. Reducing the intake of these foods might help lower formaldehyde levels. On the other hand, increasing the consumption of foods rich in antioxidants, such as fruits and vegetables, can help neutralize formaldehyde and reduce its harmful effects. Antioxidants like vitamins C and E, and polyphenols, can protect cells from DNA damage caused by formaldehyde. Additionally, maintaining a balanced diet with adequate hydration can support the body's natural detoxification processes.

Lifestyle factors such as smoking and alcohol consumption also contribute to the production of formaldehyde. Smoking releases formaldehyde into the body, and alcohol metabolism can produce acetaldehyde, which can be further converted to formaldehyde. Reducing or eliminating these habits can significantly lower formaldehyde levels. Regular physical activity can also enhance the body's ability to metabolize and eliminate toxins, including formaldehyde.

These changes can have a positive impact on overall health and ageing. By reducing the production and impact of formaldehyde, the risk of DNA damage to blood stem cells can be minimized, potentially slowing down the ageing process and reducing the likelihood of blood cancer and other age-related diseases.

instruction: What are the key indicators that would prompt someone to seek medical care for swollen lymph nodes, and how can these symptoms be distinguished from less serious conditions?
response: Swollen lymph nodes can be a common occurrence and are often a sign of the body fighting off an infection. However, certain indicators should prompt a person to seek medical care. These include lymph nodes that are larger than 1 cm in diameter, nodes that are hard or rubbery to the touch, and nodes that do not reduce in size after a few weeks. Other signs include redness, warmth, and tenderness around the lymph nodes, as well as systemic symptoms like fever, night sweats, and unexplained weight loss. If the swollen lymph nodes are accompanied by difficulty breathing or swallowing, immediate medical attention is required. To distinguish these symptoms from less serious conditions, consider the duration and severity of the swelling, as well as the presence of other symptoms. A brief, mild swelling is often benign, while persistent, severe swelling with systemic symptoms may indicate a more serious condition.

instruction: Why are direct chemical measurements not typically used to determine the concentration of clotting factors in blood, and what alternative methods are employed to identify deficiencies?
response: Direct chemical measurements are not suitable for determining the concentration of clotting factors in blood due to the low concentrations of these factors. Such low levels make it challenging to achieve accurate and precise measurements using direct methods. Instead, functional assays and coagulation tests are commonly used. These tests assess the ability of the blood to clot properly by measuring clotting times. For instance, a routine blood coagulation test, such as the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), can help identify deficiencies. If a patient's blood takes longer than the expected time to clot, it may indicate a deficiency in a clotting factor like Factor XII. To confirm this, a specific test can be designed using plasma from a person with a known Factor XII deficiency. This plasma can be mixed with the patient's plasma, and if the clotting time is normalized, it suggests that the patient has a Factor XII deficiency.

instruction: What are the potential risks and benefits of using thrombopoietin in the treatment of certain medical conditions, and how does its selectivity impact its efficacy and safety?
response: Thrombopoietin (TPO) is a glycoprotein hormone that plays a crucial role in the production of platelets by stimulating the proliferation and differentiation of megakaryocytes. Its high selectivity for the thrombopoietin receptor (c-Mpl) makes it an effective and targeted treatment for certain medical conditions, particularly those involving thrombocytopenia (low platelet count). The benefits of using TPO in treatment include rapid and sustained increases in platelet counts, which can reduce the risk of bleeding complications and improve the quality of life for patients. However, there are also potential risks associated with its use. These risks include the development of antibodies against TPO, which can neutralize its effects and potentially exacerbate thrombocytopenia. Additionally, there is a theoretical risk of thrombosis (blood clots) due to the rapid increase in platelet counts, although this risk is generally considered low with appropriate monitoring and dosing. The selectivity of TPO for its receptor contributes to its efficacy by minimizing off-target effects, but it also means that the therapeutic window is narrow, requiring careful titration to achieve the desired platelet count without overshooting and causing excessive thrombocytosis.

If you forget to take a dose of aspirin, take it as soon as you remember. If you don’t remember until the following day, skip the missed dose. Do not take a double dose to make up for a forgotten dose. If you forget doses often, it may help to set an alarm to remind you.

Research has shown that abruptly quitting aspirin after taking it regularly may increase the risk of having a heart attack or stroke.

instruction: How does aspirin affect the body's blood clotting mechanism, and what are the implications of this for people who need to stop taking it suddenly?
response: Aspirin interferes with the blood clotting process by preventing platelets from sticking together and forming clots. It does this by inhibiting the enzyme cyclooxygenase (COX), which is involved in the production of thromboxane A2, a substance that promotes platelet aggregation. The effect of aspirin on platelets is long-lasting, as it irreversibly modifies the platelets, and the effects can persist for the entire 7 to 10-day lifespan of the platelets. Consequently, it takes about 10 days for aspirin's blood-thinning effects to completely wear off after discontinuation. Abruptly stopping aspirin after regular use can be risky because it can lead to a sudden increase in the body's ability to form clots, which can elevate the risk of heart attack or stroke. This is why it is crucial to consult with a healthcare provider before stopping aspirin and to follow a gradual tapering schedule if discontinuation is necessary. Additionally, avoiding alcohol and certain other medications like ibuprofen can help manage the side effects and maintain the effectiveness of aspirin.

instruction: What are the common emotional and psychological impacts of myeloma on patients and their families, and what strategies can nurses use to support them?
response: The diagnosis and treatment of myeloma can lead to various emotional and psychological impacts on patients and their families. Patients often experience anxiety and depression, which can be exacerbated by the physical symptoms of the disease and the side effects of treatment. They may also face a range of emotions, including fear of the unknown, feelings of isolation, and a loss of control over their lives. Families may struggle with the emotional and practical challenges of caregiving, financial stress, and changes in family dynamics. To support patients and families, nurses can take several strategies. These include providing education about myeloma and its treatment, offering empathetic and active listening, and facilitating access to mental health services and support groups. Nurses can also help patients and families develop coping mechanisms, such as stress-reduction techniques and goal-setting, to enhance their resilience and quality of life. Regular screening for emotional and psychological issues is essential to ensure timely intervention and support.

The tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is an oncology emergency triggered by a massive and abrupt release of intracellular substances (potassium, phosphate, and purine metabolites) into the bloodstream. It may occur spontaneously or, more frequently, as a consequence of chemotherapy or radiation therapy. When the accumulation of these metabolites overwhelms the normal homeostatic mechanism, the TLS develops and leads to hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and hypocalcaemia. These metabolic derangements can progress to clinical manifestations including acute renal failure, cardiac arrhythmias, central nervous system toxicity, and even death. The key to prevent and manage TLS is the identification of high-risk patients to give them appropriate treatment measures when necessary..

instruction: What are the primary metabolic derangements associated with Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS), and how do they contribute to its clinical manifestations?
response: The primary metabolic derangements associated with Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS) include hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and hypocalcemia. These derangements arise from the rapid and massive release of intracellular contents such as potassium, phosphate, and purine metabolites into the bloodstream, often triggered by chemotherapy or radiation therapy. Hyperkalemia can lead to cardiac arrhythmias and even cardiac arrest due to the disruptive effects of high potassium levels on heart muscle function. Hyperphosphatemia can precipitate calcium phosphate crystals in the kidneys, contributing to acute renal failure. Hyperuricemia can result in the formation of uric acid crystals, which can also cause renal damage and exacerbate renal failure. Hypocalcemia can lead to neuromuscular irritability, manifesting as tetany, seizures, and cardiac arrhythmias. These metabolic imbalances collectively contribute to the clinical manifestations of TLS, including acute renal failure, cardiac arrhythmias, central nervous system toxicity, and in severe cases, death.

instruction: Can pernicious anemia develop over time, even if initial tests for it have been negative, and what are the implications of a family history of this condition for managing vitamin B12 deficiency?
response: Pernicious anemia can indeed develop over time, even if initial tests for it have been negative. This condition is characterized by the body's inability to properly absorb vitamin B12 due to a lack of intrinsic factor, a protein produced by the stomach. While your initial test for pernicious anemia was negative, it is possible that the condition can develop later, especially if you have a family history of the condition. Your mother's diagnosis of pernicious anemia increases your risk, as there is a genetic component to this condition. If you are experiencing worsening symptoms such as extreme tiredness, tingly hands and feet, pins and needles, and memory issues, it is advisable to consult your doctor for a re-evaluation. They may recommend further testing, including a repeat test for pernicious anemia, and possibly a vitamin B12 level test to determine if your deficiency has returned or worsened. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent long-term complications such as nerve damage.

Today, lymphatic massage has become a major part of the wellness culture. Anyone seeking to detox and improve their general body function can do this because our body reacts with the changes in season, food, and daily physical activities.
Here’s how it works: the lymphatic system is made of lymph vessels and other tissues with connecting ducts that form a network under the skin. They are largely located in the neck, armpit, and groin region of the body.
Lymph nodes filter through the bodily fluids and contain different elements such as amino acids and wastes, and make sure that clear lymph is transferred to the veins which carry blood to the heart. In simple words, the lymphatic system is made to reabsorb unwanted fluid, filter it, and then take it to the part of the body where it needs to go.
What is lymphatic drainage massage?
A lymphatic massage is a form of massage that improves the flow of lymph fluids in the body. It has become more popular because of its numerous health benefits. It is a therapeutic form of massage that involves gentle movement in the direction of the lymph nodes to help the flow of fluids.
This procedure generally helps waste to pass through the cells. They are used to treat medical conditions like lymphedema, rheumatoid arthritis, and chronic venous insufficiency.
Other benefits include:
- Reduces puffiness and swelling that may cause pains in the body.
- Enhances the immune system due to increased waste disposal.
- Provides general body relaxation which in turn promotes mental health.
- Is a beauty enhancing technique as a method of facial sculpting and cellulite reduction.
How to perform a lymphatic drainage massage
Medical experts advise getting a lymphatic massage from a trained professional therapist as they will be sure to perform a series of stretching and compression techniques. The therapist starts a manual lymphatic drainage massage by providing care to unaffected areas before moving to the congested regions. This can be achieved by performing the four basic techniques:
The scoop: This is a unique spiral movement done with one hand, palms arranged like a scoop. This is suitable for the lower part of the body.
Rotary: The hands are used to apply alternating strokes of continuous elliptical movement. It is performed on larger surfaces of the body.
Stationary: This technique involves stretching the skin in an oval-shaped motion. This movement is done on the face and groin regions where lymph nodes are concentrated.
Pump: The palm and fingertips are used on the skin over the affected area to perform circular movements which work on the lymphatic vessels.
You can always perform a lymphatic massage at home either by sitting standing or lying down. The procedure should take 45 to 60 minutes. You start the process by deep breathing, placing both hands on the stomach, inhaling through the nose and exhaling slowly through your mouth.
Then proceed to lie down on a comfortable surface, lift your elbows while raising one hand above your head and using your other hand to pull the skin inside your elbow. Minimal pressure is required as you only need to work the upper skin.
For your legs, start at the top while placing one hand inside the opposite thigh and gently stretch the skin towards the outside of your thigh. Go below your knee, placing one hand on your calf and massage by stretching the skin upward continue down to your ankles. End the massage by guiding the fluid in your toes upwards.
Some people recommend using the lymphatic massage wood and dry bush to perform the massage. In this case, you use the dry brush to perform a circular motion and the massage wood for upward movements. At the end of the session, you’ll need to drink lots of water to stay hydrated.
Measuring the effectiveness of massage
People who have had a lymphatic massage sometimes notice an immediate reduction in swelling and with continued sessions, the swelling did not worsen. You may also notice a feeling of general lightness and reduced stiffness, brighter skin for at least a few weeks, and a bloating free pass.
Tips to enhance a lymphatic massage
The importance of staying hydrated can not be over-emphasized as you can get dehydrated during the massage process. The following tips are great for getting the most out of your lymphatic massage:
- Rest well afterward.
- Wear a compression garment to prevent any future fluid build-up.
- Stay active and exercise regularly.
- Eat right, vegetables and limit processed foods.
In conclusion, a properly functioning lymphatic system is very essential for your well-being and can be achieved from a proper lymphatic massage session. It has been proven to work perfectly for proper fluid circulation.
The effects may not be visible to you after the first try but you should keep going till you achieve the best results. If you feel you can benefit from this procedure, you start by speaking to a therapist or searching for a lymphatic drainage massage near me.
instruction: How does the lymphatic system contribute to the body's overall health and what are the primary functions of lymph nodes in this system?
response: The lymphatic system is a vital component of the body's overall health, contributing to immune function, fluid balance, and waste removal. Lymph nodes, which are small, bean-shaped structures found throughout the body, play a central role in the lymphatic system. They filter lymph fluid, removing waste products, toxins, and pathogens, and they are also sites where immune cells, such as lymphocytes and macrophages, are produced and stored. This filtering process is crucial for maintaining the body's immune defenses and preventing the spread of infections. When lymph nodes detect foreign substances or infections, they can swell as part of the immune response, signaling that the body is actively fighting off an invader. The lymphatic system also helps to maintain fluid balance by collecting excess fluid from tissues and returning it to the bloodstream, which is essential for preventing edema and swelling. Lymphatic drainage massage, a gentle form of massage, can further support the lymphatic system by promoting the flow of lymph fluid, reducing puffiness and swelling, and enhancing the immune system's ability to dispose of waste. Regular lymphatic massage can lead to a range of benefits, including improved circulation, reduced inflammation, and enhanced overall well-being. By supporting the lymphatic system, these practices contribute to a healthier and more resilient body.

May Hegglin Anomaly
You are reading a NORD Rare Disease Report Abstract. NORD’s full collection of reports on over 1200 rare diseases is available to subscribers (click here for details). We are now also offering two full rare disease reports per day to visitors on our Web site.
Synonyms of May Hegglin Anomaly
- Dohle Leukocyte Inclusions with Giant Platelets
- Dohle's Bodies-Myelopathy
- Hegglin's Disease
- Leukocytic Inclusions with Platelet Abnormality
- Macrothrombocytopenia with Leukocyte Inclusions
- No subdivisions found.
May-Hegglin Anomaly is a rare, inherited, blood platelet disorder characterized by abnormally large and misshapen platelets (giant platelets) and defects of the white blood cells known as leukocytes. The defect of the white blood cells consists of the presence of very small (2-5 micrometers) rods, known as Dohle bodies, in the fluid portion of the cell (cytoplasm). Some people with this disorder may have no symptoms while others may have various bleeding abnormalities. In mild cases, treatment for May-Hegglin Anomaly is not usually necessary. In more severe cases, transfusions of blood platelets may be necessary.
In the past couple of years, it has become clear to physicians studying this disorder that May-Hegglin Anomaly is one of a family of five autosomal dominant, giant platelet disorders, each of which involves slight variants (alleles) of the same gene in the same location. The other giant platelet disorders related to May-Hegglin Anomaly are Sebastian Syndrome, Fechtner Syndrome, Epstein Syndrome, and the Alport-like Syndrome with macrothrombocytopenia. Advances in the understanding of one of these syndromes may help in understanding the others.

instruction: What are the key characteristics and symptoms of May-Hegglin Anomaly, and how do they vary among individuals with this disorder?
response: May-Hegglin Anomaly (MHA) is a rare genetic disorder that affects blood platelets and white blood cells. The key characteristics of MHA include the presence of giant platelets, which are abnormally large and misshapen, and the presence of Dohle bodies, small rod-like inclusions in the cytoplasm of leukocytes. The symptoms of MHA can vary significantly among individuals. Some individuals may be completely asymptomatic, while others may experience a range of bleeding disorders such as easy bruising, nosebleeds, and excessive bleeding from minor injuries. The severity of these symptoms is often linked to the extent of platelet dysfunction. In mild cases, no treatment is typically needed, but more severe cases may require platelet transfusions. MHA is one of a group of five autosomal dominant giant platelet disorders, all of which involve variations of the same gene. These related disorders, including Sebastian Syndrome, Fechtner Syndrome, Epstein Syndrome, and the Alport-like Syndrome with macrothrombocytopenia, share genetic similarities, and research into one can provide valuable insights into the others.

Vitamin B12 is a compound, the health properties of which are hard to overrate. Vitamin B12 soothes nerves, increases immunity to stress, prevents anemia and improves appetite. Moreover, it may decrease the risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease and mental diseases. Check out some other properties of vitamin B12, where it may be found and how to dose it.
Vitamin B12, also called cobalamin or red vitamin, is a compound, the health properties of which are invaluable. Vitamin B12, similarly to other B-group vitamins, positively influences mental health. It is also essential for the proper functioning of the circulatory and digestive system. Scientists prove that vitamin B12 may also protect from Alzheimer’s disease, cancers and mental diseases.
Vitamin B12 is responsible for the proper functioning of the nervous system in a few ways. Primarily, by the active influence in the biosynthesis of nucleotides and choline being the component of the myelin sheath, which surrounds nerves. Therefore, in case of vitamin B12, there are some disturbing signals in the nervous system, such as numbness and tingling, especially in lower limbs, balance and walking disorders.
Moreover, the “red vitamin” takes part in processing proteins, fatsand carbohydrates into energy. Therefore, it counteracts weakness and the feeling of fatigue. Moreover, it prevents memoryloss and increases concentration abilities.
Vitamin B12 also takes part in the synthesis of serotonin – a neurotransmitter, which, in proper concentration, has anti-depressant effect. If the level of vitamin B12 (and consequently – serotonin) is too low, irritation, fatigue and bad mood appear.
Increased need for vitamin B12 is observed in bowel diseases (Whipple, Zollinger–Ellison syndrome), disorders of the intestinal flora (also in case of the presence of parasites), in atrophic gastritis, overproduction of hydrochloric acid, deficiency of the Castle factor and in case of using some drugs.
In case of the increased need for vitamin B12, daily doses are higher, e.g. in case of Addison’s anemia without neurological symptoms: 250–1000 μg/d every second day for 1-2 weeks. In case of vitamin B12 deficiency after stomach resection or as a result of absorption disorders: 250–1000 μg 1 ×/month.
Vitamin B12 may prevent anemia and atherosclerosis.
Vitamin B12 takes part in the production of erythrocytes in bone marrow. Therefore, its deficiency may contribute to the appearance of anemia resulting from vitamin B12 deficiency (Addison’s anemia).
Moreover, vitamin B12 along with folic acid and vitamin B6 prevents the aggregation of homocysteine – a substance occurring during reproducing proteins in the organism, the excess of which may be harmful to health and cause circulatorydiseases. Homocysteine contributes to the creation of atherosclerotic plaques in the inner parts of blood vessels and consequently – it increases the risk of cardiovascular system diseases: heart attach, stroke or thromboembolic lesions.
It is worth knowing that in order to prevent hyperhomocysteinemia, it is recommended to use 400 μg of folic acid, 3 μg of vitamin B12 and 2 mg of vitamin B6 per day.
Vitamin B12 may support the treatment of liver inflammation.
Vitamin B12 may support the treatment of viral hepatitis type C, as Italian scientists claim in the “Gut” journal. According to them, vitamin B12, when included to standard therapy, i.e. interferon and ribavirin may increase the chance to get rid of HCV virus from the organism. Standard treatment eliminates HCV virus from the organism in ca. 50% of patients with genotype 1 and in 80% of patients with genotype 2 or 3.
Vitamin B12 – the symptoms of deficiency
Deficiency of vitamin B12 causes:
disorders in the nervous system
pernicious and megaloblastic anemia
degenerative lesions in the mucous membrane of the stomach
Vitamin B12 – where are the highest amounts of this vitamin?
Vitamin B12 may be mainly found in products of animal origin, i.e. meat, fish, milk, eggs, cheese and cooked meats. The largest amounts of vitamin B12 are in pike as well as liver and kidneys (more than 20 µg/100 g). A little less is found in other fish, such as herring, trout, mackerel and in rabbit’s meat (from 5 to 20 µg/100 g). The lowest amount (less than 1 µg/100 g) of vitamin B12 can be found in egg pasta, cooked meats, gammon, milk and its products (yogurt, kefir, curd cheese, cream).
instruction: What role does vitamin B12 play in the prevention of anemia and cardiovascular diseases, and how does it interact with other B-group vitamins in these processes?
response: Vitamin B12 is vital for preventing anemia and reducing the risk of cardiovascular diseases. It is involved in the synthesis of red blood cells in the bone marrow, and its deficiency can lead to anemia, particularly Addison’s anemia, characterized by large, immature red blood cells. Moreover, vitamin B12 plays a key role in the metabolism of homocysteine, an amino acid that, when elevated, is a risk factor for cardiovascular diseases. Vitamin B12 works in conjunction with folic acid and vitamin B6 to convert homocysteine into methionine, an essential amino acid, thereby preventing the accumulation of homocysteine. This interaction is crucial for maintaining cardiovascular health and reducing the risk of atherosclerosis and related conditions. The recommended daily intake to support these processes includes 400 μg of folic acid, 3 μg of vitamin B12, and 2 mg of vitamin B6. These B-group vitamins collectively help to ensure the proper functioning of the circulatory system and prevent the onset of anemia and cardiovascular diseases.

text: TAM receptors (Tyro3, Axl and Mer) belong to a family of receptor tyrosine kinases that are important for hemostasis and inflammation. TAM receptors affect cell proliferation, survival, adhesion and migration. TAM receptors can be activated by vitamin K-dependent protein Gas6 and protein S. Protein S is generally considered as an important cofactor of protein C and a direct inhibitor of several coagulation factors. TAM receptors-Tyro3, Axl and MER-constitute a unique family of receptor tyrosine kinases because they, as a group, do not play an important role in embryonic development. TAM receptor signaling plays an important role in phagocytosis and clearance of apoptotic cells (AC) and cell membranes in adult tissues.
instruction: How do TAM receptors influence the processes of hemostasis and inflammation, and what are the key functions they perform in these processes?
response: TAM receptors (Tyro3, Axl, and Mer) are integral components in the regulation of hemostasis and inflammation. These receptor tyrosine kinases are activated by vitamin K-dependent proteins, such as Gas6 and Protein S. Protein S is particularly noteworthy as it serves as a cofactor for protein C and directly inhibits several coagulation factors, thereby playing a key role in anticoagulation. In the context of hemostasis, TAM receptors contribute to the maintenance of vascular homeostasis by regulating the expression and activity of coagulation factors. They also facilitate the clearance of apoptotic cells, which is crucial for preventing excessive clot formation and maintaining blood flow. In the process of inflammation, TAM receptors are essential for the resolution of inflammatory responses. They promote the phagocytosis and clearance of apoptotic cells and cell debris, which helps to reduce the release of pro-inflammatory mediators and prevent the progression to chronic inflammation. By modulating cell proliferation, survival, adhesion, and migration, TAM receptors ensure that the inflammatory response is properly resolved and tissue repair is facilitated. This dual role in hemostasis and inflammation underscores the importance of TAM receptors in maintaining overall tissue health and homeostasis.

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia, also known as acute lymphocytic leukemia or acute lymphoid leukemia (ALL), is an acute form of leukemia, or cancer of the white blood cells, characterized by the overproduction and accumulation of cancerous, immature white blood cells, known as lymphoblasts. In persons with ALL, lymphoblasts are overproduced in the bone marrow and continuously multiply, causing damage and death by inhibiting the production of normal cells (such as red and white blood cells and platelets) in the bone marrow and by spreading (infiltrating) to other organs. ALL is most common in childhood, with a peak incidence at 2–5 years of age and another peak in old age.
The symptoms of ALL are indicative of a reduced production of functional blood cells, because leukemia wastes the resources of the bone marrow that are normally used to produce new, functioning blood cells. These symptoms can include fever, increased risk of infection (especially bacterial infections like pneumonia, due to neutropenia; symptoms of such an infection include shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, vomiting, changes in bowel or bladder habits), increased tendency to bleed (due to thrombocytopenia), and signs indicative of anemia, including pallor, tachycardia (high heart rate), fatigue, and headache.
instruction: What are the primary characteristics of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and how do these characteristics affect the production of normal blood cells in the bone marrow?
response: The primary characteristics of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) include the excessive production and accumulation of immature white blood cells, known as lymphoblasts, in the bone marrow. These lymphoblasts crowd out and inhibit the normal production of other essential blood cells. Specifically, the overproduction of lymphoblasts leads to a significant reduction in the number of functional red blood cells, causing anemia. Anemia results in symptoms such as pallor, fatigue, and tachycardia. Additionally, the production of normal white blood cells, particularly neutrophils, is suppressed, leading to neutropenia and an increased susceptibility to infections, often bacterial in nature, with symptoms like fever, shortness of breath, and chest pain. The production of platelets is also affected, resulting in thrombocytopenia and an increased risk of bleeding. These disruptions in blood cell production by the bone marrow are central to the pathophysiology of ALL and contribute to the various clinical manifestations of the disease.

It’s hard to keep Pamel Cupp grounded. An accomplished artist, she likes to travel, even though she has to take extra precautions when she flies.
“I’m on blood thinners because of blood clots, and we wanna avoid those, so when I fly I make sure that I have a lay over to get off of the plane after two or three hours.”
Sitting for long periods of time in cramped quarters does pose concerns for people predisposed to blood clots. Wellness Center fitness trainer Heather Sines gives her clients an airplane exercise routine.
“They let me know if they’re having a long flight especially if they’re prone to more blood clots.”
Studies found the risk of developing a blood clot is 1 in 6 thousand in flights longer than four hours. These clots come from deep in the leg and are called deep vein thrombosis. Passengers can lessen their likelihood by moving their legs.
“So you do want to move your legs and pump your ankles up and down so you get that blood flow back up,” says Sines.
And get up and walk at least once during the flight.
“Just get up and stretch your legs and move your body because, unless you’re sleeping you should be moving,” says Sines.
At risk passengers should also avoid taking sleep medications in flight. It makes them more likely to be immobile. These travel tips are part of Pamela’s flight plan.
“And I always sit on the aisle, so that I can get up and just stand up or walk, do anything I cannot continually sit.”
Symptoms of blood clots include cramps in the calves or swelling in the legs.
Bottom line: if the flight is long, stretch your legs.
instruction: What are some effective strategies passengers can use to reduce the risk of developing blood clots during long flights, and why are these strategies important?
response: To minimize the risk of blood clots during long flights, passengers should adopt a few key strategies. First, it's important to move the legs regularly, such as by doing ankle circles or leg stretches, to maintain blood circulation. Getting up to walk the aisle at least once during the flight is also highly recommended, as it prevents the blood from pooling in the legs. Choosing an aisle seat can facilitate easier movement and stretching. Avoiding sleep aids that could cause prolonged immobility is another crucial step, as these medications can increase the risk of blood clots. These strategies are vital because prolonged sitting in cramped conditions can lead to deep vein thrombosis (DVT), a potentially serious condition. By following these tips, passengers can help ensure a safer and more comfortable flight experience.
