ATGAM Sterile Solution contains lymphocyte immune globulin, anti-thymocyte globulin [equine]. It is the purified, concentrated, and sterile gamma globulin, primarily monomeric IgG, from hyperimmune serum of horses immunized with human thymus lymphocytes. ATGAM is a transparent to slightly opalescent aqueous protein solution. It may appear colorless to faintly pink or brown and is nearly odorless. It may develop a slight granular or flaky deposit during storage. (For information about in-line filters, see Infusion Instructions in the DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION SECTION.)
Before release for clinical use, each lot of ATGAM is tested to assure its ability to inhibit rosette formation between human peripheral lymphocytes and sheep red blood cells in vitro. In each lot, antibody activity against human red blood cells and platelets is also measured and determined to be within acceptable limits. Only lots that test negative for antihuman serum protein antibody, antiglomerular basement membrane antibody and pyrogens are released.
Each milliliter of ATGAM contains 50 mg of horse gamma globulin stabilized in 0.3
molar glycine to a pH of approximately 6.8.
INDICATIONS AND USAGE
Renal TransplantationATGAM Sterile Solution is indicated for the management of allograft rejection in renal transplant patients. When administered with conventional therapy at the time of rejection, it increases the frequency of resolution of the acute rejection episode. The drug has also been administered as an adjunct to other immunosuppressive therapy to delay the onset of the first rejection episode. Data accumulated to date have not consistently demonstrated improvement in functional graft survival associated with therapy to delay the onset of the first rejection episode.
ATGAM is indicated for the treatment of moderate to severe aplastic anemia in patients who are unsuitable for bone marrow transplantation.
When administered with a regimen of supportive care, ATGAM may induce partial or complete hematologic remission. In a controlled trial, patients receiving ATGAM showed a statistically significantly higher improvement rate compared with standard supportive care at 3 months. Improvement was defined in terms of sustained increase in peripheral blood counts and reduced transfusion needs.
Clinical trials conducted at two centers evaluated the 1-year survival rate for patients with severe and moderate to severe aplastic anemia. Seventy-four of the 83 patients enrolled were evaluable based on response to treatment. The treatment groups studied consisted of 1) ATGAM and supportive care, 2) ATGAM administered following 3 months of supportive care alone, 3) ATGAM, mismatched marrow infusion, androgens, and supportive care, or 4) ATGAM, androgens, and supportive care. There were no statistically significant differences between the treatment groups. The 1-year survival rate for the pooled treatment groups was 69#. These survival results can be compared with a historical survival rate of about 25# for patients receiving standard supportive care alone.
The usefulness of ATGAM has not been demonstrated in patients with aplastic anemia who are suitable candidates for bone marrow transplantation or in patients with aplastic anemia secondary to neoplastic disease, storage disease, myelofibrosis, Fanconis syndrome, or in patients known to have been exposed to myelotoxic agents or radiation.
To date, safety and efficacy have not been established in circumstances other than renal transplantation and aplastic anemia.
Do not administer ATGAM Sterile Solution to a patient who has had a severe systemic reaction during prior administration of ATGAM or any other equine gamma globulin preparation.
Because ATGAM Sterile Solution is an immunosuppressive agent ordinarily given with corticosteroids and antimetabolites, watch patients carefully for signs of leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, or concurrent infection. Several studies have suggested an increase in the incidence of cytomegalovirus infection in patients receiving ATGAM(1). In one study it has been found that it may be possible to reduce this risk by decreasing the dosage of other immunosuppressive agents administered concomitantly with ATGAM. If infection occurs, institute appropriate adjunctive therapy promptly. On the basis of the clinical circumstances, a physician should decide whether or not therapy with ATGAM will continue.
The safety and effectiveness of ATGAM have been demonstrated only in renal transplant patients who received concomitant immunosuppressive therapy and in patients with aplastic anemia.
Dilution of ATGAM in dextrose injection, USP, is not recommended, as low salt concentrations may result in precipitation. The use of highly acidic infusion solutions is also not recommended because of possible physical instability over time.
When the dose of corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants is being reduced, some previously masked reactions to ATGAM may appear. Under these circumstances, observe patients especially carefully during therapy with ATGAM. ATGAM
instruction: What are the key indications for the use of ATGAM Sterile Solution, and how does it contribute to the management of these conditions?
response: ATGAM Sterile Solution, containing lymphocyte immune globulin (anti-thymocyte globulin [equine]), is primarily indicated for two key conditions: the management of allograft rejection in renal transplant patients and the treatment of moderate to severe aplastic anemia in patients unsuitable for bone marrow transplantation. In renal transplantation, ATGAM is used to increase the frequency of resolution of acute rejection episodes when administered with conventional therapy. It can also be used as an adjunct to other immunosuppressive therapies to delay the onset of the first rejection episode, although data on long-term graft survival are inconclusive. For aplastic anemia, ATGAM, when administered with supportive care, can induce partial or complete hematologic remission, as evidenced by a statistically significant improvement in peripheral blood counts and reduced transfusion needs. Clinical trials have shown a 1-year survival rate of 69% for patients treated with ATGAM, compared to a historical survival rate of about 25% with standard supportive care alone. ATGAM's immunosuppressive properties help in managing these conditions by suppressing the immune system's attack on the transplanted organ or the patient's own bone marrow, thereby improving outcomes.

instruction: What are the potential clinical applications of the HEMASCREEN test, and how might it impact the diagnosis and management of blood-related conditions?
response: The HEMASCREEN test, which employs E.M.® Technology, offers significant potential in clinical settings, particularly in the areas of transfusion medicine and prenatal care. By using magnetized red blood cells and an Indirect Antiglobulin Test (IAT), the HEMASCREEN test can efficiently detect IgG antibodies that are fixed on red blood cells. This capability is essential for pre-transfusion testing, as it helps identify antibodies in the patient’s plasma or serum that could react with donor blood, leading to hemolytic transfusion reactions. The test’s accuracy and reliability can improve the safety of blood transfusions, ensuring that only compatible blood products are used. In the prenatal context, the HEMASCREEN test can screen for maternal antibodies that may cause hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN). Early detection of these antibodies allows for timely intervention, such as the administration of intravenous immunoglobulin or close monitoring of the pregnancy. Furthermore, the test can be used in the diagnosis and management of autoimmune hemolytic anemias, where the presence of autoantibodies can lead to the destruction of red blood cells. By providing rapid and accurate results, the HEMASCREEN test can facilitate timely and effective treatment, ultimately improving patient outcomes and reducing the risk of complications.

Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) is a low-grade lymphoproliferative disorder characterized by the presence of an immunoglobulin M monoclonal protein in the blood and monoclonal small lymphocytes and lymphoplasmacytoid cells in the marrow. The disease is uncommon and there is a lack of clear diagnostic criteria. WM is treatable but not curable and long-term survival is possible. Therefore, the treating physician needs to carefully balance the risks and benefits of treatment. Treatments are aimed at relieving symptoms resulting from marrow infiltration and the hyperviscosity syndrome. Therapies available for initiation of treatment include alkylating agents, purine nucleoside analogs, and rituximab. Chlorambucil has been the mainstay of treatment for many years and remains useful, especially in older patients. Rituximab has become an important new therapy for this disease because of its positive treatment responses, acceptable toxicity, and lack of therapy-associated myelosuppression and myelodyspLasia. Currently, rituximab is being combined with chemotherapy. Other options of treatment include interferon and corticosteroids. Emerging therapies include stem cell transplantation (autologous; and allogeneic) for younger patients. Currently, there are few comparative data on which to state an absolute opinion concerning the best available treatment for patients with WM.

instruction: What are the key considerations for a physician when deciding on the treatment for a patient with Waldenström macroglobulinemia, and how do these considerations impact the choice of therapy?
response: In treating a patient with Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM), a physician must carefully evaluate several key considerations to guide the choice of therapy. WM is a treatable but not curable condition, characterized by the presence of an immunoglobulin M monoclonal protein and specific cellular changes in the bone marrow. The primary considerations include the patient's age, overall health, and the severity of symptoms such as marrow infiltration and hyperviscosity syndrome. For older patients, chlorambucil has been a traditional and effective choice due to its manageable side effects and lower risk of myelosuppression and myelodysplasia. For younger patients, rituximab has emerged as a crucial treatment due to its high efficacy and low toxicity, often used in combination with chemotherapy to enhance outcomes. Other treatment options include interferon and corticosteroids, which may be considered based on the patient's specific condition. Emerging therapies, such as autologous and allogeneic stem cell transplantation, are being explored for younger patients who can tolerate more intensive treatments. Given the lack of clear diagnostic criteria and limited comparative data, the physician must individualize the treatment plan, balancing the potential benefits and risks to optimize the patient's quality of life and long-term survival.

instruction: What are the common treatments and medications available for conditions like spleen enlargement and ascites, and how effective are they in managing these issues?
response:
Spleen enlargement and ascites are complex conditions that require a multifaceted approach to treatment. For spleen enlargement, the primary focus is on addressing the underlying cause. If the enlargement is due to an infection, antibiotics or antiviral medications can be effective. For conditions like liver disease or hematologic disorders, treatments might include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or immunosuppressive drugs. In severe cases, a splenectomy might be necessary, although this is typically reserved for situations where other treatments have failed.

Ascites, the accumulation of fluid in the abdominal cavity, is often managed with diuretics such as spironolactone and furosemide. These medications help reduce fluid retention by increasing urine output. In cases where diuretics are not sufficient, paracentesis, a procedure to remove excess fluid, may be performed. Lifestyle changes, such as a low-sodium diet, are also crucial in managing ascites.

The effectiveness of these treatments can vary. Diuretics are generally effective for managing ascites, but they may need to be adjusted over time. For spleen enlargement, the success of treatment depends on the underlying cause and the severity of the condition. It's important for your grandma to have regular follow-ups with her healthcare provider to monitor her condition and adjust the treatment plan as needed.

The most common containers for blood samples are blood vacuum tubes. The blood vacuum tubes differ from other tubes because of the shape of the lid. The lid is not screwed like an ordinary lid, instead it is held tight by a rubber sealing. Normally the lid is never loosened because of the vacuum inside the tube that draws exactly the blood the tube needs when you penetrate the center of the lid with a needle. Considering the often long distance with many bumps on the way from taking the blood sample to the analyzing machine, these tubes are more secure and offer optimal control.
Blood vacuum tubes are often transported by the staff or sent through a traditional pneumatic transportation system. An alternative method of transporting blood tubes, is via the Tempus600 system designed for individual transportation of small clinical samples. The samples are sent directly from the ward to the laboratory, exactly as they are - no risk of mis-delivery, loss of samples or contamination of the system because of loose lids. Both vacuum tubes and tubes with screw lid can be used in the Tempus600 system.
instruction: How does the design of blood vacuum tubes ensure the secure transport of blood samples over long distances with many bumps?
response: The design of blood vacuum tubes is optimized to ensure the secure transport of blood samples, especially over long distances with many bumps. The primary feature is the rubber sealing lid, which provides a tight and airtight seal, preventing any leakage or contamination. Unlike screw lids, the rubber sealing lid is less likely to loosen or come off during transport. Additionally, the vacuum inside the tube is critical. It draws the exact amount of blood needed when the needle pierces the lid, ensuring a precise and consistent sample. The vacuum also helps maintain the sample's stability by minimizing movement and exposure to external conditions. These design elements, combined with the use of systems like the Tempus600, which is designed for individual and direct transportation of small clinical samples, further enhance the security and integrity of the blood samples during transport.

An Examination of Non-Hodgkins Lymphoma
Cancer is a life-threatening disease that is prevalent in our time. One of which is known as non-Hodgkins lymphoma or NHL. It is a cancer that affects the lymphatic system and develops in the lymphoid tissue, which contain lymphocytes that are found all over the body.
Tlymphocytes on the other hand destroy cancer cells as well as viruses, fungi, and bacteria. They produce a chemical called cytokinesis which attracts white blood cells to help destroy harmful microorganisms. Research posted at www.cancer.org by the Cancer Society claims that non-Hodgkins lymphoma develop from B lymphocytes 85% of the time, and the remaining 15% from T lymphocytes.
Since lymphoid tissue is found in all the areas of the body, non-Hodgkins lymphoma can originate almost anywhere in the body. It commonly develops on the lymph nodes, spleen, digestive tract, and tonsils. Diagnosis can be difficult because there are at least thirty different types of lymphoma. It is a fast growing type of cancer that can spread quickly if not diagnosed immediately. Treatment depends on which type of non-Hodgkins lymphoma is present, the rate that it is growing, or if it has infected surrounding tissues.
Since every case of non-Hodgkins lymphoma is unique, treatment is often difficult and complicated. Treatment used on one case may not necessarily work on another. It is safer to obtain a second opinion before any treatment should begin. This is important especially if there are questions or doubts about the recommendations being made.
Before undergoing any major treatment or surgery consider getting a second opinion as it may spell the difference between death and a full recovery. Visit the American Cancer Society at www.cancer.org, the National Caner Institute at www.cancer.gov, and www.lymphomafocus.org, for more information on non-Hodgkins lymphoma. These websites offer critical information on signs and symptoms, early diagnosis, and various treatments and interventions.

instruction: How does the diversity of lymphoid tissue locations in the body impact the diagnosis and treatment of non-Hodgkins lymphoma?
response: The widespread distribution of lymphoid tissue in the body has a profound impact on the diagnosis and treatment of non-Hodgkins lymphoma (NHL). Because lymphocytes, which are the primary cells affected by NHL, are found in multiple organs and tissues, the cancer can originate in various locations such as the lymph nodes, spleen, digestive tract, and tonsils. This diversity makes it challenging to diagnose NHL, as there are numerous subtypes, each with distinct clinical and biological features. The rapid growth of NHL further complicates matters, necessitating timely and accurate diagnosis to prevent the cancer from spreading. Treatment strategies must be tailored to the specific type of NHL, its growth rate, and the extent of its spread. Due to the unique nature of each case, obtaining a second opinion is crucial to ensure the most effective and appropriate treatment plan. Patients and their families can find comprehensive information and support through reputable sources like the American Cancer Society, National Cancer Institute, and Lymphoma Focus.

I first started running about nine years ago, to lose weight after having my second child. It began with jogs around my neighborhood. Over time I increased my mileage. Before I knew it, I was running full 26.2-mile marathons. I've finished 18 so far, including eight straight years in the Los Angeles Marathon.
Last fall, I received a diagnosis of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. Since then, I've been fighting off the disease with help from the City of Hope medical team. It's a wonderful place, and I feel lucky to be in their care.
My doctor at City of Hope tells me that those years of running have helped me enormously in handling the aggressive treatment needed to battle lymphoma. And I continued, completing shorter distances on weekends between sessions of chemotherapy.
I had signed up for February's Pasadena Marathon before my diagnosis. Running is my sanity, and it's important to me that I keep racing. My doctor cautioned me against tackling the entire 26.2 miles. So, with her blessing, I arranged to run the half-marathon instead. It's hard for me to describe the exhilaration I felt after completing the course.
I'm looking forward to the chance to support City of Hope by joining in the All-Star Game Charity 5k & Fun Run this July. I want to be an inspiration, a ray of hope for someone else battling cancer.
The way I see it, marathons are about enduring hardships, and life is a marathon. I'm not ready to be done with mine.
Stand Up To Cancer
Why am I running? Because when I see a "bad guy" that has hurt my friends and family, I want to chase that villain down. I'm running because cancer isn't going to slow down on its own. Cancer doesn't take vacations or go to the movies. Cancer doesn't care that you are getting married next week, or that you just landed a promotion at work, or that you were accepted into your top choice for college. Cancer doesn't care that your wife just had a baby. Hell, it doesn't even care if you're human...I'm running for my eight-pound dog who, believe it or not, is a breast cancer survivor. I'm running for my 90 year old grandmother who is also a breast cancer survivor and still bakes the best lemon cake in the world. I'm running in support of the SU2C researchers who, in their own way, are running as fast as they can in their labs to find treatments that work. I'm running because we can't sit on the sidelines and wait for someone else to run for us, because we can't let another minute go by without doing something, anything. I consider myself very lucky; cancer hasn't claimed the life of a best friend or close family member of mine...yet. And I know all too well that it is a game of numbers. If I don't run now to help fight cancer, then one day I will lose someone I love. It could even be me.
Jonathan W. Simons, MD
President and CEO
Prostate Cancer Foundation
My entire career as a doctor and scientist has been dedicated to caring for patients and conducting research to end prostate cancer as a cause of suffering and death. Prostate cancer strikes one out of every 6 American men and is an enormous American health crisis.
Just down the hall, one of my closest teammates here at the Prostate Cancer Foundation, Dan Zenka, recently had a routine PSA test and biopsy that led him to a cancer diagnosis and then surgery to remove his prostate. With his early diagnosis and treatment, I believe Dan will be with us and his family for many, many years to come. Each year, 27,000 U.S. men are not as fortunate.
As vice president of communications for PCF, Dan has chosen not to be silent, but to share his story with the millions of men we serve through his recently launched cancer blog: www.mynewyorkminute.org.
I am running for Dan, his wonderful family, and the thousands of patients I have taken care of over the years. I run because Dan is so courageous to talk to others about his story. Even at my slow, creaky, lumbering, jogging pace, I will remind myself with every stride, that we are going to finish this race - we will see the day when prostate cancer is no longer a problem for families, their fathers, grandfathers, brothers and sons. On July 11th, with the support of the MLB All-Star 5K Run in Anaheim, PCF's team - Zenka's Zoomers, will be sprinting faster to find a cure.
It all started five years ago after a great night celebrating New Year's with family. The under wire in my bra had left kind of a mark under my left breast, and so when I was checking it I noticed a lump. I called my doctor and saw him right away. He immediately referred me to have a mammogram and ultrasound. This was followed up by a biopsy.
Never in a million years did I imagine that the doctor would call me a few days later to tell me that I had triple negative breast cancer. I started chemotherapy - hard core chemotherapy that was scheduled every two weeks to shrink the tumors before surgery was even beneficial. That's right. You heard it: tumors, plural. There were three infiltrating tumors growing in my breast. Surgery was followed by radiation. I was 33 years old.
I am a proud breast cancer survivor celebrating my 5 year anniversary this summer, and I Race because it is my passion. I Race so that everyone knows that early detection is important - it's the key to surviving and thriving. My three daughters, ages 15, 11 and 7, understand the significance of all of this. I Race, so that by the time they grow up, there is a cure. My family and friends race with me. It's not just the grandmas and great aunts who are getting breast cancer. Young women are affected, too. I was one of them.
Why I am running first of all to support cancer charities. I started running in 2008 trying to overcome a weight problem. I weighed 200 lbs. and when I first started I could only walk for 5 minutes I can now run 4 miles and I enjoy running so much that if I do not go for my morning run I just do not feel right. Iwould be honored to be a part of the 2010 Major League Baseball All-Star Game Charity 5k & 1 Mile Fun Run. Because I do run for fun and fitness.
Our son Nathan was diagnosed with Stage IV Testicular cancer at the age of 18 in May 2008. He has been fighting this disease for two years. He has undergone five surgeries three different types of chemotherapy treatments and radiation. He is such a courageous young man who never complains and inspires me to be the best person I can be. He keeps on living his life to the fullest. He is my hero. I wish for a cure for all cancers in the world so people don't have to die from this horrible disease.
I have formed a team in honor of my beautiful daughter Victoria Vargas. Victoria passed away on March 1 2010. While cancer did not contribute to her passing I have resolved to honoring her by contributing to worthy causes in her name. For the 2010 All-Star Game Charity 5K I have formed "Victoria's All-Stars" which is a team comprised of friends and family that will walk to raise money for this worthy cause. Victoria's legacy will be honored by people coming together in her name to raise money to fight this disease which impacts so many.
I run for my husband other cancer fighters survivors and all the families that have a loved one battling cancer. I run to be one step closer to defeating cancer so that no one has to go through the pain and hardship this disease can cause. I run to "pay it forward" to all the people who have supported my family during a trying time of our lives. I run to make a difference...
instruction: How can physical activities like running contribute to both physical and mental resilience in the face of serious health challenges, such as cancer?
response: Engaging in physical activities such as running can profoundly impact both physical and mental resilience when facing serious health challenges like cancer. Physically, running enhances cardiovascular health, boosts the immune system, and improves overall physical strength. This is crucial for individuals undergoing cancer treatment, which can be physically taxing. The author of the text shares that their years of running have significantly aided in managing the aggressive treatment for non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. Running can also help mitigate common side effects of cancer treatments, such as fatigue and muscle weakness. Mentally, running serves as a powerful stress reliever and a means to maintain a sense of normalcy and control. The author describes running as their 'sanity' and emphasizes the psychological benefits of continuing to race, even while undergoing chemotherapy. Completing races, like the half-marathon the author ran, can provide a sense of accomplishment and boost self-esteem, which are vital for mental well-being. Running can thus act as a dual support system, enhancing both physical and mental resilience in the face of serious health challenges.

NEW BRUNSWICK, N.J. – A Johnson & Johnson drug has won approval for treating the blood cancer multiple myeloma in patients who’ve failed three prior therapies and have few options.
Darzalex (DAR’-zah-lecks) is the first biologic drug and first monoclonal antibody — a genetically engineered drug designed to target diseased tissue and spare healthy cells nearby — approved for multiple myeloma. Darzalex helps certain immune system cells attack cancer cells by binding to a protein on their surface.
The Food and Drug Administration granted accelerated approval based on two small studies that showed Darzalex reduced or eliminated tumors in about one-third of patients for about seven months, on average. J&J’s Janssen biologic drug unit is conducting further testing.
For patients who respond to Darzalex, a year’s treatment costs $134,550, excluding discounts negotiated by payers.
instruction: How might the high cost of Darzalex treatment impact patient access and the broader healthcare system, and what measures can be taken to ensure affordability and availability for those in need?
response: The high cost of Darzalex, at $134,550 per year, poses significant challenges for patient access and the broader healthcare system. For patients, the financial burden can be overwhelming, leading to delayed treatment or non-adherence, which can exacerbate the progression of multiple myeloma. For the healthcare system, the high cost can lead to increased insurance premiums and strain on public healthcare programs, such as Medicare and Medicaid, which may struggle to cover the expenses. To mitigate these issues, several strategies can be implemented. First, payers and healthcare providers can negotiate with Johnson & Johnson to secure discounts and rebates. Second, policies that promote transparency in drug pricing and regulate price increases can be enacted. Third, the development and approval of biosimilars can provide more affordable alternatives. Finally, patient assistance programs and subsidies can be established to help those who are most in need, ensuring that cost does not become a barrier to accessing this potentially life-saving treatment.

instruction: What are the general guidelines for monitoring and retesting blood parameters when initial results show minor deviations from the normal range, and how does a healthcare provider determine the necessity for follow-up tests?
response:
When initial blood parameters show minor deviations from the normal range, healthcare providers follow specific guidelines to determine the necessity for follow-up tests and monitoring: 
1. **Clinical Correlation**: The provider will correlate the lab results with the patient's clinical history, symptoms, and any recent health events. For instance, if the patient has been recently ill or under stress, minor deviations may be transient and not indicative of a serious condition. 
2. **Repeat Testing**: Minor deviations often prompt a repeat of the tests within a defined period, typically 4-6 weeks, to assess if the changes are persistent or resolve on their own. In your case, the slightly elevated platelet count (431) and slightly low MPV (7.1) could be due to a recent viral infection, as suggested by the slightly elevated lymphocyte count (45.6). 
3. **Comprehensive Review**: The provider will review all relevant parameters together, as some values can influence each other. For example, platelet count and MPV are interconnected, and both can be affected by viral infections or other transient conditions. 
4. **Risk Assessment**: The provider will assess the overall risk based on the patient's medical history and the nature of the deviations. If the deviations are minor and there are no concerning symptoms, the risk is generally low. 
5. **Patient Education**: Clear communication with the patient is essential to ensure they understand the results and the rationale for follow-up testing. Your provider may recommend repeating the tests in a month to monitor for any changes, but there is no immediate cause for concern given the minor deviations observed.

Also found in: Dictionary, Thesaurus, Medical.
an increase in the total quantity of blood in the human body. A distinction is made between polycythemia vera, in which the increase in erythrocytes, up to 8–10 million in 1cu mm of blood, is greater than the increase in the total volume of blood plasma, and hypervolemia, which is characterized chiefly by an increase in the volume of plasma. The latter may be of cardiac origin or may be due to water retention in the vascular system after copious drinking. The normal ratio of the volume of blood cells to that of plasma is 45:55.
an increase in the number of erythrocytes in the blood. Spurious, or relative, polycythemia results from a reduction in the volume of blood plasma and is caused by loss of fluid, as from heavy perspiration or from diarrhea. Secondary polycythemia is characterized by an absolute increase in the number of erythrocytes, as with oxygen deficiency in the mountains, heart disease, or pulmonary emphysema. Secondary polycythemia accompanied by an increase in the volume of blood plasma is called polycythemia vera, or erythremia.
instruction: What are the primary differences between polycythemia vera and hypervolemia, and how do these conditions affect the ratio of blood cells to plasma in the human body?
response:
Polycythemia vera and hypervolemia are two distinct conditions that affect the ratio of blood cells to plasma differently. Polycythemia vera is a myeloproliferative disorder characterized by an absolute increase in the number of red blood cells (erythrocytes), often reaching up to 8–10 million per cubic millimeter of blood. This increase in erythrocytes is greater than the increase in the volume of blood plasma, leading to a higher ratio of blood cells to plasma. The normal ratio of blood cells to plasma is typically 45:55, but in polycythemia vera, this ratio is significantly altered, resulting in a more viscous blood that can lead to various clinical complications such as thrombosis.

Hypervolemia, on the other hand, is primarily characterized by an increase in the volume of blood plasma. This can occur due to cardiac issues or water retention in the vascular system after excessive fluid intake. In hypervolemia, the total blood volume increases, but the number of blood cells remains relatively unchanged. As a result, the ratio of blood cells to plasma is diluted, leading to a lower ratio compared to the normal 45:55. This condition can affect blood viscosity and hemodynamics, potentially leading to issues such as hypertension and edema.

instruction: What are the potential benefits and risks of using aspirin to prevent blood clots in patients with Covid-19, and how might this treatment impact patient outcomes?
response: Using aspirin to prevent blood clots in patients with Covid-19 is a promising but complex intervention. **Potential Benefits:** Aspirin acts as an antiplatelet agent, which can help reduce the formation of blood clots. Given that a high percentage of Covid-19 deaths (nearly 80%) are associated with thrombosis, aspirin could play a crucial role in mitigating this risk. This inexpensive and readily available drug could be particularly beneficial in resource-limited settings. **Potential Risks:** However, the use of aspirin is not without risks. One of the primary concerns is the increased risk of bleeding, especially in the gastrointestinal tract. Patients with a history of peptic ulcers or other bleeding disorders may be at higher risk. Additionally, the combination of aspirin with other anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs could exacerbate this risk. **Impact on Patient Outcomes:** The impact of aspirin on patient outcomes would depend on several factors, including the severity of the patient's condition, their overall health, and the presence of other comorbidities. Clinical trials, such as the one being conducted in British hospitals, are essential to determine the efficacy and safety of aspirin in this context. If the trials yield positive results, aspirin could become a standard part of the treatment regimen for Covid-19 patients, potentially reducing the incidence of severe complications and improving survival rates. However, careful monitoring and individualized treatment plans will be necessary to maximize benefits while minimizing risks.

instruction: What are the primary differences between acute and chronic leukemia, and how do these differences affect the progression and treatment of the disease?
response: Acute and chronic leukemia differ significantly in their progression and treatment due to the nature of the cell maturation and growth patterns. Acute leukemia, such as Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia (ALL) and Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML), involves the rapid proliferation of immature blood cells, which can quickly overwhelm the body's normal blood cell production. This rapid progression necessitates immediate and aggressive treatment, often including chemotherapy, radiation, and sometimes stem cell transplants. In contrast, chronic leukemia, such as Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) and Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML), involves the slower accumulation of more mature but abnormal blood cells. Symptoms may be mild or absent initially, allowing for a more measured and long-term treatment approach, which can include targeted therapies, immunotherapy, and periodic monitoring. The differences in the disease's pace and cell maturity directly influence the urgency and intensity of the treatment strategies.

text:
Among the chronic myeloproliferative disorders, polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia are unique because of their association with thrombohemorrhagic manifestations and their relatively indolent clinical course. Patients with essential thrombocythemia may not have a significant shortening of life-expectancy and most may not require specific therapy. However, patients with polycythemia vera have a significant risk of transformation of polycythemia vera into acute leukemia or postpolycythemic myelofibrosis (or both). 'High-risk-for-thrombosis' patients with either polycythemia vera or essential thrombocythemia require specific therapy with a platelet-lowering agent to prevent thrombotic complications. Currently, the standard agent used for this is hydroxyurea. However, its teratogenic and leukemogenic potential has been of concern. As a result, new platelet-lowering agents are being evaluated in the treatment of polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia. Anagrelide and interferon alfa are two such agents and have been shown to be effective in reducing platelet counts in patients with chronic myeloproliferative disorders. The putative mechanism of action of these drugs, their specific activity in polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia, side-effect profile, and current indications are discussed herein.

instruction: What are the primary differences in the clinical course and treatment requirements between polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia, and how do these differences impact patient management?
response: The clinical course and treatment requirements for polycythemia vera (PV) and essential thrombocythemia (ET) differ in several key aspects, which significantly impact patient management. PV is characterized by an increased production of red blood cells, leading to hyperviscosity and a higher risk of thrombotic events. This condition also has a higher risk of progression to more severe disorders, such as acute leukemia or post-polycythemic myelofibrosis. On the other hand, ET is marked by an elevated platelet count, which can increase the risk of thrombosis but generally to a lesser degree than in PV. Patients with ET may not have a significant reduction in life expectancy and often do not require specific therapy unless they are at high risk for thrombosis. For high-risk patients with either condition, the standard treatment involves the use of a platelet-lowering agent, typically hydroxyurea. However, concerns about the teratogenic and leukemogenic potential of hydroxyurea have led to the evaluation and use of alternative agents such as anagrelide and interferon alfa. These agents are effective in reducing platelet counts and are considered for patients who cannot tolerate hydroxyurea or are at higher risk of its side effects. In summary, the management of PV is more intensive and focused on preventing disease progression and thrombotic events, while the management of ET is more conservative and often less aggressive, depending on the patient's risk factors.

instruction: How does iron deficiency impact the body's ability to produce healthy red blood cells, and what are the broader health implications of this deficiency?
response: Iron deficiency affects the body's ability to produce healthy red blood cells by limiting the production of hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein within red blood cells. When there is a lack of iron, the bone marrow cannot produce enough hemoglobin, resulting in smaller and paler red blood cells (microcytic and hypochromic). This condition, known as iron deficiency anemia, reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, leading to symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, and shortness of breath. The broader health implications of iron deficiency anemia are significant and can include cognitive impairment, immune system weakness, and increased susceptibility to infections. In severe cases, it can also lead to heart problems, such as an enlarged heart or heart failure, as the heart must work harder to pump oxygenated blood to the body. Additionally, iron deficiency in pregnant women can increase the risk of premature birth and low birth weight.

Bleeding disorder is an acquired or an inherited condition, which is characterized by excessive bleeding in the persons affected by the disorder.
In our body, blood circulates inside the blood vessels called the veins, arteries and capillaries. If there is a crack or damage of the vessel then bleeding occurs into the organs or externally.
Under normal conditions, our body resorts to its own mechanism to cope with bleeding through a process called hemostasis. During this process the blood vessels constrict to decrease blood flow and platelets in the blood accumulate to form a plug. This is then stabilized by a film of fibrin that forms a barrier. This barrier remains in place till the injury is fully healed.
The process of clot formation, involving a range of clotting factors, occurs sequentially in a coagulation ‘cascade’. The clot is dissolved (fibrinolysis) once the wound is healed.
In people with bleeding disorders, the clotting process is impaired and this results in spontaneous bleeding. If a component that aids in clotting is missing, deficient or is dysfunctional then it results in excessive bleeding.
The disorders are first detected during early childhood and the resultant bleeding can be very severe.
Bleeding conditions do not have a permanent cure. They can, however, be managed.

instruction: What are the primary challenges in managing bleeding disorders, and why is it difficult to find a permanent cure for these conditions?
response: The primary challenges in managing bleeding disorders revolve around the intricate nature of the hemostasis process and the genetic roots of these conditions. When a blood vessel is damaged, the body initiates hemostasis to stop bleeding, involving vasoconstriction, platelet aggregation, and the formation of a fibrin clot. In individuals with bleeding disorders, one or more components of this process are compromised, leading to excessive and potentially life-threatening bleeding. The management of these disorders is complex because it requires continuous monitoring and intervention, such as regular infusions of clotting factors to maintain hemostasis. The genetic basis of many bleeding disorders, such as hemophilia, means that these conditions are lifelong and currently lack a permanent cure. While advancements in gene therapy offer hope, they are still under development and face significant hurdles, including ensuring long-term efficacy and safety. As a result, the current approach focuses on symptom management and preventing complications, rather than achieving a permanent cure.

instruction: How does the diagnostic process for hemolytic anemia differ from that of other types of anemia, and what specific tests are used to identify the underlying causes?
response:
The diagnostic process for hemolytic anemia is more specialized and comprehensive compared to other types of anemia due to the unique nature of the condition. Hemolytic anemia involves the premature destruction of red blood cells, which can be caused by various factors such as genetic disorders, immune system issues, or environmental factors. The diagnostic process typically begins with a Complete Blood Count (CBC) to identify anemia. If anemia is confirmed, further specific tests are conducted to pinpoint the cause and severity of hemolytic anemia. These tests include:

1. **Reticulocyte Count**: Measures the number of immature red blood cells, which helps determine if the bone marrow is responding to the anemia by producing more red blood cells.
2. **Peripheral Blood Smear**: Microscopic examination of the blood to identify abnormal red blood cell shapes, such as sickle cells or spherocytes, which can indicate specific types of hemolytic anemia.
3. **Coombs' Test**: Detects antibodies that may be attacking red blood cells, which is crucial for diagnosing autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
4. **Haptoglobin and Bilirubin Levels**: Low haptoglobin and high bilirubin levels can indicate hemolysis, as these are byproducts of red blood cell breakdown.
5. **Hemoglobin Electrophoresis**: Identifies different types of hemoglobin, useful for diagnosing genetic disorders like sickle cell anemia and thalassemia.
6. **Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH) Test**: Detects red blood cells that lack certain proteins, leading to increased destruction.
7. **Osmotic Fragility Test**: Evaluates the fragility of red blood cells, which can be increased in conditions like hereditary spherocytosis.
8. **Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) Deficiency Test**: Checks for the absence of the G6PD enzyme, which can cause hemolysis in certain conditions.
9. **Urine Test**: Detects the presence of hemoglobin and iron in the urine, which can indicate intravascular hemolysis.
10. **Bone Marrow Biopsy**: In some cases, a bone marrow biopsy may be necessary to assess the bone marrow's ability to produce healthy red blood cells, though this is often a last resort if other tests are inconclusive.

These tests are essential for differentiating hemolytic anemia from other types of anemia, such as iron-deficiency anemia or anemia of chronic disease, and for identifying the specific underlying cause, which is crucial for appropriate treatment.

instruction: How does myelosuppression, a common side effect of chemotherapy, impact the dosage and frequency of chemotherapy treatments, and what are the current strategies to manage it?
response: Myelosuppression, a common side effect of chemotherapy, significantly impacts the dosage and frequency of chemotherapy treatments. This condition involves the suppression of bone marrow function, leading to a decrease in the production of blood cells, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. As a result, patients may experience anemia, increased susceptibility to infections, and a higher risk of bleeding. These complications often necessitate dose reductions or treatment delays to allow the bone marrow to recover. However, reducing the dosage or frequency can compromise the effectiveness of the chemotherapy. To manage myelosuppression, current strategies include the use of growth factors such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) to stimulate white blood cell production, and transfusions of red blood cells or platelets to address anemia and bleeding risks. Additionally, prophylactic antibiotics may be prescribed to prevent infections. The research by Professor Wally Langdon at the University of Western Australia (UWA) offers a promising new approach to combat myelosuppression, potentially allowing for more effective and consistent chemotherapy treatments.

Furthermore, iron isinvolved in the synthesis of serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine and even collagen.The most well-knowncondition of iron deficiency is of course anemia, which is associated withfeelings of weakness and fatigue. Other conditions associated with irondeficiency include Plummer-Vinson syndrome, a condition characterized bydifficulty in swallowing solid food due to the presence of a thin, web-likemembrane growing across the upper passageway of the esophagus. Those withPlummer-Vinson syndrome are at an increased risk of cancer of the esophagusand stomach, and iron supplementation has been shown to prevent this syndrome.
Who Is At Risk? Pregnant and menstruating womenare often at risk of iron deficiency (and consequently anemia), as are infants, adolescents, endurance athletes, and those under any other conditionof growth and/or fatigue generating an increased cellular demand for oxygen.The loss of iron â€“ and thus the need for supplementation â€“ also occurs duringconditions of blood loss such as uterine bleeding in post-menopausal women on hormone replacement therapy, gastrointestinal bleeding, and bleeding fromtrauma or surgery. Some iron loss can also occur through mucosal excretionsand skin sloughing.
Iron Metabolism The proper metabolism ofiron is exceptionally important and highly biologically regulated due to thefact that the body has no way of excreting excess amounts of it. Iron absorption can vary considerably, ranging from 10-35% for someone withsufficient iron stores, to as high as 95% for those with iron deficiencies.Upon ingestion, iron shifts between its two oxidative states â€“ ferrous (II)and ferric (III). This shift back and forth via single electron-transferreactions, while making iron essential in the electron transport chain, canalso generate reactive oxygen species hydroxyl radicals. It is in the form offerric (III) however, that iron is bound to transferrin, a liver-generatedprotein that is primarily responsible for distributing iron throughout thebloodstream. It eventually enters the cell mitochondria where it is combinedwith protoporphyrin to form heme for the purpose of hemoglobin synthesis.Between 70-90% of this tranferrin-bound iron is designated for hemoglobinsynthesis, with the majority of the remainder used for the electron transferchain.
Excess iron is stored in the body as ferritin, a unique protein whose main function is the storage of iron and is located mainly in the liver but also in the spleen, bone marrow,intestines and other organs. This iron can be released from ferritin andre-transported into the plasma by transferrin if the demand for hemoglobin iswarranted. The body has a very limited capacity to excrete excess iron, withonly tiny amounts being excreted through the kidneys, liver, bile ducts andgall bladder.

The subjects in the study group were reported to performsignificantly better than those in the placebo group on learning and memorytests.
Infantile Breath Holding Expiratory apnea or BreathHolding Spells (BHS) is a condition affecting infants that is characterized by spells of involuntary breath-holding, usually during a stressful event thatelicits crying on the part of the child. Children with thisdisorder who were given 5 mg of iron per kg of bodyweight each day for 16weeks experienced 88% complete or partial improvement â€“ compared with 6% inthe placebo group.

instruction: How does iron deficiency impact cognitive function and immune health, and what are some of the broader health implications of iron deficiency beyond anemia?
response: Iron deficiency has far-reaching effects on cognitive function and immune health, extending beyond the well-known condition of anemia. In cognitive function, iron is essential for the development and maintenance of the nervous system. It is involved in the synthesis of neurotransmitters like serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine, which are crucial for mood, learning, and memory. Research has demonstrated that iron supplementation in iron-deficient adolescent girls improved their cognitive performance on memory and learning tests. Regarding immune health, iron is necessary for the synthesis of DNA and the production of immune cells, which are critical for mounting an effective immune response. Iron deficiency can compromise the immune system, making individuals more vulnerable to infections and illnesses. Beyond anemia, iron deficiency can contribute to other health issues such as Plummer-Vinson syndrome, a condition that causes difficulty swallowing and increases the risk of esophageal and stomach cancer. Furthermore, iron deficiency can lead to longer hospital stays, as evidenced by a study showing that patients with functional iron deficiencies had hospital stays more than twice as long as those without. Iron deficiency can also affect infants, leading to conditions like breath-holding spells, which were significantly reduced with iron supplementation. These broader health implications highlight the importance of maintaining adequate iron levels for overall health and well-being.

instruction: What are the primary clinical manifestations and complications of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH), and how do they affect the quality of life and long-term prognosis of patients?
response: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH) is a rare acquired chronic hemolytic anemia characterized by intravascular hemolysis, which leads to the breakdown of red blood cells and the release of hemoglobin into the bloodstream. The primary clinical manifestations of PNH include hemoglobinuria (red or dark urine due to hemoglobin), abdominal pain, smooth muscle dysfunction, and thrombosis. Hemoglobinuria, particularly noticeable in the morning, is a classic sign due to nocturnal hemolysis. Other symptoms may include fatigue, pallor, shortness of breath, and jaundice. Thrombosis, a significant complication, can occur in both arterial and venous vessels and is a leading cause of mortality in PNH patients. Chronic hemolysis can also lead to iron deficiency anemia and bone marrow failure. The quality of life for PNH patients is often compromised due to the chronic nature of the disease, frequent hospitalizations, and the need for regular blood transfusions. Long-term prognosis varies, with a median survival of about 10 years, but this can be improved with treatments like eculizumab, which reduces hemolysis and improves quality of life, although it does not significantly affect overall mortality.

instruction: How do multidisciplinary care and community partnerships contribute to improving the quality of life for people living with haemophilia and other rare blood disorders?
response: The integration of multidisciplinary care and community partnerships significantly enhances the quality of life for individuals with haemophilia and other rare blood disorders. Multidisciplinary care teams, composed of specialists such as hematologists, orthopedists, and physiotherapists, offer a comprehensive approach to managing the condition. This team-based approach ensures that patients receive coordinated care, which can lead to better outcomes and reduced complications. For instance, hematologists can manage clotting factor replacement therapy, while orthopedists can address joint issues and prevent long-term damage. Physiotherapists play a vital role by designing exercise regimens that improve joint health and reduce the risk of bleeding episodes. Community partnerships, on the other hand, are essential for providing support and resources outside the clinical setting. These partnerships can involve local hospitals, support groups, and advocacy organizations, which can offer educational programs, financial assistance, and emotional support. For example, community-based programs can provide training on self-infusion techniques, which can empower patients to manage their condition more independently. Additionally, advocacy groups can work to improve access to care and treatment, ensuring that patients have the necessary resources to lead fulfilling lives. Together, these efforts create a supportive network that enhances the overall well-being and quality of life for individuals with rare blood disorders.

I wrote it all off and blamed turning 30, early morning wake-ups, a busy work schedule, etc. I made up excuses to validate feeling like crap. This is something that I talk about all the time as a yoga teacher and I this was an instance where I wasn’t practicing it in my own life. There is nothing wrong with waving the white flag and seeking help (and this applies to MANY areas of life!). It is not a sign weakness.

All three of these supplements can be found at CVS and the best part is that they come with a money-back guarantee. If they don’t work for you simply return them for a full refund. I am taking a few other supplements as well that I will share with you in another post.
So, how am I feeling now? AMAZING! After starting treatment for my anemia, I made 2014 my best year ever as a runner. I surprised myself with how strong and happy I felt running and set a new 5K PR, ran my first half marathon in four years and set a huge PR doing it. And so far 2015 has been great too! instruction: What are the benefits and potential risks of taking supplements like iron and B12 for treating anemia, and how can one determine the right dosage and type of supplement to use?
response: Supplements like iron and B12 are essential for managing anemia, but they come with their own set of benefits and risks. **Benefits:** Iron supplements are crucial for treating iron-deficiency anemia, helping to increase hemoglobin levels and improve energy and overall well-being. B12 supplements are vital for the production of red blood cells and can boost cognitive function, mood, and energy. **Risks:** Overconsumption of iron can lead to iron toxicity, which can damage organs, especially the liver. Excessive B12 can mask other deficiencies, such as folate deficiency, and may cause skin reactions or allergic responses. **Determining the Right Dosage and Type:** To determine the right dosage and type of supplement, it's essential to consult a healthcare provider. They can perform blood tests to identify your specific needs and recommend the appropriate dosage. Start with the lowest effective dose and adjust based on your symptoms and test results. Choose high-quality supplements from trusted sources, such as CVS, which offers a money-back guarantee. Consider forms of iron and B12 that are well-absorbed, such as ferrous gluconate for iron and methylcobalamin for B12, to maximize effectiveness.

What is positive Allen’s test?
A positive Allen test means that the patient may not have an adequate dual blood supply to the hand, which would be a contraindication for catheterization, radial forearm flap harvest, or any procedure that may result in occlusion of the vessel.
Why do we do Allen test?
Before drawing blood for an arterial blood gas test, your health professional will make sure that both arteries are open and working correctly. A procedure called the Allen test may be used to find out if the blood flow to your hand is normal.
What is a normal Allen test?
Allen test. Normal (positive) Your hand quickly becomes warm and returns to its normal colour. This means that one artery alone will be enough to supply blood to your hand and fingers. Abnormal (negative)
What do you do if the Allen test is negative?
Negative modified Allen test – If the hand does not flush within 5-15 seconds, it indicates that ulnar circulation is inadequate or nonexistent; in this situation, the radial artery supplying arterial blood to that hand should not be punctured.
What is Allen test in nursing?
(ăl′ĕn) 1. A bedside test used to evaluate the patency of the arteries of the hand before arterial puncture. The patient elevates the hand and repeatedly makes a fist while the examiner places digital occlusive pressure over the radial and ulnar arteries at the wrist.
Which Pulse site is used for Allen test?
Allen’s test is performed by occluding both radial and ulnar arteries at the wrist, emptying the hand of blood by repeatedly making a fist, and releasing one of the arteries.
How do you check circulation in your fingers?
How to check: Compare the temperature of both sides. If fingers or toes are cold, put a blanket on to cover the fingers or toes and check again in one hour. Normal: Pink within 3 seconds or less. Less than 3 seconds is rapid.
How far under the skin is the radial artery?
The anterior wall of the typical radial artery is 3 mm under the skin, so a lot of depth is not necessary.
instruction: What are the clinical implications of a negative Allen test, and what actions should be taken if this result is observed?
response: A negative Allen test suggests that the ulnar artery is not providing adequate collateral circulation to the hand, which is crucial for maintaining blood flow when the radial artery is occluded. This finding has important clinical implications, especially for procedures that involve the radial artery, such as arterial blood gas sampling or catheterization. If the Allen test is negative, it is contraindicated to puncture the radial artery, as this could lead to compromised blood flow to the hand and potential complications like ischemia or necrosis. Instead, alternative sites for the procedure should be considered, such as the brachial artery or the contralateral hand if it has a positive Allen test. It is also advisable to conduct further vascular assessments to rule out any underlying conditions that might be affecting the patient's blood supply.

instruction: What are the potential benefits for patients who receive stem cell transplants from younger, healthier donors, and how does this influence the importance of recruiting such donors?
response: Receiving stem cell transplants from younger, healthier donors can significantly enhance patient outcomes. Younger donors generally provide stem cells with higher regenerative potential, which can lead to more successful engraftment and a quicker recovery process. Moreover, younger donors are less likely to have accumulated genetic or environmental damage, reducing the risk of complications such as graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) and other post-transplant issues. This improved compatibility and reduced risk of complications translate to better survival rates and a higher quality of life for the patients. The importance of recruiting younger, healthier donors is emphasized by the need to expand the donor pool, ensuring that more patients have access to potentially life-saving transplants. Initiatives like the GenDx Stem Cell Donor Recruitment Week are vital in this effort, as they raise awareness and encourage young, fit individuals to sign up as potential donors, ultimately contributing to the success of stem cell transplantation programs.

Innovate UK will provide a grant of approximately 1.3 million GBP to a research consortium led by Plasticell for a project entitled ‘Ex-vivo expansion of cord blood and bone marrow stem cells”. The consortium includes the University of Oxford and the Cell Therapy Catapult.
While bone marrow is currently the primary source of stem cells for haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), donor cells have to be immunologically matched to the recipent, resulting in demand far outstripping supply. In contrast, donated cord blood is plentiful and contains a high proportion of stem cells with a lower risk of tissue rejection despite immunological mismatch. HSCT from cord blood is currently limited by the low number of total cells present in each donated unit.
Using CombiCult®, Plasticell has tested millions of combinations of cell culture components to develop cord blood expansion media which amplify stem cells by up to 100-fold. This grant will allow the consortium to develop a clinically compliant process to expand cord blood stem cells ex vivo using Plasticell’s media, allowing more patients to be treated with this life-saving therapy.
Commenting on the award, Dennis Saw, Chief Executive of Plasticell, said:
“Using CombiCult®, our team of stem cell scientists is successfully tackling some of the most difficult problems in regenerative medicine, as is demonstrated by the development of highly effective cord blood expansion media. Since 2007, Plasticell has been awarded a number of competitive grants from the Technology Strategy Board, now Innovate UK, which have funded research projects costing an approximate 8.3 mln GBP in total. These awards recognise our industry experience and continued innovation at the cutting edge of stem cell research & development.”
instruction: What are the primary challenges associated with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) from bone marrow, and how does cord blood offer a potential solution to these challenges?
response: One of the main challenges in haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) using bone marrow is the stringent requirement for immunological matching between the donor and recipient. This necessity often leads to a shortage of suitable donors and can delay the transplantation process, which is particularly critical in time-sensitive medical conditions. Another challenge is the potential for graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) due to the immunological mismatch. Cord blood, on the other hand, is a promising alternative source of stem cells because it is more readily available, and the stem cells it contains have a lower risk of causing tissue rejection, even in the absence of a perfect immunological match. However, the use of cord blood for HSCT is limited by the relatively low number of total cells in each donated unit. To overcome this limitation, Plasticell has developed a high-throughput stem cell technology called CombiCult® that has successfully tested millions of cell culture components to create expansion media capable of amplifying cord blood stem cells by up to 100-fold. With support from a grant by Innovate UK, the consortium led by Plasticell, including the University of Oxford and the Cell Therapy Catapult, aims to develop a clinically compliant process for ex vivo expansion of cord blood stem cells, thereby making this therapy more widely available to patients in need.

Serology tests uses various methods to measure and characterise antibodies, antigens, and other immunological substances in blood and other body fluids.
Antibodies play an important role in the innate and acquired immune responses. Levels of antibody production are increased in infective or inflammatory conditions, and we can utilise this phenomenon to diagnose disease and sometimes also to stage disease progression. The detection and characterisation of antibodies can indicate infection with specific pathogens (bacteria, viruses or fungi) which are difficult to culture or expensive to detect with other methods such as molecular tests. It can also be used to diagnose inflammatory conditions including autoimmune diseases, where antibodies are produced that may damage tissues. Antibodies (also called immunoglobulins) are mostly very specific. For instance, if a patient is infected with the influenza virus, the antibodies will be identifiable as against influenza, and can be distinguished from the type of antibody produced in response to another type of infection (e.g. measles).
There are different classes of these immunoglobulins e.g. IgM, IgG, IgA and IgE, and identifying this various classes of antibodies can help us to determine the stage or progression of disease.
When a patient is for instance infected by a microorganism for the first time, antibodies of the class IgM are initially produced. IgM antibodies are thus usually an indication of an acute infection. As time goes by a class switch takes place and IgG antibodies will be produced. During this phase one could find both IgM and IgG antibodies present in the blood of an infected patient. The IgM response tends to decline within approximately 1 to 2 months, although low levels can persist for a year or more in certain infections. IgG antibodies are much more long-lasting, and can persist for the life span of the patient. Serology tests can therefore determine whether a person is currently infected, or was perhaps previously infected by a certain organisms, or is already immune to these organisms. Serology can also be used to determine the blood type of a person by detecting certain proteins (antigens) on the blood cells of the person, and can help to determine whether a patient has an immune deficiency (when there will be a lack of antibodies).
According to this model, the following is usually true
|Organism-specific IgM||Organism-specific IgG||Status|
|Absent||Absent||Susceptible to organism|
|Present||Absent or present||Current or very recent infection|
|Absent||Present||Past infection *|
* This often, but not always, indicates immunity to subsequent infection
Many pathogen specific factors will also influence the interpretation of serology results, for instance the incubation period of the infection, as antibodies may still be absent at the time that a patient first presents with an infection. In contrast, in infections with long incubation periods (a month or longer), both IgM and IgG might be present at the onset of symptoms.
In reinfection and reactivation serologic diagnosis is even more complicated than initial infections. It is therefore important to recognise the difficulties associated with some serological tests, and to consult us for advise in the use and interpretation of these tests, as required.
instruction: In what ways can serology tests be used beyond diagnosing infections, such as in determining blood type or identifying immune deficiencies?
response:
Serology tests can be used beyond diagnosing infections in several ways. One key application is in determining blood type. Blood typing involves detecting specific antigens on the surface of red blood cells, which can be done using serological methods. For example, the ABO blood group system is determined by the presence or absence of A and B antigens. Serology tests can identify these antigens, ensuring safe blood transfusions and reducing the risk of transfusion reactions.

Another important use of serology tests is in identifying immune deficiencies. Immune deficiencies occur when the immune system is not functioning properly, often due to a lack of antibodies. Serology tests can measure the levels of different classes of immunoglobulins (IgM, IgG, IgA, and IgE) in the blood. Low levels of these antibodies can indicate an immune deficiency, helping healthcare providers diagnose and manage conditions such as primary immunodeficiency disorders. This information is crucial for developing appropriate treatment plans and monitoring the effectiveness of interventions.

instruction: How do the risk factors for mesenteric vein thrombosis differ from those of other vascular conditions, and what are the typical clinical presentations of this uncommon disease?
response: Mesenteric vein thrombosis (MVT) is a rare vascular condition with unique risk factors and clinical manifestations. Unlike other vascular conditions, which often involve systemic factors like atherosclerosis or hypertension, MVT is frequently associated with specific intra-abdominal and hematological factors. These risk factors include infections, inflammation, malignancies, and hematological disorders such as myeloproliferative syndromes, protein C or S deficiencies, and antithrombin III or plasminogen activator deficiencies. The clinical presentation of MVT typically involves acute abdominal symptoms, including severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. The pain is often diffuse but can be localized, and patients may exhibit signs of peritoneal irritation such as tenderness and guarding. Diagnostic imaging, particularly CT or MRI, is crucial for identifying enlarged mesenteric veins and characteristic findings like bowel wall thickening and edema, which are key to confirming the diagnosis of MVT.

Medicare coverage woefully underfunds cell acquisition for bone marrow and cord blood transplants.
-- August 10 2016
The National Marrow Donor Program® (NMDP)/Be The Match®, which operates the nation's Be The Match Registry® of potential adult volunteer marrow donors and donated umbilical cord blood units, today expressed disappointment that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) did not establish policy changes to address the deficits marrow and cord blood transplant centers incur for the cost of acquiring the cells used in transplants in the final hospital inpatient prospective payment system (IPPS) rule for CY2017.
"We are disappointed that CMS does not address chronic underfunding of bone marrow and cord blood transplants for Medicare beneficiaries in the inpatient setting, where the majority of these life-saving transplants occur," said Jeffrey W. Chell, M.D., chief executive officer of the NMDP/Be The Match. "These transplants are often the last therapeutic option patients with a blood cancer or other blood disorder have and the only chance for a cure. We had hoped CMS would have included a way to ensure that the reimbursement rate does not create a barrier to access in the final rule."
NMDP/Be The Match urges CMS to find a way to address this problem in the inpatient setting without waiting until next year. The NMDP/Be The Match, along with the American Society of Blood and Marrow Transplant, cord blood banks, transplant centers, and patient advocates have asked CMS to reimburse hospitals for the cost of acquiring cells for transplant using the same method Medicare relies upon to reimburse hospitals for the cost of acquiring solid organs. Medicare currently pays solid organ acquisition costs for kidney, heart, heart-lung, liver, lung, pancreas, and intestinal (or multivisceral organs) transplants on a reasonable cost basis and separate from the prospective payment rate.
Despite the lack of a solution in the final inpatient hospital payment rule, the NMDP/Be The Match remains hopeful that the problem will be addressed in the hospital outpatient setting. The HOPPS proposed rule, on which CMS is still seeking comments, would adopt a new method for determining the payment amount for bone marrow and cord blood transplants that would better account for the cost of acquiring these cells. Even though the vast majority of transplants occur in the inpatient setting, there are a limited number each year that can be successfully performed in the outpatient setting.
"While we were encouraged when CMS chose to increase cell acquisition and transplant rates in the outpatient setting, which we applauded as a first step toward improving care and recognizing the acute underfunding for procurement and transplant for the outpatient setting, we are puzzled as to why CMS neglected to take a similar positive step forward for the inpatient setting, which is where most transplants occur since hospital stays are often required," Chell added. "We are deeply concerned that for another year hospitals will be expected to perform transplants without adequate reimbursement, as the costs exceed the amount Medicare will pay them. This disconnect between cost and reimbursement rates places tremendous strain on our nation's transplant programs and seriously threatens access for Medicare patients in need of transplant for survival."
About the National Marrow Donor Program® (NMDP)/Be The Match®
The NMDP/Be The Match is the global leader in providing a cure to patients with life-threatening blood and marrow cancers such as leukemia and lymphoma, as well as other diseases. The nonprofit organization manages the world's largest registry of potential marrow donors and cord blood units, connects patients to their donor match for a life-saving marrow or umbilical cord blood transplant, educates health care professionals and conducts research through its research program, CIBMTR® (Center for International Blood and Marrow Transplant Research®),so more lives can be saved. NMDP/Be The Match also provides patient support and enlists the community to join the Be The Match Registry®, contribute financially and volunteer.
instruction: What are the potential consequences of Medicare's underfunding of bone marrow and cord blood transplants for patients and transplant centers, and how might this issue be addressed?
response: The chronic underfunding of bone marrow and cord blood transplants by Medicare has far-reaching consequences for both patients and healthcare providers. For patients, the lack of adequate reimbursement can create significant barriers to accessing these critical treatments, especially for those with life-threatening blood cancers and disorders. This can result in delayed or denied transplants, which can be a matter of life and death. For transplant centers, the financial burden of performing transplants without full reimbursement can lead to operational challenges, including reduced funding for staff, equipment, and research. This can ultimately threaten the viability of transplant programs, leading to closures and further reducing patient access. To address this issue, Medicare could consider aligning its reimbursement policies with those for solid organ transplants, where the costs of cell acquisition are covered on a reasonable cost basis. Additionally, CMS could expedite the adoption of new payment methods in both inpatient and outpatient settings to better reflect the true costs of these procedures and ensure sustained access to life-saving transplants.

instruction: What are some natural methods to increase a low platelet count, and how do these methods work to improve blood clotting?
response: Natural methods to increase a low platelet count focus on dietary and lifestyle changes that support the production and function of platelets. One effective approach is to increase the intake of foods high in essential nutrients like iron, vitamin K, and vitamin D. Iron is crucial for the formation of hemoglobin and overall blood health; it can be found in red meat, spinach, and lentils. Vitamin K, which plays a key role in blood clotting, is abundant in leafy green vegetables like kale and spinach. Vitamin D, which can be obtained from sunlight exposure and foods like fatty fish and fortified dairy products, helps regulate the immune system and can support platelet production. Additionally, staying hydrated and avoiding alcohol and tobacco can reduce the risk of platelet destruction. These methods work by providing the body with the necessary building blocks for platelet production and by creating an environment that supports their function and longevity, thus improving blood clotting.

instruction: What are the primary physiological and pathological processes in which Tribbles proteins are known to play a role, and how do these processes impact cell function?
response: Tribbles proteins, including TRIB2, play significant roles in both physiological and pathological processes, primarily through their interactions with signal transduction pathways. These proteins are known to modulate the activity of various signaling pathways, which in turn impact cell function in several ways. One of the primary physiological roles of Tribbles proteins is in the regulation of cell apoptosis, particularly in hematopoietic cells. TRIB2 has been shown to induce apoptosis in these cells, which is crucial for maintaining proper hematopoietic homeostasis and preventing the accumulation of damaged or unnecessary cells. Additionally, TRIB2 is up-regulated by inflammatory stimuli in myeloid cells, suggesting a role in the immune response and inflammation. Pathologically, TRIB2 has been identified as an oncogene that can cause acute myelogenous leukemia (AML). This occurs through the inactivation of the transcription factor C/EBPalpha (CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein alpha), which is essential for the differentiation and function of myeloid cells. By disrupting C/EBPalpha, TRIB2 contributes to the uncontrolled proliferation and survival of myeloid cells, leading to the development of AML. Thus, the impact of Tribbles proteins on cell function is multifaceted, influencing both normal cellular processes and disease states.
