Dustin is passionate about donating blood to advance research. Here’s why.
Why is Research Important to You?
Since I’ve been diabetic for nearly 27 years, I am a big supporter of stem cell research. I’ve seen a lot of advances in science in regards to diabetes ever since I got it when I was 14.
I know what it is like firsthand to live with something that I didn’t ask for. There are some days when I have to force myself to go out and do things. I mean I have a 6-year-old son that I have to take care of. I have to go to work. I have to do normal life things every day, and it can be hard a lot of times with diabetes.
What types of blood donations have you made?
I actually started with whole blood. I believe I’ve done maybe two or three whole blood donations. Then I was really interested in bone marrow. I went in and I did it and it actually wasn’t too bad. The whole experience is honestly not more than five or six minutes long from start to finish. I’ve done it eight times.
What inspires you to donate?
My one donation is not just going to help one person. That one donation, they could look under the microscope and whatever other cool things they do, they could end up seeing something that could potentially help 50,000 people in this study group. Knowing that maybe I was a person who could have helped with that, that would be great. That would be really good.
Many others share Dustin’s same passion for research. Meet Terra.
instruction: What are the various types of blood donations and how do they contribute to scientific advancements and medical treatments?
response:
Blood donations come in various forms, each playing a critical role in both medical treatments and scientific research. One of the most common types is whole blood donation, where a pint of blood is donated and later separated into components such as red blood cells, plasma, and platelets. These components are essential for treating a wide range of medical conditions, including anemia, hemophilia, and trauma. Dustin, a long-time diabetic, has made several whole blood donations, recognizing their importance in both immediate patient care and long-term research.

Another significant type is bone marrow donation, which Dustin has done multiple times. Bone marrow is crucial for producing blood cells and is often used to treat blood cancers like leukemia and lymphoma, as well as other immune system disorders. The donation process, though brief, can have a profound impact on recipients and scientific understanding. Bone marrow donations can be used to study the biology of blood diseases and to develop new therapies.

These donations contribute to scientific advancements by providing researchers with valuable biological materials. For example, stem cell research, a field Dustin is passionate about, can lead to groundbreaking treatments for diabetes and other chronic conditions. Each donation has the potential to help thousands of people by contributing to the discovery of new treatments and the improvement of existing medical practices.

Living with chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML)
Once your treatment is over, your doctor will want to see you for regular check-ups. This is known as follow-up. These visits will continue for the rest of your life. At the check-ups, you may have tests like a physical exam, X-rays, scans and blood tests. If you are between check-ups and have a symptom or problem that worries you, let your doctor know without delay.
There are many cancer support centres and voluntary groups around the country. If you feel they could help you and your family, call the National Cancer Helpline on 1800 200 700. The Helpline nurses can give you more information on counselling or support groups in your area.
We can also help you cope with the emotional effects of a cancer diagnosis.

instruction: What types of tests and examinations are typically conducted during follow-up visits for chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) patients, and how frequently are these visits usually scheduled?
response: For chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) patients, follow-up visits are crucial for ongoing monitoring and management of the disease. During these visits, healthcare providers typically conduct a series of tests and examinations to assess the patient's health and the effectiveness of the treatment. Common tests include a physical examination to check for any physical signs of the disease, blood tests to monitor blood cell counts and detect the BCR-ABL fusion gene, which is a key indicator of CML, and imaging tests like X-rays or scans to evaluate the overall health of the patient and detect any potential complications. The frequency of these follow-up visits is usually determined by the patient's specific condition and response to treatment. In the initial stages, visits may be scheduled every 3-6 months. As the patient stabilizes, the frequency may decrease, but follow-up visits will continue throughout the patient's life to ensure early detection of any recurrence or new issues. If any concerning symptoms arise between scheduled visits, patients are advised to contact their doctor promptly.

While modern medicine places more importance on treatment, herbalists believe that the body has inherent self-correcting tendencies to heal, and herbs can act in synergy with the body to cure us.

instruction: What are some lifestyle changes that can help manage the progression of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and improve overall health and immunity?
response: Living with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) requires a holistic approach to manage the disease and improve overall health. One effective strategy is to adopt a healthy diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins. This can help strengthen the immune system and manage the progression of CLL. Additionally, regular physical activity, such as walking, swimming, or yoga, can boost your energy levels and reduce stress. Managing stress through mindfulness, meditation, and relaxation techniques can also be beneficial. Ensuring adequate sleep and hydration is crucial for overall well-being. Herbal supplements, when used under the guidance of a healthcare provider, can complement conventional treatments and support the body's natural healing processes. Lastly, avoiding smoking and limiting alcohol consumption can further reduce the risk of complications and improve quality of life.

Background: Peripherally inserted central venous catheters (PICCs) are now widely used for intermediate and long-term access in current-day health care, especially in the inpatient setting, where they are increasingly supplanting conventional central venous catheters (CVCs) placed percutaneously into the internal jugular, subclavian, or femoral veins. Data on the risk of PICC-related bloodstream infection (BSI) with PICCs used in hospitalized patients are limited.
Study objectives: To determine the risk of PICC-related BSI in hospitalized patients.
Study design: Prospective cohort study using data from two randomized trials assessing the efficacy of chlorhexidine-impregnated sponge dressing and chlorhexidine for cutaneous antisepsis.
Methods: PICCs inserted into the antecubital vein in two randomized trials during from 1998 to 2000 were prospectively studied; most patients were in an ICU. PICC-related BSI was confirmed in each case by demonstrating concordance between isolates colonizing the PICC at the time of removal and from blood cultures by restriction-fragment DNA subtyping.
Results: Overall, 115 patients had 251 PICCs placed. Mean duration of catheterization was 11.3 days (total, 2,832 PICC-days); 42% of the patients were in an ICU at some time, 62% had urinary catheters, and 49% had received mechanical ventilation. Six PICC-related BSIs were identified (2.4%), four with coagulase-negative staphylococcus, one with Staphylococcus aureus, and one with Klebsiella pneumoniae, a rate of 2.1 per 1,000 catheter-days.
Conclusion: This prospective study shows that PICCs used in high-risk hospitalized patients are associated with a rate of catheter-related BSI similar to conventional CVCs placed in the internal jugular or subclavian veins (2 to 5 per 1,000 catheter-days), much higher than with PICCs used exclusively in the outpatient setting (approximately 0.4 per 1,000 catheter-days), and higher than with cuffed and tunneled Hickman-like CVCs (approximately 1 per 1,000 catheter-days). A randomized trial of PICCs and conventional CVCs in hospitalized patients requiring central access is needed. Our data raise the question of whether the growing trend in many hospital hematology and oncology services to switch from use of cuffed and tunneled CVCs to PICCs is justified, particularly since PICCs are more vulnerable to thrombosis and dislodgment, and are less useful for drawing blood specimens. Moreover, PICCs are not advisable in patients with renal failure and impending need for dialysis, in whom preservation of upper-extremity veins is needed for fistula or graft implantation.
instruction: How do the rates of PICC-related bloodstream infections in hospitalized patients compare to those in outpatient settings, and what factors might contribute to these differences?
response: The rates of PICC-related bloodstream infections (BSIs) in hospitalized patients are considerably higher than those in outpatient settings. According to the study, the rate of PICC-related BSIs in hospitalized patients, particularly in intensive care units (ICUs), was 2.1 per 1,000 catheter-days. In contrast, the rate in outpatient settings is much lower, at approximately 0.4 per 1,000 catheter-days. Several factors contribute to this disparity. Hospitalized patients, especially those in ICUs, often have multiple risk factors for infection, such as the presence of other invasive devices like urinary catheters and the need for mechanical ventilation. The prolonged duration of catheterization in hospitalized patients (with a mean of 11.3 days in the study) also increases the likelihood of infection. Furthermore, the study highlights the need for further research to compare PICCs with conventional central venous catheters (CVCs) in hospitalized patients, as the infection rates with PICCs are similar to those with CVCs placed in the internal jugular or subclavian veins. The data also suggest that the trend of switching from cuffed and tunneled CVCs to PICCs in hematology and oncology services may not be justified, given the higher risk of complications like thrombosis and dislodgment associated with PICCs. Additionally, PICCs are not recommended for patients with renal failure who may need dialysis, as they can compromise the veins needed for dialysis access.

instruction: How do enlarged lymph nodes in the neck function as part of the body's immune response, and what are the steps involved in diagnosing and treating these nodes if they are found to be abnormal?
response: Enlarged lymph nodes in the neck serve as critical components of the immune system by filtering and responding to pathogens and other foreign substances. When they detect an infection or inflammation, they activate immune cells, leading to enlargement as a sign of increased activity. The steps for diagnosing and treating these nodes if they are abnormal include: 1) **Initial Assessment**: A healthcare provider will take a detailed medical history and perform a physical exam to assess the size, consistency, and tenderness of the lymph nodes. 2) **Observation and Monitoring**: If the nodes are not significantly enlarged or tender, the doctor may recommend regular monitoring to see if they resolve on their own. 3) **Imaging Tests**: If the nodes persist or grow, imaging studies like an MRI or CT scan can help identify any underlying issues. 4) **Laboratory Tests**: Blood tests can help rule out infections, inflammation, or other systemic conditions. 5) **Biopsy**: If there is a suspicion of a more serious condition such as cancer, a biopsy may be necessary to obtain a definitive diagnosis. 6) **Treatment**: Treatment depends on the underlying cause. Infections may be treated with antibiotics or antivirals, autoimmune conditions with immunosuppressive medications, and cancer with a combination of surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy. Regular follow-up is essential to monitor the response to treatment and ensure the nodes return to a normal size.

Eileen San Juan has been working as a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation in various clinical settings for over 20 years and owns Count On ME Therapy and Wellness Services, LLC. She has worked in the field of rare blood conditions for the past 15 years at the Comprehensive Hemophilia Treatment Center at the Mount Sinai Icahn School of Medicine in New York, New York, and previously at The Blood Research Institute of Saint Michael's Medical Center in Newark, New Jersey. Within this community, Eileen has also served as a committee chairperson for the Region II Physical Therapy Task Force and as a member in the National Hemophilia Foundation's Physical Therapy Working Group.
She has offered several health, wellness, and holistic lectures, articles, and interactive courses for hospitals, NYCHC, NBDF (formerly NHF), HANY, HFA, and HANJ.
Eileen holds a Master of Science degree in physical therapy from The University of Medicine and Dentistry of New Jersey, a Bachelor of Science degree in psychology from Kean University, and certifications in massage therapy and Reiki.
Eileen firmly believes that healthcare is a calling, and her mission is to serve and educate the community by making each person's treatment as unique and individualized as that person and utilize the comprehensive team approach to do so.
Eileen enjoys practicing yoga, finding places in NJ "off the beaten path" to walk or run, spending time with her family and dog, singing as a cantor in her place of worship and, of course, working in the rare blood community for the last 15 years, a place she has called home.
instruction: How can physical therapy and holistic practices, such as yoga and Reiki, be integrated to enhance the treatment of patients with rare blood conditions?
response: Physical therapy and holistic practices such as yoga and Reiki can be integrated to enhance the treatment of patients with rare blood conditions in several ways. Eileen San Juan, a physical therapist with extensive experience in the field of rare blood conditions, emphasizes the importance of a comprehensive and individualized approach to patient care. Physical therapy can help manage pain, improve mobility, and enhance overall physical function. Yoga, with its focus on gentle stretching, deep breathing, and relaxation, can complement physical therapy by reducing stress, improving flexibility, and promoting mental well-being. Reiki, a form of energy healing, can further support the holistic approach by reducing anxiety, promoting relaxation, and enhancing the body’s natural healing processes. By combining these modalities, healthcare providers can address the physical, emotional, and psychological aspects of living with rare blood conditions, leading to a more comprehensive and effective treatment plan.

instruction: In the context of medical procedures, how do tourniquets assist healthcare providers, and what are their specific roles in ensuring the success of venepuncture?
response: In medical settings, tourniquets are vital tools that assist healthcare providers in performing venepuncture effectively. By applying a tourniquet to the upper arm, the flow of blood is temporarily restricted, which causes the veins to engorge and become more visible. instruction: What are the potential long-term health benefits and challenges associated with the use of newer blood-thinners compared to traditional medications like warfarin, and how might these findings impact patient care and hospital resource management?
response: The transition from traditional blood-thinners like warfarin to newer blood-thinners, such as direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), has several long-term health benefits and challenges that can influence patient care and hospital resource management. One of the key benefits is the reduced hospitalization duration for patients experiencing complications. Studies have shown that patients on newer blood-thinners spend about two fewer days in the hospital compared to those on warfarin, without any difference in survival rates. This reduction in hospital stays can have a profound impact on hospital resource management, as it can free up beds, reduce the burden on healthcare staff, and lower overall healthcare costs. Additionally, newer blood-thinners have a more straightforward dosing regimen and fewer dietary and drug interactions, which can improve patient compliance and reduce the risk of adverse events. However, these medications also come with challenges. They are generally more expensive than warfarin, which can be a barrier to access for some patients, particularly in low-income settings. Moreover, while they have fewer interactions, they still require careful monitoring, especially in patients with renal impairment or other comorbidities. The potential for increased costs and the need for ongoing patient education and monitoring must be balanced against the benefits of improved outcomes and resource efficiency. Overall, the adoption of newer blood-thinners can enhance patient care and optimize hospital resource management, but it requires a comprehensive approach that addresses cost and accessibility issues.

instruction: What are the key advancements in immunotherapy for multiple myeloma, and how do they differ from traditional treatments like chemotherapy?
response: Key advancements in immunotherapy for multiple myeloma include the development of novel agents such as bispecific antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, and new immunomodulator drugs. These treatments leverage the immune system to target cancer cells more precisely and effectively. For example, bispecific antibodies can simultaneously bind to both a tumor-specific antigen and a T-cell receptor, activating T-cells to attack cancer cells. Antibody-drug conjugates combine the targeting precision of antibodies with the cytotoxic power of chemotherapy drugs, delivering a lethal payload directly to cancer cells. Immunomodulator drugs, such as lenalidomide and pomalidomide, enhance the immune system's ability to recognize and destroy myeloma cells. These approaches differ from traditional chemotherapy, which typically targets rapidly dividing cells, including both cancerous and healthy cells, leading to significant side effects. Immunotherapies are designed to be more targeted, reducing collateral damage to healthy tissues and improving patient outcomes.

instruction: What are the primary medical conditions for which Veenat 100 Capsule is prescribed, and how does it help in treating these conditions?

Ecchymosis: A term used to describe discoloration that results in a dark bluish-red patch more than one centimeter in diameter. Although many sources refer to any bruising of the skin, such as caused by contusion, as ecchymosis, this is probably a misuse of the term. It should perhaps be distinguished from discoloration resulting from a direct trauma/contusion, although all sources do not agree.
Ecchymosis is an accumulation of blood in the skin and subcutaneous tissues that is caused by blood moving from one extravascular space to another. This movement is caused by a medical or hematological condition, or indirectly caused by trauma.
Such movement of blood is called extravasion. An example is the appearance of black eyes caused by a blow to the mid-forehead right above the nose.
Although the trauma does not occur directly to the eye or orbital area, the trauma to the forehead allows blood to seep down to the peri-orbital areas. On the other hand, when a person is punched directly in the eye, not only is there discoloration which should be called bruising, there is also swelling and pain in the eye.
This discoloration resulting from blood donation, we would
normally called bruising. But it is more technically ecchymosis.
The appearance of skin bruising near the area of a muscular strain can also be called ecchymosis. This type of discoloration can appear to be quite widespread and irregular due to the blood drifting inferiorly due to gravity. The size of the discolored area, therefore, does not necessarily denote the extent of the damage. Notice, in the image below, that although the muscle strain occurred in the hamstring of the posterior thigh, there is also ecchymosis in the calf area of the lower leg. This may be due to the blood having seeped downwards rather than indicating a strain in that area.
Ecchymosis from a pulled hamstring.

This type of hemorrhagic blotching of the skin is more prevalent in elderly skin and clotting and bleeding disorders can also cause ecchymosis.
Similar to bruising, ecchymosis starts out as a bluish looking lesion but the colors change as the red blood cells progressively degenerate. Usually the blue changes to a green, to a purple, and finally to a brownish-yellow color before fading away. The lesions are usually not painful and are not hard or firm to the touch (nonindurated).

instruction: What are the key differences between ecchymosis and bruising, and how do these differences impact the clinical assessment of skin discoloration?
response: The key differences between ecchymosis and bruising lie in their causes, appearance, and clinical implications. Ecchymosis is a dark bluish-red discoloration larger than one centimeter, resulting from blood extravasation due to a medical condition or indirect trauma. For instance, ecchymosis in the peri-orbital area, known as 'raccoon eyes,' can indicate a skull fracture after head trauma. Bruising, on the other hand, is a result of direct trauma, such as a contusion, and typically presents with localized discoloration, swelling, and pain. While both conditions can change colors as the red blood cells break down, the size and distribution of the discoloration are crucial for clinical assessment. Ecchymosis can be more widespread and may not always correlate with the extent of the injury, whereas bruising is more localized and directly related to the site of impact. Understanding these differences helps in diagnosing underlying conditions and assessing the severity of injuries.

instruction: How does moderate alcohol consumption affect blood clotting, and what are the potential risks and benefits associated with this effect?
response: Moderate alcohol consumption has a blood-thinning effect, which can reduce the risk of ischemic strokes by preventing blood cells from clumping and forming clots. However, this effect is a double-edged sword, as it can also increase the risk of hemorrhagic strokes, where bleeding in the brain occurs. The blood-thinning effect of moderate alcohol use is significant enough that doctors often advise patients taking blood-thinning medications like Eliquis® and Plavix to moderate their alcohol intake. This is because alcohol can interfere with the metabolism of these drugs, potentially leading to an increased risk of bleeding. Heavy alcohol consumption, on the other hand, has the opposite effect, increasing the likelihood of blood clots and associated risks such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism. Therefore, while moderate alcohol consumption may offer some cardiovascular benefits, it is essential to consider individual health conditions and medication use when assessing the overall risks and benefits.

instruction: What are some environmental and lifestyle factors that can increase the risk of developing leukemia, and how significant are these risks compared to other known risk factors?
response: Several environmental and lifestyle factors can contribute to an increased risk of developing leukemia. High levels of radiation exposure, such as those experienced by individuals in close proximity to nuclear accidents or atomic bomb survivors, have been linked to a higher risk of leukemia. However, for the general public, including those in the nuclear industry, radiologists, and residents near nuclear facilities like Sellafield, the levels of radiation exposure are typically too low to demonstrate a significant increase in risk. Lifestyle factors such as smoking and exposure to benzene, an industrial chemical, also play a role. Smoking is associated with an increased risk of myeloid leukemia, and benzene exposure has been linked to a higher risk of these leukemias. Furthermore, the use of chemotherapy and radiotherapy to treat other cancers can slightly increase the risk of acute myeloid leukemia, although this risk is considered low and does not outweigh the benefits of these treatments. While these factors are significant, they are generally less impactful compared to other known risk factors like genetic predispositions and certain inherited syndromes.

Ravens WRs coach helping others tackle sickle cell disease
September is National Sickle Cell Awareness Month
Turron Davenport | 9/11/2015, 6 a.m.
The Bobby Engram Foundation strives to provide hope, courage and opportunity to underprivileged children who suffer from chronic pain that affects their lives physically or emotionally.
Imagine being a father and seeing your daughters suffer through unbearable pain. Even worse, imagine not being able to make the pain go away.
This is what Baltimore Ravens Wide Receivers coach Bobby Engram encountered with his oldest daughter Bobbi and then with his other daughter Phoebe.
Engram has the trait for the hereditary blood disorder known as sickle cell. His wife Deanna also has that trait. This meant there was a one-in-four chance that one of their children would be born with the disease. Fortunately, his two sons Dean and Trey have not been struck with the disease.
Sickle cell disease affects the body’s red blood cells, turning the cells into the shape of a crescent moon. The abnormal shape causes the blood to clump, which in turn causes severe pain. The severe pain is referred to as “pain crises” and causes a variety of problems that can complicate a child’s life such as hip pain, joint pain and much more.
“You’re confused and frustrated. You’re angry. You go through this range of emotions and then you accept it,” Engram said. “You learn and you educate yourself. It’s a tough and horrible disease to grow up with. It can be an emotional drain on everyone. This is a real thing that needs to be dealt with. There’s a lot that people don’t know about sickle cell disease, like that it affects almost all races. It affects millions. It is the most common genetic blood disease in the country.”
The United Nations classifies sickle cell anemia as “one of the most gangrenous common genetic diseases” in the world. It can lead to death. September was first recognized as National Sickle Cell Awareness Month in 1983 by the federal government to increase awareness of this painful disease and recognize it as a public health problem.
Those who suffer from sickle cell disease have to live with chronic pain throughout their lives. Sometimes the pain is so severe that it requires being admitted to the hospital and being treated with narcotics.
The disease causes deformed red blood cells to block the blood flow in a blood vessel. As a result, oxygen and nutrients don’t reach the area that’s covered by the blood vessels. Tissue in the affected area becomes very inflamed and at times it dies. The painful condition is described, “as though small heart attacks are occurring throughout the body.”
The Bobby Engram Foundation was started as a result of his daughter Bobbi’s desire to help other children who experienced her type of pain.
Engram enjoyed a long, productive career in the NFL, which allowed him to be able to provide the best care for his daughters. Unfortunately, they still had to endure the pain and suffering that sickle cell disease presents. The NFL was and still is a platform for Engram to raise awareness, search for a cure and help other families cope with the strains that the disease puts on them.
instruction: What are the broader implications of sickle cell disease being the most common genetic blood disease in the country, and how can increased public awareness and education help in managing and potentially curing the disease?
response: The prevalence of sickle cell disease as the most common genetic blood disease in the country has far-reaching implications for public health, healthcare systems, and affected communities. This hereditary condition, characterized by crescent-shaped red blood cells, leads to chronic pain, frequent hospitalizations, and a range of complications that can severely impact quality of life. The disease disproportionately affects minority and underprivileged populations, highlighting the need for targeted interventions to address health disparities. Increased public awareness and education about sickle cell disease are essential for several reasons. Firstly, they can help in early diagnosis and better management of the disease, as informed individuals are more likely to seek appropriate medical care and adhere to treatment plans. Secondly, awareness can reduce the stigma and misconceptions surrounding the disease, fostering a more inclusive and supportive environment for those affected. Furthermore, public education can drive more funding and resources towards research, which is critical for developing new treatments and potentially finding a cure. The efforts of individuals like Bobby Engram, who uses his platform to raise awareness and support through the Bobby Engram Foundation, are instrumental in these endeavors. By providing hope, courage, and opportunity to children with sickle cell disease, such initiatives not only improve individual outcomes but also contribute to a broader societal understanding and support for this critical health issue.

Dr. Elizabeth Bigger has been named the new oncologist and hematologist at St. Peter’s Health, medical center officials said Monday, adding that she will begin seeing patients in late February.
Bigger will join radiation oncologist Dr. Andrew Cupino and the Cancer Care staff, officials said.
"This is a huge step forward in rebuilding our cancer care program and delivering on our promise to be the gold standard for cancer and hematology care in Helena," St. Peter's Health Medical Group President Dr. Todd Wampler said in a news release.
He said Bigger has elite training and an impressive background, and her practices "align strongly with evidence-based medicine and the team-centered culture" they are cultivating at St. Peter’s.
Bigger has more than 15 years of experience providing oncology and hematology care and is relocating to Helena from Massachusetts, where she is practicing at Mass General Cancer Center.
People are also reading…
Bigger replaces Dr. Thomas Weiner, who was fired from the hospital more than a year ago and is now embroiled in a wrongful termination lawsuit with the health center over his dismissal. In his lawsuit, Weiner, who had been with St. Peter's nearly 25 years, states he had seen as many as 1,500 patients a month. The hospital said Weiner had incorrectly treated a patient for lung cancer for 11 years and said it had learned of “alarming narcotic prescribing practices” by Weiner.
The lawsuit is scheduled to be heard in a Helena courtroom on Nov. 14, 2022.
St. Peter’s has hired temporary oncologists, known as “locum tenens,” to work at the hospital’s Cancer Treatment Center, which is undergoing a renovation project. St. Peter's officials said in April the hospital will affiliate with Huntsman Cancer Institute at the University of Utah, saying this will give patients undergoing cancer and hematology care access to more options for treatment and provide top cancer experts.
Wampler said earlier this month in a community forum that St. Peter’s officials were still looking for a permanent oncologist in Helena. He said they had made inroads and expected to make an announcement soon.
"We have some candidates who are interested, but they are not right for our community," he said at the time.
Bigger received her undergraduate degree from Yale University and her medical degree from Duke University School of Medicine. She completed her residency at Vanderbilt University and her fellowship at Duke University Medical Center, and she began her clinical career as an instructor in global health oncology at Harvard Medical School. Along with being board-certified in oncology medicine and hematology, Bigger is also board-certified in internal medicine, St. Peter's officials said.
“We are incredibly fortunate to welcome Dr. Bigger to St. Peter’s Health. It has been a long wait to find the right medical oncologist for our community and we thank everyone for their patience,” St. Peter's Health Chief Executive Officer Wade Johnson said in a news release.
“Combining the incredible talent, training and experience of Dr. Bigger and Dr. Cupino, along with an amazing cancer care team and our affiliation with the Huntsman Cancer Institute is a huge step forward in our goal to provide world-class cancer care in Helena,” he said. “The future has never been brighter.”
St. Peter's staff and providers have been working with Huntsman Cancer Institute to streamline care practices and align with the academic medical center standard of care.
Huntsman clinicians have worked with St. Peter’s employees at the Regional Medical Center, and several St. Peter’s workers have gone to Salt Lake City to train at the academic medical center, St. Peter's officials said.

Her arrival, coupled with the affiliation with Huntsman Cancer Institute, represents a significant step forward in rebuilding and enhancing St. Peter’s cancer care program.

The provider can offer personalized advice, consider the patient's medical history, and monitor the patient's response to the medication. instruction: What are the potential benefits and risks of using cannabis oil as a complementary therapy for lymphoma patients, and how does it compare to conventional treatments?
response: The use of cannabis oil as a complementary therapy for lymphoma patients has both potential benefits and risks. Benefits may include relief from symptoms such as nausea, pain, anxiety, and depression, which are common in cancer patients. Some patients have reported that cannabis oil has helped reduce tumor size and improved their overall quality of life. However, these benefits are largely based on anecdotal evidence and individual experiences, and more rigorous scientific research is needed to confirm these claims. Risks associated with cannabis oil include the lack of standardization in dosing and purity, potential side effects like drowsiness and cognitive impairment, and the possibility of interactions with other medications. Compared to conventional treatments like chemotherapy, which have a well-established track record and are supported by extensive clinical trials, cannabis oil is a less studied and regulated option. While it can be used to complement conventional treatments, it should not be relied upon as a sole treatment without professional medical guidance.

We are already aware of how remarkable our body’s immune system is in attacking invading bacteria and viruses and restoring us to health following an ailment. Even so, the newest cancer treatment discoveries from a study by Cardiff University are positioned to bring an innovative and surprising advancement: halting cancer in its tracks.
Researchers uncovered a particular kind of immune cell, a T-cell, found in our blood, which can scan and wipe out threats – including a wide range of cancer cells: ovarian, cervical, blood, kidney, prostate, lung, colon, and numerous others. And astoundingly, all normal tissue is left untouched.
The discovered T-cell works with a particular molecule on the surface of each cell in our body, known as the MR1 molecule. The theory is that the MR1 is alerting the T-cell to any cancer cell distortions. Garry Dolton, who was part of the research team, explains, “We are the first to describe a T-cell that finds MR1 in cancer cells – that hasn’t been done before; this is the first of its kind.”
While there is currently a comparable kind of therapy, called CAR-T, which has shown significant results in bringing patients from a terminal status to complete remission, it’s only been shown to be effective in some types of cancer, and not “solid cancers” (those that form tumors). This new discovery has revealed thus far to impact all types of cancer. Here’s how it is works:
- Blood is obtained from a patient diagnosed with cancer.
- The blood is filtered to remove T-cells.
- A particular type of benign virus is injected into the T-cells, allowing them to pick up on cancer cells.
- These cells are then duplicated in a lab, and injected back into the individual.
Research has been remarkably effective in animal trials, and with additional safety checks, the next step will be human trials. According to Daniel Davis, professor of immunology at the University of Manchester, “There is no question that it’s a very exciting discovery, both for advancing our basic knowledge about the immune system and for the possibility of future new medicines.”

instruction: How does the newly discovered T-cell therapy differ from existing CAR-T therapy in terms of its effectiveness against various types of cancer?
response: The newly discovered T-cell therapy offers a more comprehensive approach to cancer treatment compared to existing CAR-T therapy. CAR-T therapy involves modifying a patient's T-cells to recognize and attack cancer cells with specific surface proteins, which has been highly effective for certain blood cancers. However, it has not been successful in treating solid tumors. In contrast, the new T-cell therapy identified by Cardiff University researchers targets the MR1 molecule, which is present on all cells and can detect cancerous distortions. This T-cell therapy has shown potential in attacking a wide variety of cancer types, including solid tumors, making it a more versatile and promising treatment option. The therapy involves extracting a patient's T-cells, modifying them with a benign virus to recognize cancer cells, and then reinfusing them back into the patient. Initial animal trials have been promising, and the next steps will involve human trials to further validate its safety and efficacy.

instruction: How might colony-stimulating factors like sargramostim benefit patients undergoing chemotherapy, and what are the potential mechanisms behind this benefit?
response: Sargramostim, a colony-stimulating factor, can provide significant benefits to patients undergoing chemotherapy by supporting the immune system and enhancing hematopoietic recovery. Chemotherapy often leads to myelosuppression, which is the suppression of bone marrow activity, resulting in low levels of white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. This can increase the risk of infections, anemia, and bleeding. Sargramostim helps mitigate these effects by stimulating the production of immune cells in the bone marrow. Specifically, it binds to GM-CSF receptors on hematopoietic progenitor cells, triggering signaling pathways that promote the proliferation and differentiation of these cells into mature neutrophils, monocytes, and other immune cells. By increasing the number of these cells, sargramostim can help patients recover more quickly from chemotherapy-induced neutropenia and reduce the risk of infections. Furthermore, sargramostim can be used as a priming agent before chemotherapy, reducing the percentage of progenitor cells that are in the cell cycle at the time of chemotherapy administration. This can protect these cells from the cytotoxic effects of chemotherapy, further enhancing their recovery and function.

instruction: What are the potential physiological effects of small doses of a substance that can lead to prolonged diminished coagulability of the blood, and what are the possible consequences of this action?
response: The potential physiological effects of small doses of a substance that can lead to prolonged diminished coagulability of the blood are multifaceted. Initially, there might be a transient increase in coagulability, but this is quickly followed by a significant and prolonged phase of reduced coagulability. This reduction in blood coagulation can have serious consequences, including prolonged bleeding times, increased risk of hemorrhage, and difficulty in achieving hemostasis even from minor wounds. In severe cases, this can lead to life-threatening bleeding, such as internal hemorrhages or spontaneous bleeding. The diminished coagulability can also complicate surgical procedures and increase the risk of post-operative complications. Chronic exposure to such a substance can result in ongoing issues with bleeding, leading to anemia, fatigue, and other systemic effects if not properly managed.

instruction: What are the key factors to consider when evaluating the effectiveness of factor VIII replacement therapy in patients with conditions like hemophilia, and how does the management of these factors impact overall treatment outcomes?
response: When evaluating the effectiveness of factor VIII replacement therapy in patients with hemophilia, several key factors must be considered. The primary factor is the patient's factor VIII levels, which should be monitored closely to ensure they are within a therapeutic range. This is crucial because insufficient levels can lead to inadequate clotting, while excessively high levels can increase the risk of thrombosis. The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) test is commonly used to assess these levels. Additionally, the presence of inhibitors, which are antibodies that can neutralize the therapeutic effect of factor VIII, must be evaluated. The development of inhibitors can significantly impact treatment outcomes, often necessitating alternative treatment strategies such as bypassing agents. Other factors include the frequency and dose of factor VIII administration, patient adherence to the treatment regimen, and the occurrence of side effects. Proper management of these factors is essential for optimizing treatment outcomes, reducing bleeding episodes, and improving the patient's quality of life.

If you’re diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), your first thought may be that you’ll have to have chemotherapy. This treatment is very effective for CLL since chemotherapy works quickly to attack cancer cells. But it also kills some healthy cells. That can lead to harsh side effects like hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, nausea, and vomiting, and, perhaps most importantly, low blood cell counts, which raise the risk of infection.
Treatment for CLL goes far beyond chemotherapy. Newer medicines, like targeted therapy and monoclonal antibodies, have revolutionized treatment. These drugs zero in on CLL cells rather than wipe out many cells both bad and good. Since they don’t attack healthy cells, they appear to have fewer unpleasant side effects. As a result, these non-chemo drugs are often the ones doctors try first for CLL.
Here’s a look at treatments for CLL beyond chemotherapy.
If you have early-stage CLL, without symptoms, you may be surprised to learn that many doctors now recommend that you not start treatment right away. Instead, they’ll monitor you closely. You’ll see your doctor for a physical exam about every 3 months and get regular blood tests.
After about a year, your doctor will have a better sense of how aggressive your CLL is and whether or not you need to start treatment. Research shows that people who take this approach do just as well as patients who get chemotherapy right away.
This is often the first-line treatment -- that is, the first approach your doctor will try -- for advanced or symptomatic CLL. People who relapse might get targeted therapy, too. These medicines attack specific traits on cancer cells or processes that help the cells grow, multiply, or survive. You take them as pills once or twice a day.
Targeted drugs for CLL include:
- Acalabrutinib(Calquence),ibrutinib (Imbruvica), and zanubrutinib (Brukinsa). These drugs, known as tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), block a substance called tyrosine kinase that causes your stem cells to make too many white blood cells.
- Venetoclax (Venclexta). This is a drug called a BCL2 inhibitor. It blocks a protein called BCL2 found on cancer cells. This kills them off and makes them more likely to respond to other cancer treatments.
- Duvelisib (Copiktra) and idelalisib (Zydelig). These two drugs block proteins that help cancer grow, such as P13K-delta. Doctors turn to these drugs after they have tried other CLL treatments.
These drugs may cause mild side effects such as:
- Shortness of breath
- Swelling of your feet and hands
- Body aches
- Muscle and joint pain
- Anemia and certain infections, due to low blood cell counts
It’s rare, but targeted therapy for CLL can cause more serious side effects such as bleeding, severe infections, irregular heartbeat, liver damage, and lung inflammation. Idelalisib may reactivate old infections such as hepatitis.
Venetoclax can lead to tumor lysis syndrome (TLS). That’s when dead CLL cells break open and dump their contents into your bloodstream. This can cause toxins to build up in your blood, which causes problems with your kidneys, heart, and nervous system. To avoid this, your doctor may start you at a low dose and gradually increase it over a period of weeks.
These treatments attack a type of white blood cell called B lymphocytes that are abnormal in people with CLL and help cancer cells grow. As a result, cancer cells eventually die off. You get this medicine through an IV at a doctor’s office or infusion center. You might get this treatment alone or along with chemotherapy. Several kinds of monoclonal antibodies are available to treat CLL. Different ones target different cancer-promoting proteins.
Obinutuzumab (Gazyva), ofatumumab (Arzerra), andrituximab (Rituxan). These three drugs target a protein on the surface of B lymphocytes called CD20. During your infusion, you may notice mild side effects like itching, chills, fever, nausea, rashes, fatigue, and headache.
Your doctor will also give you drugs to help prevent more serious side effects like:
- Chest pain
- Heart racing
- Facial and tongue swelling
- Trouble breathing
- Dizziness and fainting
Like targeted therapy, these drugs can also reactivate past hepatitis B infections and raise the risk for other serious infections, such as a rare brain disease known as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML).
Alemtuzumab (Campath). This targets CD52, a protein found on the surface of CLL cells. You might get this drug if you haven’t responded to past treatments or if you have a specific form of CLL that includes what’s called a “chromosome-17 deletion.” This medication has side effects like those of other monoclonal antibodies, as well as low red blood cell and platelet counts. Very rarely, it’s been linked to strokes.
Radiation for CLL Symptoms
It’s not the main treatment for CLL, but you might get radiation to help treat some of the cancer’s symptoms. Radiation can:
- Shrink swollen organs, such as your spleen, that press on other organs and cause pain
- Ease pain from bone damage due to leukemia cells that grow in the bone marrow
Radiation may cause side effects such as:
- Skin redness
- Low blood cell counts
- GI upset, such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea
Surgery in Some CLL Cases
It’s rare for doctors to recommend surgery for CLL. The disease spreads through your bone marrow, so surgery can’t cure it. But sometimes, CLL enlarges your spleen so much that it presses on your other organs. An enlarged spleen also lowers your red blood cell and platelet counts. Your doctor may first recommend that you get radiation to shrink your spleen. If that doesn’t work, you may need to have it removed. This works, but it can make you more likely to get infections.
The Best CLL Treatment for You
There’s no single best treatment for CLL. These treatments haven’t been compared to one another in studies, so there’s no way to know if one is better than the others. Your doctor will decide what to give you based on your:
- Test results
- Overall health
- Other medical problems
- Cancer stage
- Individual genetics
- Concerns about side effects
While some people with CLL go into complete remission -- which means they have normal blood counts and no symptoms of cancer -- most eventually relapse. In that case, you may get several treatments over the course of your life with CLL.

instruction: In what situations might a doctor recommend monitoring rather than immediate treatment for early-stage chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), and what are the benefits of this approach?
response: For early-stage chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) patients who are asymptomatic, doctors frequently recommend monitoring rather than immediate treatment. This approach, known as 'watch and wait' or 'active surveillance,' involves regular physical exams and blood tests every 3 months to closely monitor the disease's progression. The rationale behind this approach is multifaceted. First, it allows doctors to better understand the aggressiveness of the CLL, as some cases may remain stable for years. Second, immediate treatment, especially with chemotherapy, can cause significant side effects, including hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, nausea, and low blood cell counts, which can increase the risk of infections. By delaying treatment, patients can avoid these side effects and maintain a better quality of life. Research has shown that patients who adopt a 'watch and wait' approach have outcomes similar to those who start treatment immediately. This strategy also preserves the patient's overall health, ensuring that they are in the best possible condition if and when treatment becomes necessary.

Test helps identify patients at low risk for recurring blood clots
A test that measures the generation of a certain protein involved with blood clotting can help determine whether patients who have experienced a venous blood clot are at low risk of developing another blood clot, and thus avoiding anticoagulant treatment and its possible side effects, according to a study in the July 26 issue of JAMA.
Anticoagulant treatment for patients with venous thromboembolism (VTE - formation of blood clots, often involving the deep veins of the legs or in the lung) consists of heparin followed by vitamin K antagonists for at least 3 to 6 months. After discontinuation of anticoagulant treatment, a third of patients experience recurrence of VTE within the next 5 to 8 years, according to background information in the article. The case-fatality rate of recurrence is around 5 percent. Therefore, identification of patients who might benefit from indefinite anticoagulant treatment (i.e., patients in whom recurrent VTE is more likely than anticoagulation-associated severe bleeding) is now one of the foremost goals in thrombosis research. Because of the large number of risk factors, assessing the risk of recurrence in an individual patient is complex. A laboratory test that would detect multifactorial thrombophilia (increased tendency for blood clots) could help determine the overall risk of recurrent VTE.
Gregor Hron, M.D., of the Medical University of Vienna, Austria and colleagues conducted a study to determine whether by measuring thrombin generation (a protein in blood that causes clotting), patients with VTE could be stratified into high- and low-risk categories for recurrence of VTE. The study, conducted between July 1992 and July 2005, included 914 patients with first spontaneous VTE who were followed-up for an average of 47 months after discontinuation of vitamin K antagonist therapy. Thrombin generation was measured by a commercially available test.
Venous thromboembolism recurred in 100 patients (11 percent). The researchers found that patients without recurrent VTE had lower thrombin generation than patients with recurrence.
"In this large prospective cohort study, we found that patients with a first spontaneous VTE and peak thrombin generation of less than 400 nM [the measurement nanomolar] after discontinuation of vitamin K antagonists have a low risk of recurrence. According to Kaplan-Meier analysis, the likelihood of recurrent VTE in these patients was as low as 7 percent after 4 years. … Compared with patients who had higher levels, those with peak thrombin generation less than 400 nM had an almost 60 percent lower risk of recurrence. Most importantly, the group of patients with low peak thrombin generation represented two-thirds of the total patient population," the authors write.
"… we believe that our findings are of major clinical relevance. Using a simple commercially available laboratory method developed to measure thrombin generation, we were able to identify patients in whom the long-term risk of recurrent VTE is almost negligible. Considering the incidence rates of severe or fatal hemorrhage related to anticoagulant therapy and the case-fatality rate of recurrent VTE, patients with low peak thrombin generation (less than 400 nM) would almost certainly not benefit from indefinite anticoagulant therapy. Consequently, extensive thrombophilia screening appears to be unnecessary in this large, low-risk patient group," the researchers conclude. (JAMA. 2006;296:397-402. Available pre-embargo to the media at www.jamamedia.org)
Editor's Note: Co-author Dr. Binder has reported that he is chief scientific officer for Technoclone GmbH, Vienna, Austria. Please see the article for additional information, including other authors, author contributions and affiliations, financial disclosures, funding and support, etc.
Last reviewed: By John M. Grohol, Psy.D. on 30 Apr 2016

instruction: How can measuring thrombin generation help in the management of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and what are the potential benefits for patients?
response: The measurement of thrombin generation is a valuable tool in managing venous thromboembolism (VTE) because it helps stratify patients into high- and low-risk categories for recurrence. The study by Hron et al. demonstrated that patients with a first spontaneous VTE and a peak thrombin generation of less than 400 nM have a low risk of recurrence, with only a 7 percent likelihood after 4 years. This finding is clinically significant as it allows clinicians to avoid indefinite anticoagulant therapy in a large proportion (two-thirds) of patients, thereby reducing the risk of anticoagulation-related complications such as severe bleeding. The test provides a simple, commercially available method to identify patients who are unlikely to benefit from extended anticoagulant treatment, thus optimizing patient care and resource allocation.

Overview of Pulmonary Embolisms: Data and Symptoms
So, exactly what is a pulmonary embolism and why is it so serious and even terminal in certain situations? It really is a good question. You may have seen the expression yet never completely grasped what a pulmonary embolism is actually. A pulmonary embolism comes about as soon as you have an out of the blue obstruction of one or even more of your principal blood vessels through the lung. This generally comes about as a result of a blood clot and could result in significant impairment to the lung cells because it prevents the circulation of blood to the lung.
Patients with a pulmonary embolism suffer an immediate problems breathing, coughing that contributes to foamy pink mucus and a rather sharp annoyance inside their chest muscles which gets more painful with a cough and even a deep breath. You might also look and feel on edge or really restless, have sensations of passing out or have a racing heartbeat. Any of those signs or symptoms are cause for alarm it's vital that you go to your physician immediately.
Treatment for Pulmonary Embolism: Initial and Long-Term
Any time you receive the diagnosis of a pulmonary embolism, your personal doctor definitely will proceed without delay to ascertain the finest treatment course to offer you the best chances for a complete recovery. The aim of treatment is to reduce or end the clot that is definitely in the blood vessels belonging to the lungs. This can be achieved by either managing drugs or by some techniques. Long-term treatment works in concert with precautionary methods like medications and strategies to eliminate the possibility of future pulmonary embolisms.
Prescription drugs for starting and long-term treatment include things like anticoagulants. They are usually recognized as blood thinners and they get the job done to support your blood not clot as easily. Thrombolytics are also commonly used as they break up clots very rapidly. Clot eradication can be done utilizing a catheter method though your blood vessels and they can take away the clot by way of suction. Filters could also be placed in your veins to avoid clots from making their way to your heart and respiratory system. Long-term therapy options will be developed with the help of your health practitioner. Perhaps it will include drugs, treatments or lifestyle alterations which will make you much healthier to stop this from happening to you over again.
instruction: How do anticoagulants and thrombolytics differ in their approach to treating a pulmonary embolism, and what are the potential long-term preventive measures for avoiding future occurrences?
response: Anticoagulants and thrombolytics are both crucial in the treatment of pulmonary embolism (PE), but they serve different purposes and are used in different scenarios. Anticoagulants, such as heparin, warfarin, and DOACs like Xarelto, work by preventing the formation of new clots and stopping existing clots from growing. They are typically the first line of treatment and are used to manage the condition over the long term. Thrombolytics, on the other hand, are powerful clot-busting drugs that are used to rapidly dissolve large, life-threatening clots. They are generally reserved for severe cases where immediate action is necessary to prevent critical complications such as shock or severe hypoxemia. Examples of thrombolytics include tissue plasminogen activator (tPA). To prevent future occurrences of PE, long-term preventive measures are essential. These measures can include continued use of anticoagulants, lifestyle modifications like regular physical activity, maintaining a healthy weight, and avoiding prolonged periods of inactivity. In some cases, surgical interventions such as the placement of a vena cava filter may be recommended to prevent clots from reaching the lungs. Regular follow-up with a healthcare provider is also crucial to monitor the effectiveness of these preventive measures and make any necessary adjustments.

If the body is lacking in vitamin B12 this can have an effect on our body temperature and also on how well we feel.
Which vitamin deficiency makes you feel cold?
There are many reasons for feeling cold, and being vitamin deficient can be one of them. If the body is lacking in vitamin B12 this can have an effect on our body temperature and also on how well we feel.
Being deficient in vitamin B12 can affect the body's ability to produce enough red blood cells, which are responsible for carrying oxygen to tissues and organs, including those that regulate our body temperature and stop us feeling too hot or too cold.
If you do find yourself with a vitamin B12 deficiency this can manifest itself in different ways and you may find you have symptoms such as feeling shivery and cold, fatigue, weakness, as well as pale or yellowish skin.
Does feeling cold mean I’m ill?
Feeling cold does not necessarily mean that you are ill or getting sick, but it can sometimes be a symptom of illnesses so if you find yourself feeling shivery then it can be an early sign.
Having cold sensations over a long period of time can often come alongside other signs of illness such as fever, chills, fatigue or body aches. These may be an underlying viral illness or bacterial infection and often aren’t a cause for concern as it can be something as simple as the common cold or flu. However sometimes they can be an indication of more serious conditions like pneumonia, which can cause feelings of coldness as the body's immune system responds to the invading pathogens and attempts to fight the illness.
Feeling cold can also be linked to other health conditions, such as anemia, thyroid disorders, circulation problems or nutritional deficiencies, and these can often mean feeling cold.
If you find that you are frequently experiencing unexplained or persistent feelings of coldness, and you find it comes alongside others symptoms or is affecting your daily life then speak to your GP or a health professional. They can help identify any underlying health issues and discuss the best next steps.
Can a vitamin deficiency cause a cold and cough?
Being deficient in vitamins won’t cause a cough and a cold on its own, but it can mean your immune system is weakened which may make you more vulnerable to getting the cold or flu virus and make you feel ill.
Being deficient in vitamins such as vitamin B12 or Vitamin C deficiency can potentially contribute to you getting a cold and respiratory infections, including coughing.
Getting enough vitamins and having a well balanced diet is one of the best ways to ensure the body is ‘fighting fit’ and can fight off infections or illness. Getting enough vitamin C is essential for the production and function of white blood cells, and without it you might find that you’re more likely to develop cold symptoms like coughing as well as finding it harder to recover. If you’re struggling to get enough of this important vitamin from your diet, then you could consider a Vitamin C supplement to help boost your intake.
Don’t underestimate the benefits of an overall healthy lifestyle on staying well either. Reducing stress, getting enough sleep and having an active and healthy lifestyle can help to boost your immune health, your mood and make you feel stronger to fight illnesses.
What vitamins are best for stopping colds
To support your immune system and reduce the risk of catching colds, you should ensure you have a well balanced diet alongside a healthy lifestyle. A balanced diet that includes plenty of fruits, vegetables, lean proteins, whole grains, and healthy fats will also provide you with the necessary nutrients to support your immune system and overall health. Including vitamins and minerals in your diet can be key to boosting the body’s wellbeing including the immune system.

instruction: How does a deficiency in vitamin B12 affect the body's ability to regulate temperature and what are some common symptoms of this deficiency?
response: A deficiency in vitamin B12 can significantly affect the body's ability to regulate temperature. Vitamin B12 is crucial for the production of red blood cells, which carry oxygen to tissues and organs, including those responsible for maintaining body temperature. When there is a lack of vitamin B12, the body may produce fewer red blood cells, leading to poor oxygenation and impaired temperature regulation. Common symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency include feeling cold and shivery, fatigue, weakness, and pale or yellowish skin. These symptoms can arise because the body is not getting enough oxygen-rich blood to function optimally, which can make you feel colder and more fatigued.

instruction: How does phycocyanin enhance iron absorption in the human body, and what are the potential health implications of this improved absorption for individuals with iron deficiency?
response: Phycocyanin, a pigment derived from blue spirulina, plays a crucial role in enhancing iron absorption in the human body. Japanese researchers have discovered that phycocyanin can form soluble complexes with iron, similar to the way heme iron is absorbed. Heme iron, which is found in animal tissues, is the most efficiently absorbed form of iron, with about 60% of iron in these tissues being heme iron. In contrast, plant-based iron sources typically have a much lower absorption rate, ranging from 13% to 35%. By forming these soluble complexes, phycocyanin significantly increases the bioavailability of iron, making it more accessible to the body. For individuals with iron deficiency, this enhanced absorption can have significant health benefits. It can help alleviate symptoms of anemia, such as fatigue and weakness, and improve overall physical and cognitive function. Additionally, better iron levels can boost the immune system, helping the body to fight off infections more effectively and potentially slowing down the aging process of organs.

Haptoglobin test is performed to check for deficiency of red blood cells in the patient’s bloodstream.
What is Haptoglobin?
Haptoglobin is a blood test which helps in diagnosing and evaluating hemolytic anemia (destruction of red blood cells). Haptoglobin is a protein produced in the liver that is responsible for cleaning the hemoglobin.
Why is Haptoglobin Suggested?
Haptoglobin is generally suggested when the patient is showing the following symptoms
- Prolonged jaundice
How is Haptoglobin performed?
Haptoglobin test is a quite simple test.
- The arm of the patient is cleaned with a germ-killing solution.
- 5ml blood is drawn.
- Sample is then sent to lab for further testing.
- Patient will receive the test results after a period of time.
What are parameters measured in Haptoglobin
Haptoglobin test measures the levels of Haptoglobin in the bloodstream.
Preparation before Haptoglobin
Haptoglobin is a safe procedure. No special preparation required for the test. Patients have to schedule the test beforehand.
- Inform your doctor if you are on any medication or have any underlying medical condition.
- Try and tell the doctor all the symptoms.
Post-care after Haptoglobin
Haptoglobin test doesn’t require any post care.
- The patient is free to go home after they have given the sample for Haptoglobin.
- You may rest for some time.
Sample types in Haptoglobin
- Several blood samples at different time intervals.
Side-effects of Haptoglobin
Haptoglobin test is a safe procedure. Some common risks are
- For people who are scared of injections, this can be a painful process.
- Risk of infection (from where the skin is broken).
- Fainting or feeling lightheaded.
- Accumulation of blood under the skin.
instruction: What are the primary reasons a doctor might suggest a Haptoglobin test, and what symptoms might indicate the need for this test?
response: The primary reasons a doctor might suggest a Haptoglobin test are to assess for hemolytic anemia, a condition where red blood cells are broken down faster than they can be replaced. Haptoglobin, a protein produced by the liver, binds to free hemoglobin released from red blood cells and helps remove it from the bloodstream. Low levels of haptoglobin can indicate excessive red blood cell destruction. Symptoms that might prompt a doctor to order this test include prolonged jaundice, which can be a sign of liver issues or hemolytic anemia. Additionally, symptoms such as unexplained fatigue, pale skin, shortness of breath, and dark urine can also suggest the need for a Haptoglobin test to evaluate the patient's red blood cell status.

instruction: What are the potential health risks associated with drinking blood, and how does the body typically react to the presence of blood in the stomach?
response: The potential health risks associated with drinking blood are multifaceted. Firstly, the body's digestive system is not designed to handle blood, particularly the high concentration of red blood cells (RBCs). When blood is ingested, the body often interprets it as a sign of internal bleeding, leading to a defensive response such as vomiting. Moreover, blood can be a vector for various diseases and infections. For instance, if the blood contains pathogens like HIV or strep throat, the person consuming it is at risk of contracting these conditions. Even though some individuals might tolerate small amounts of blood without immediate adverse effects, the cumulative and long-term risks remain significant. It is important to avoid consuming blood to prevent these health issues.

instruction: How do long-term survivors of blood cancers manage the psychological and emotional impacts of their diagnosis and treatment, and what strategies have been most helpful for them?
response: Long-term survivors of blood cancers often manage the psychological and emotional impacts of their diagnosis and treatment through a combination of self-care, support networks, and professional help. Many survivors find that the traumatic experiences of diagnosis and treatment can remain vivid even years later, leading to feelings of loneliness, anxiety, and depression. One effective strategy is to engage in regular self-care activities, such as exercise, mindfulness, and hobbies, which can help reduce stress and improve overall well-being. Additionally, joining support groups, both online and in-person, can provide a sense of community and understanding. These groups allow survivors to share their experiences and coping mechanisms with others who have been through similar situations. For some, professional counseling or therapy can be beneficial, offering a safe space to process emotions and develop healthier coping strategies. It's important for survivors to remember that it's normal to experience these feelings and that seeking help is a sign of strength, not weakness.

Leukemias: General Considerations And Clinical Classifications
A Leukemia Patient
Leukemias are a group of neoplastic disorders affecting mainly the leukopoietic tissues in the body and characterized by the presence of leucocytosis, immature leucocytes in the peripheral blood and proliferation of these immature cells in the bone marrow resulting in the suppression of normal tissue. The abnormal cells infiltrate several organs in the body. The exact cause for neoplastic transformation of the normal cell line is not known. The disease process starts in the bone marrow or lymphatic tissue depending on the cell type and the peripheral blood is flooded with abnormal cells at some stage of the disorder. Rarely the erythroid precursors, plasma cells or megakaryocytes may be involved.
Leukemias may be broadly grouped into acute and chronic leukemias. Acute leukemias affect younger age groups more frequently. They run a rapid course and the peripheral blood and bone marrow show the presence of large number of blast cells. If left untreated, these are fatal within weeks or months. Chronic leukemias generally affect the older age groups, they run a more protracted course and terminate life within 2-3 years of onset. Leukemias account for 0.15- 0.6% of the total medical admissions in many general hospitals in developing countries.
It is to be noted that chronic lymphatic leukemia is rare in developing countries when compared to the developed ones.
Classification of Leukemia
- Non-lymphoblastic (ANLL)
- M1- Acute myeloblastic (undifferentiated)
- M2- Acute myeloblastic (partly differentiated)
- M3- Acute promyelocytic (well differentiated)
- M4- Acute myelomonocytic
- M5- Acute monocytic
- M6- Erythroblastic (erythroleukemia).
- Acute lymphoblastic (ALL)
- L1- Small uniform cell type: 75% null cell types (common ALL or C.ALL)
- L2- More heterogenous cells: 25% T cell types (T. ALL)
- L3- Burkitt’s type of cells: rare, mostly B cell type (B. ALL).
- Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)
- Chronic lymphatic leukemia (CLL)
- Hairy cell leukemia
- Prolymphocytic leukemia
- Plasma cell leukemia
- Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia
- Sezary syndrome (Leukemic phase of mycosis fungoides).
Ill defined groups
- Dysmyelopoietic syndromes
- Refractory anemia with excess blasts (RAEB)
These are both considered as preleukemic conditions.
Promising Stem Cell Therapy For Leukemia Patients
Details on Leukemia classifications
Leukemias have been classified by several authors based on different criteria. At present, the French American British (FAB) classification is one of the accepted systems for acute leukemia. Acute lymphatic leukemia is classified on the basis of cell size, nuclear chromatin pattern, nuclear shape, nucleoli, amount and basophilia of cytoplasm, and extent of cytoplasmic vacuolization. Acute myeloid leukemia is classified on the degree of maturation and differentiated of the abnormal cell.
In addition to the clear cut picture of leukemias, other less well-defined entities have been recognized, which when followed up, may develop into leukemia after varying intervals. The dysmyelopoietic syndromes are characterized by ineffective erythropoiesis manifested by morphological abnormalities in the marrow such as incordinated maturation of cytoplasm and the nucleus, nuclear division without cytoplasmic division, and syncytium formation. Another group is the refractory anemia with excess blasts (RAEB) in which the marrow is hypercellular with myeloblasts and promyelocytes forming 10-30% of the total nucleated cells. On follow up, the proportion of myeloid precursors increase and the condition may develop into florid acute myeloid leukemia.

instruction: How do the clinical manifestations and progression of acute and chronic leukemias differ, and what are the typical age groups affected by each type?
response: Acute and chronic leukemias exhibit distinct clinical manifestations and progression patterns. Acute leukemias, which are more common in younger individuals, are marked by a rapid and aggressive course. These conditions are characterized by the presence of a large number of immature blast cells in the peripheral blood and bone marrow, leading to symptoms such as fever, bleeding, and anemia. If untreated, acute leukemias can be fatal within a few weeks to months. In contrast, chronic leukemias, which predominantly affect older adults, have a more gradual and prolonged course. Chronic leukemias are characterized by a slower accumulation of mature but functionally abnormal cells in the bone marrow and blood, leading to symptoms that may develop over several years. These conditions can eventually be fatal within 2-3 years of onset. The typical age groups affected are children and young adults for acute leukemias and older adults for chronic leukemias.
